sections.title: Discussion
sections.text: The two-metal ion mechanism for nuclease activity is the most widely accepted ( 15 ). This mechanism is appealing as it is generally applicable for diverse nucleases including ribozyme catalyzed RNA splicing-even in the absence of chemical groups with pKa near neutrality as general base or acid for a phosphoryl transfer reaction. The position of the metal ions dictates its functional role- M A is located closer to the nucleophile while M B is near the 3′ O leaving group separated by ca 4Å. As expected, water molecules at the active site are crucial while carboxylates on polar groups coordinate the metal ions and exclude the water molecule from M B . Thus, both metal ions play significant but distinct roles. The identity of the metal cofactor in this context can also be rationalized in terms of the physico-chemical requirements. Mn, a transition element with less stringent coordination restraints, is associated with relaxed substrate specificity and rescue of defective enzymes ( 37 ). Mixed metal ions are particularly suited in this scenario ( 38 ). M A in this case drives the reaction by deprotonating the nucleophile (a water molecule). This hydrolytic reaction can also occur in the absence of a general base ( 39 ). M B stabilizes the penta-covalent transition state and destabilizes the ground state of a scissile phosphate for cleavage ( 37 ). In the absence of M A , for example in the ββα-Me nucleases, a His residue serves as a general base to deprotonate and activate a nucleophilic water ( 17 , 40 , 41 ). Others, like the HUH nuclease, employ Tyr as the nucleophile to cleave DNA substrates ( 42 ). ββα-Me nucleases are catalytically highly efficient enzymes. On the other hand, the catalytic efficiency of RNase J2 is significantly lower than RNase J1, effectively condemning it as an inactive enzyme ( 19 , 20 , 21 ). Retaining the structural metal co-factor M B in RNase J2 appears to have different implication(s). While M B in the two-metal ion catalytic mechanism facilitates the departure of the leaving group, that role in RNase J2 is performed by H80. M B , in RNase J2, stabilizes the overall structure. Indeed, removal of this metal cofactor alters domain orientation. That said, a single metal can contribute either directly or indirectly to catalysis. In the case of RNase J2, where M B plays a structural role, it is likely that substrate binding could potentially alter the active site enabling direct interactions of the substrate with the metal ion ( Figs. S10 and S11 ). It is worth noting in this context that recent studies on the nuclease EndoV and I-PpO-I suggested different roles for the single metal ion at the active site. EndoV utilizes a Mg ion for substrate stabilization through indirect interaction facilitated by a water molecule ( 43 ). In the case of I-PpO-I, the Mg ion directly coordinates with the substrate and helps in the departure of the leaving group ( 44 ). The finding that the role of the metal ion in RNase J2 is more towards overall structural integrity than the reaction mechanism per se thus suggests a different reaction mechanism than that proposed for other single metal ion containing nucleases. Weak metal cofactor binding, as in the case of the H78A mutant, was seen to enhance enzymatic activity suggesting that conformational flexibility could be a factor in dictating the activity levels of RNase J enzymes. Interestingly, RNase J2 H78A, despite having a bound Mn ion (albeit low occupancy), shows interdomain reorientation like that of apo RNase J2. This appears plausible as of all the active site residues, the H78-Mn pair has the lowest bond dissociation energy ( Table 1 ). Furthermore, the structures of active site mutants suggest that alternate rotamer preferences of all active site residues (except H78) are limited. This aspect could also be noted from the ensemble models fitted into the electron density map of diffraction data collected at room temperature. Overall, in these ensemble models, only the loop regions at the interface of the β-lactamase and β-CASP domains show significant variation and at the active site, H78 is the most dynamic. ( Fig. S6 ). It thus appears likely that mutation of this residue to Ala removes a steric deterrent leading to higher catalytic activity in the case of the RNase J2 H78A mutant. Even otherwise, we note multiple factors that could pre-dispose wild-type RNase J2 to be a sluggish enzyme when compared to RNase J1. First, the site of substrate entry in RNase J2 is negatively charged, limiting substrate recruitment ( Fig. S12 ). Second, the relative orientation of catalytic residues. For example, superposing the substrate-bound structure of RNase J (PDB - 4XWW) on RNase J2, the orientation of Lewis acid (H80), scissile phosphate, and Lewis base (E166) in RNase J2 is different ( Fig. S12 ). Finally, in RNase J2, HOMO, and LUMO are localized around several active site residues suggesting the possible involvement of multiple residues in catalysis. Indeed, the structural and biochemical data strongly support the hypothesis that RNase J2 is not really a one-metal cofactor nuclease in the sense that the metal ion does not have a direct role in nuclease activity. This is significantly different from the more catalytically active paralog, RNase J1 ( Fig. S7 ). From a functional perspective, it is interesting to note that RNase J2 plays a critical role in the CRISPR-Cas mechanism ( 45 , 46 ). RNase J1, on the other hand, is an important player in RNA turnover in S. aureus ( 21 ). Differences in the reaction mechanisms and catalytic activity levels thus appear to dictate the functional roles for the two S. aureus RNase J paralogs.

sections.title: Protein purification and crystallization
sections.text: Mutations were introduced into the rnjB gene using primers compiled in Table S2 . The plasmid (pETDuet1) containing the gene of interest was transformed into Escherichia coli BL21 star (DE3) expression strain. The E. coli cultures were grown at 37 °C and induced with 0.3 mM of Isopropyl-D-1-thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG) at an OD 600nm of 0.5 to 0.6. The cells were harvested by centrifugation at 4000 rpm, 4 °C. The pellet was resuspended in lysis buffer (25 mM Tris pH 8.0, 600 mM NaCl, 10% Glycerol, 2 mM β-mercaptoethanol, containing 2 mM Phenylmethylsulfonyl fluoride). The protein was subsequently stepwise eluted at varying concentrations of imidazole (maximum 500 mM imidazole). The eluted protein was subjected to another round of purification by passing through a Hi-prep 16/60 Sephacryl S-200 column (GE Healthcare). The protein was finally stored in 25 mM Tris-HCl pH-8.0, 250 mM NaCl, 10% Glycerol, and 2 mM β-mercaptoethanol. Crystallization of mutant RNase J2 enzymes was performed using the micro-batch method at 20 °C. Trial grids for crystallization were set up around the condition containing 100 mM trisodium citrate pH-5.6, 20% isopropanol, and 20% polyethylene glycol 4000. 40% formamide was used as an additive in the crystallization drop. The volumetric ratio of protein (8–10 mg/ml), precipitant, and additive was 2:2:0.4.

sections.title: Data collection and structure determination
sections.text: Diffraction data reported here were recorded both at the home source and at the XRD2 beamline of the Elettra Sincrotrone ( Table S4 ). The in-house X-ray source for recording diffraction data was a Rigaku FRE Cu K-alpha (1.54Å) X Ray generator equipped with a Rigaku-IV++ Axis detector ( Rigaku Holdings Co ). Diffraction images were indexed and integrated using iMosflm and scaled using SCALA ( 47 , 48 ). PHASER-MR (molecular replacement) was used to obtain phase information using Staphylococcus epidermidis RNase J2 wild type (PDB: 6K6W ) as a search model. The model was subsequently built using coot ( 49 ) and refined using REFMAC ( 42 ) and/or Phenix ( 31 ). In the case of data recorded at room temperature, crystals were mounted in glass capillaries (Hampton Inc) with sealed ends. The capillary containing a single crystal was subjected to X-ray diffraction at the home source. Ensemble refinement was performed using Phenix ( 31 ). Illustration of the structures were prepared using Pymol (The PyMOL Molecular Graphics System, Version 3.0 Schrödinger, LLC) and Chimera ( 50 ).

sections.title: Estimation of the protonation state of histidine from high-resolution crystal structures
sections.text: A detailed procedure for the estimation of protonation state from crystal structures is described in Banerjee et al. 2022 ( 28 ). Briefly, high-resolution structures were refined using REFMAC5, where restraints for histidine residues were removed. By default, REFMAC5 always considers both nitrogens of the histidine ring to be protonated; therefore, it was necessary to remove these restraints for the histidine residues. Four stereochemical parameters of the histidine imidazole ring were used to determine its protonation state as described ( 51 ). The stereochemical parameters are bond lengths Cε1- Nε2(X1Å), Nδ1-Cε1(X2Å) and the endocyclic angles -Nδ1- (X3 degrees) and -Nε2- (X4 degrees). Based on these parameters, the following functions were derived- his1 = −37.31X1 + 15.57X2–0.64X3 + 0.76X4 + 17.30 his2 = −2.16X1–6.08X2 + 0.56X3 + 0.42X4–94.46 A negative his1 value suggests that the Nδ1 group is protonated. In the case of a positive value of Nδ1, the his2 value is calculated. A negative his2 value suggests that only the Nε2 atom is protonated. Both N atoms are protonated when his1 and his2 values are positive ( 51 ).
path: Estimation of the protonation state of histidine from high-resolution crystal structures

sections.title: RT-FeDEx assay for RNase J2 and its mutants
sections.text: RT-FeDEx assays for RNase J2 and its mutants were performed as mentioned as described earlier ( 25 ). A 30 nt long RNA labeled at the 3′ end with a fluorophore group FAM (6-Carboxyfluorescein) (5′ ACUCACUCACUCAGGUUUUUUUAAUUAUCC 3′) was synthesized. It was hybridized to a synthesized 17 nt long DNA labeled at the 5′ end with a quencher molecule TAM (Carboxytetramethylrhodamine) (3′ CCAAAAAAATTAATAGG 5′). The annealing of the two strands was performed in a buffer containing 10 mM TRIS pH 7.5, 50 mM NaCl, and 50 mM KCl at 55 °C with a gradual decrease in the temperature over the period of 45 min. The assay was performed using a thermal cycler (RT-PCR machine). The annealed substrate was incubated with the enzyme at 30 °C. The assay was performed in a buffer containing 30 mM TRIS pH7.5, 100 mM NaCl and 100 mM KCl. The reaction mixture consisted of 1 μM of enzyme and 0.5 μM of substrate in 20 μl of volume. The activity of RNase J2 at different pH was estimated using the same approach but in a different buffer system with 30 mM Bis-Tris propane (pH5.5, pH6, pH6.5, pH7.5 and pH9), 100 mM NaCl and 100 mM KCl.
path: RT-FeDEx assay for RNase J2 and its mutants

sections.title: Cloning of rnjB mutants for transformation in a rnjB deletion strain
sections.text: S. aureus strains PR01-01 (WT) and PR01 to 04 ( ΔrnjB ) were generous gifts from Dr P. Redder ( 52 ). Different rnjB mutants were cloned into an E. coli - S. aureus shuttle vector, pRMC2 ( 53 ). The vector backbone was modified by introducing a rbs (ribosome binding site). PR01 to 04 ( ΔrnjB ) electrocompetent cells were prepared as described by Löfblom and colleagues ( 54 ). The plasmid DNA containing different rnjB mutants was electroporated into competent S. aureus cells. The cells were revived in TSB (tryptic soy broth) media containing 500 mM of sucrose at 37 °C for 3 hours. After incubation the cells were plated on TSB plate containing 10 μg/ml of chloramphenicol.
path: Cloning of rnjB mutants for transformation in a rnjB deletion strain

sections.title: Hemolysis assay
sections.text: A single colony of different constructs were inoculated in TSB media containing 30 μg/ml of chloramphenicol and were incubated at 37 °C overnight. 1% (v/v) of the overnight culture was added to fresh TSB containing 30 μg/ml chloramphenicol. At an OD 600 of 0.5, the secondary cultures were induced with 1 μg/ml of AHT (anhydrotetracycline) followed by incubation at 37 °C for 9 hours. Post induction, the OD 600 of each culture was measured and normalized. 2 μl of each culture having the same OD 600 was spotted onto sheep blood agar plate (Himedia). The plate was incubated at 37 °C for 24 hours followed by incubation at 4 °C for another 24 hours. Images were taken using Olympus SZ61 stereomicroscope and the zone was clearance (difference between outer and inner diameter) was quantified using ImageJ ( 55 ).

sections.title: Bacterial RNA isolation and relative expression of genes by RT-qPCR
sections.text: Total RNA was isolated from different rnjB mutants induced cultures. The culture pellet was resuspended in 400 μl of lysis buffer (30 mM TRIS pH 8.0, 1 mM EDTA, 0.2 mg/ml lysostaphin, 0.2 mg/ml proteinase K, 0.1 mg/ml lysozyme) followed by incubation at 37 °C for 30 min. Subsequently, RNeasy mini kit (Qiagen) was used for further processing of the samples as per manufacturer protocol. The RNA yield was quantified using a NanoDrop spectrophotometer (Thermo Scientific). 1 μg of RNA was used for cDNA conversion using QuantiTect Reverse Transcriptase kit (Qiagen). Real time quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR) was carried out in iQ5 cycler (Bio-Rad) to estimate the relative gene levels. The reaction mix consists of SYBR green mix, cDNA and corresponding primers. Relative transcripts levels were calculated with the ΔΔCt method using 16S rRNA was used as internal control. The primers used for RT-qPCR are listed in Table S3 .

sections.title: Input files
sections.text: The structures of RNase J1 (PDB: 6K6S ) and RNase J2 (PDB: 6K6W ) paralogs were prepared using a protein preparation wizard ( 56 ) by adding hydrogens, bond orders, and disulfide bonds to the protein structure. Missing residues and loops were added to the structure with the help of the prime routine ( 57 ). The protonation state of all titratable residues was modified using PropKa at neutral pH ( 58 ). The structure was subsequently energy minimized using the OPLS2005 forcefield ( 59 ).

sections.title: MD simulations
sections.text: MD simulations were performed for enzymes with the bound metal cofactors using AMBER20 ( 60 ). As the enzyme was coordinated with Mn as a metal cofactor, MCPB.Py ( 61 ) a Python-based metal parameter builder was used. This builder employs a bonded model approach to generate a forcefield for the metal center of the enzyme. The structure of both enzymes was immersed in an orthorhombic water box of 12 Å using the TIP3P water model ( 62 ). The solvated system was neutralized by adding seven and 5 Na ions in the case of RNase J1 and J2, respectively. For long-range electrostatic interactions, the particle mesh Ewald method was employed with a cut-off value of 12 Å. Two-step minimization was performed to remove unfavorable contacts. The first step was partial minimization with restraints while these were removed in the second minimization step. Each minimization was performed using the steepest descent method for 5000 steps followed by another 5000 steps using the conjugate gradient method. Further, the Langevin thermostat ( 63 ) was used to gradually heat the system from 0 to 300 K at a constant volume of 500 ps. Production dynamics were carried out using NPT ensemble for the period of 50 ns each, and for every 2 fs trajectories were recorded. The SHAKE algorithm ( 64 ) was utilized during the simulation to retain hydrogen bonding interactions. The conformer after 50 ns MD simulations (in the case of both RNase J paralogs) was taken as the initial structure for QM/MM minimization ( Fig. S13 ).

sections.title: QM/MM minimization
sections.text: For both paralogs, the QM/MM minimization was performed using AMBER20 ( 60 ) with Gaussian16 ( 65 ) as an interface for 1000 steps; in which the first 500 steps were performed using the steepest descent method followed by the conjugate gradient method. The QM region of RNase J1 consists of two Mn ions along with the coordinating residues (His74, His76, Asp78, His79, His142, Asp164 and His390) while the rest of the enzyme is considered as MM region. For RNase J2, the QM region consists of His76, His78, His80, His144 and Glu166 along with the Mn cofactor. For both paralogs the QM cutoff value was fixed at 12 Å. The electrostatic embedding scheme has been employed to describe the charges between QM and MM atoms and the link atom approach has been applied for QM and MM interface atoms. The QM calculations were performed using Density functional theory B3LYP method ( 66 ) employing a 6 to 311G∗∗ basis set ( 67 ). The MM region on the other hand employed the AMBERff19SB forcefield ( 68 ). During minimization, the Shake algorithm was not introduced. The particle mesh Ewald method was used to define long-range electrostatics. Further, from the last snapshot of QM/MM minimization, for the QM region residues, single point energy calculations were performed using Gaussian16, and the wavefunction obtained was used for further charge density and electrostatic property calculations.

Protein Structure & Enzyme Engineering.title: Structural basis of nearest-neighbor cooperativity in the ring-shaped gene regulatory protein TRAP from protein engineering and cryo-EM
Protein Structure & Enzyme Engineering.abstract: SignificanceHomo-oligomeric proteins are ubiquitous in biology, and their function is often regulated by ligands that bind cooperatively, via poorly understood mechanisms. Aha TRAP is a bacterial protein that assembles into dodecameric rings and is responsible for sensing changes in cellular tryptophan concentration, and for downregulating its production when levels are elevated. By fusing two subunits via a flexible linker, we assembled protein rings in which every other of its twelve ligand binding sites could be altered. Monitoring ligand binding by native mass spectrometry revealed that disabling every other site disrupts cooperative ligand binding. Cryo-EM of these engineered proteins revealed how ligand binding events alter the structure of neighboring sites to enable cooperative binding.
Protein Structure & Enzyme Engineering.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

figure_captions.label: fig1
figure_captions.caption: Dodecameric TRAP from Alkalihalobacillus halodurans ( Aha ) exhibits strong nearest-neighbor (NN) cooperativity in Trp binding. ( A ) Crystal structure of the ligand-activated Aha TRAP 12-mer (PDB:3ZZL) shows 12 bound Trp ligands (spheres) located between adjacent protomers (cartoon). Adjacent Trp binding sites are separated by ~12 Å via a seven-strand β-sheet that connects the protomers. Inset : Loops BC and DE that enclose the Trp binding site of one protomer connect it to adjacent Trp binding sites. ( B ) Configurations and parameters of the nearest-neighbor (NN) statistical thermodynamic model applied to TRAP. Each ligand binding site can populate one of four possible energy states: a reference empty state (state 0), and states bound with no occupied neighbors (state N0), bound with a single occupied neighbor (state N1), or bound with two occupied neighbors (state N2). Statistical weights ω are assigned relative to the reference state 0, with S = K 0 [L], where K 0 = exp(-Δ G 0 / RT ) is the equilibrium association constant, [L] is the free ligand concentration and α = exp(-Δ G α / RT ) is the NN interaction term that relates the affinity of a site with an occupied neighbor to an isolated site ( α = K N1 / K N0 ). In the NN model, the interaction energy for binding between two occupied neighbors is just 2Δ G α , and the corresponding statistical weight is α 2 S . ( C ) ( Top ) The NN interaction term α defines thermodynamic coupling between adjacent Trp binding sites in Aha TRAP. ( Bottom ) Deconvolved native mass spectrum of a mixture of 60 µM Aha TRAP sites with 40 µM Trp; fitting a series of such spectra using the NN model revealed an interaction term α = 256, corresponding to nearest-neighbor interaction of −3.3 kcal/mol ( 16 ).

figure_captions.label: fig2
figure_captions.caption: Design of linked dTRAP to enable control over nearest-neighbor configurations. ( A ) Primary sequence of tandem Aha dTRAP-linked protomers. Secondary structural elements observed in the crystal of the wild-type protein, PDB ID 3ZZL are indicated schematically. The Gly-Ser linker is gray, residual C-terminal TEV-cleavage site is black. Thr49 and Thr52, mutated to Ala to disrupt Trp binding are indicated by “*”. ( B ) Hydrogen bonds between the sidechain hydroxyls of Thr49 and Thr52 and the Trp ligands, as observed in the crystal, PDB ID 3ZZL. ( C ) Rosetta model of dTRAP based on PDB ID 3ZZL. The 10-residue linker is predicted to be at the base of the TRAP ring and not interfere with Trp or RNA binding. Protomers colored as in A .

figure_captions.label: fig3
figure_captions.caption: Linked dTRAP retains native structure and cooperative ligand binding. ( A ) Comparative 2D 1 H- 15 N TROSY-HSQC NMR spectra of TRAP WT and linked dTRAP, recorded at 600 and 800 MHz, respectively, in the absence ( Left ) and presence ( Right ) of saturating Trp. The general similarity in peak positions indicates that introduction of the linker has a minimal impact on the structure of the oligomeric TRAP ring, and that Trp binding is minimally perturbed. ( B ) Wild-type (WT) and dTRAP exhibit similar apparent Trp binding affinities as monitored by CD at 228 nm and fit with a two-state model (6.5 ± 1.0 µM; 4.5 ± 1.4 µM, respectively). ( C ) Native mass spectra of dTRAP (1.7 µM) titrated with 0-48 µM Trp. Increased Trp concentration in each titration shifts the population from apo (Trp 0 , circle) to holo (Trp 12 , square). ( D ) Deconvolved zero-charge mass spectra over a range of Trp concentrations for TRAP ( Left ) and dTRAP ( Right ). The experimental spectra (color) are superimposed on simulated data (gray) derived from best-fit NN model parameters. In both spectra, the dominant populations comprise the apo-state (0 Trp) and the holo-state (12 Trp), indicating strong positive cooperativity. The best-fit NN interaction terms α = 256 and α = 123, correspond to RT ln α = 3.3 and 2.9 kcal/mol at 25 °C, respectively ( 16 ).

figure_captions.label: fig4
figure_captions.caption: Eliminating the nearest-neighbor interaction disrupts cooperativity in dTRAP. ( A ) Comparative 2D 1 H- 15 N-correlated NMR spectra of WT-WT and WT-Mut dTRAP in the absence and presence of Trp. Top Left , WT-WT and WT-Mut adopt similar structures in the absence of Trp. Top Right , WT-WT in the absence and presence of Trp. Bottom Left , WT-Mut in the absence and presence of Trp; lack of perturbations reflects a binding defect. Bottom Right , WT-WT and WT-Mut in the presence of Trp contrasts with their similarity in the absence. ( B ) RNA filter-binding data as a function of protein concentration for dTRAP variants toward an idealized (GAGUU) 11 single-stranded leader RNA, in the presence of 1 mM Trp. The RNA binding affinities of WT, WT-WT, and WT-Mut were not distinguishable under these conditions of excess Trp (20 ± 5, 26 ± 5, 29 ± 9 nM, respectively), whereas the Mut-Mut variant did not bind RNA over the same range of TRAP concentrations. ( C ) ITC of Trp into dTRAP variants. The thermogram for WT-WT dTRAP is biphasic, indicative of cooperativity. Thermograms of dTRAP WT-Mut and Mut-Mut exhibit small and no enthalpy changes, respectively. ( D ) Deconvolved zero charge native MS spectra of Trp-dTRAP titrations (at 12 µM sites) reveal strong positive cooperative binding for WT-WT dTRAP ( Left ) (high abundance in both apo- and holo-state), whereas dTRAP WT-Mut cannot be saturated at > 10-fold stoichiometric excess under these conditions ( Right ).

figure_captions.caption: Cryo-EM of dTRAP and WT-Mut dTRAP reveal ligand-dependent ordering. Electron potential maps from single-particle reconstruction of cryo-EM images from Trp-free apo-dTRAP (EMD-44472), Trp-loaded holo WT-Mut (EMD-44473), and Trp-loaded holo dTRAP (EMD-44468) colored by local resolution, from 3 to 7 Å using a rainbow heatmap. figure_captions.label: fig6
figure_captions.caption: Ligand-dependent density in dTRAP-linked protomer maps reveal loop stabilization. Left : Views of apo dTRAP ( A ), holo WT-Mut ( B ), and holo dTRAP ( C ) maps of a linked protomer colored by local resolution. Middle : models of dTRAP variants fitted into the maps. The two linked protomers are colored differently. Right : Close-up views of the BC and DE loops. Density corresponding to the BC and DE loops is mostly missing in apo dTRAP, partially discernable for the DE loops in Trp-bound WT-mutant, and much better defined in holo dTRAP. figure_captions.label: fig7
figure_captions.caption: Cooperativity through population shifts induced by nearest-neighbor binding in TRAP. x -axis, idealized one-dimensional conformational coordinate; y -axis, free energy; lower energy conformations (states) are more populated. In the absence of Trp (0 0 0, Top ), the BC and DE loops sample a wide range of isoenergetic conformations, most of which do not favor Trp binding. The conformational landscape of a Trp-bound site (0 1 0, Bottom ) is narrow and deep, populating conformations corresponding to the Trp-bound state. Binding of a ligand to a neighbor (0 0 1) alters the free energy landscape of a site, favoring the bound state, but also populating other states, such as those that allow binding. Next-nearest-neighbor binding (0 0 01, dashed line) may also result in a population shift, exerting a smaller magnitude cooperative effect. Free energy curves are offset for clarity.

sections.title: Engineered Linked TRAP Dimers (dTRAP) Enable Control Over Nearest-Neighbor Configurations.
sections.text: To manipulate the NN effect in TRAP, we engineered pairs of tandemly linked Aha TRAP subunits fused with flexible linkers, here termed dTRAP ( Fig. 2 ). Because Trp binds between adjacent protomers, in dTRAP one of the Trp binding sites lies at the interface connected by the linker, while the other binding site is between linked dimers. By introducing mutations to disable Trp binding on either the N- or C-terminal protomer, only every other site would be competent for Trp binding, and the potential for NN interaction would be eliminated ( Fig. 2 B and C ). In the crystal structure of Aha TRAP ( 28 ), the side chain hydroxyls of Thr49 and Thr52 from the DE loop of each protomer are observed to hydrogen bond with one of the carboxyl oxygens of the bound Trp ligand. Mutation to Ala of both of these residues, T49A/T52A, is expected to strongly weaken Trp binding to that site ( 36 , 37 ). To avoid perturbing the structure and thermodynamics of Trp binding by TRAP, we experimented with three different linker lengths for fusing C- to N-terminus two Aha TRAP protomers with flexible Gly-Ser linkers (GGGS, GGGSGGG, and GGGGSGGGGS) ( 38 , 39 ). We then evaluated the resulting fusion proteins in terms of recombinant expression yield, in vitro solubility, and Trp- and RNA-binding capabilities ( SI Appendix , Fig. S2 ). Based on those criteria, and guided in part by loop modeling with Rosetta ( 40 ) and AlphaFold2 ( 41 ) ( Fig. 2 , SI Appendix , Fig. S3 ), we selected for biochemical characterization a fusion construct with the 10-residue linker (Gly 4 Ser) 2 .

sections.title: Aha dTRAP Retains Native Oligomeric Structure and Strong Cooperativity in Trp Binding.
sections.text: By several measures, linking together two WT protomers with the (G 4 S) 2 linker did not significantly disrupt the structural integrity of the protein ring, or its ligand binding capacity. Two-dimensional 1 H- 15 N-correlated NMR spectra were recorded for both the ligand-free apo and ligand-saturated holo states of both Aha TRAP and dTRAP ( Fig. 3 A ). Aha TRAP protomers comprise 76 amino acids and both apo and holo spectra feature the number of signals expected for a single chain, indicating that the protein exhibits C12 cyclic symmetry. Although additional signals are expected from the linker and C-terminal protease site in dTRAP ( Fig. 2 ), most signals superposed well in both apo and holo states, indicating that introduction of the linker does not perturb the overall structure of the protein; broader signals in the spectrum of apo dTRAP suggest some weak aggregation under the NMR conditions. Circular dichroism (CD) spectrum of TRAP is sensitive to Trp binding ( 42 ), and similarity of the Trp-dependent CD spectra indicates that the linked protein dTRAP binds Trp similarly to the WT protein, with similar apparent dissociation constants ( Fig. 3 B ). ITC data also showed that these two proteins share similar biphasic trends, indicative of cooperative binding ( SI Appendix , Fig. S4 ). We have found nMS to be particularly useful for quantifying cooperativity in TRAP ( 11 , 16 ) and those spectra revealed similar strong cooperativity in dTRAP compared to TRAP ( Fig. 3 D ). Native mass spectra of both proteins recorded in the absence of Trp yielded a dominant set of signals corresponding to the mass of the oligomeric apo proteins (TRAP: 111,449 Da expected, 111,454 observed; dTRAP: 110,355 Da expected, 110,394 observed). MS signals from dTRAP were broader than those of WT TRAP 12 , reflecting a higher degree of adduct formation. Differences between expected and measured masses are likely the result of attempts to use cool MS tuning to avoid restructuring of the complex and associated adducting with salts and solvents, in addition to uncertainty in the specific charging species; i.e., H + , Na + , K + . While nonspecific ligand binding is sometimes observed in nMS experiments ( 43 – 45 ), the absence of signals attributable to superstoichiometric Trp:site complexes, and insensitivity of the spectra to low activation energy indicated that a correction for nonspecific binding is not necessary. Across a range of Trp concentrations, nMS signals from the apo and fully loaded holo states (dTRAP with 12 bound Trp, expected: 112,805 Da, observed: 112,832 Da; TRAP with 12 bound Trp: 113,899 Da expected, 113,903 observed) dominated both sets of spectra ( Fig. 3 C and D ). Depletion of partially loaded states of the oligomer is a defining feature of positive cooperativity ( 16 ), indicating that both TRAP and dTRAP exhibit strong positive cooperativity under those conditions. Populations of Trp n -TRAP 12 states obtained from the nMS peak heights were fit with the NN binding model ( 10 , 11 , 16 ) using the standard deviation from three replicates as an estimate of precision. Best fit parameters to the NN models yielded for Aha TRAP a NN cooperativity strength α = 256 ± 87 and for dTRAP α = 123 ± 5; intrinsic affinities K 0 were 720 ± 140 µM and 240 ± 90 µM, respectively.
path: Aha dTRAP Retains Native Oligomeric Structure and Strong Cooperativity in Trp Binding.

sections.title: Eliminating NN Interactions Impairs Trp Binding.
sections.text: To produce dTRAP variants incapable of NN interactions, dual T49A/T52A mutations were introduced either on the N-terminal or C-terminal protomer ( Fig. 2 ) to generate Mut-WT or WT-Mut dTRAP proteins, or at both sites to generate a Mut-Mut dTRAP variant. We expressed and purified each of these dTRAP variants and performed preliminary characterization. Each protein construct eluted from a size exclusion column with the apparent molecular weight (MW) expected of a TRAP dodecamer (here with six linked dTRAP). Heteronuclear NMR spectra of WT-WT, WT-Mut, and Mut-WT dTRAP were highly congruent in the absence of Trp ( Fig. 4 A and SI Appendix , Fig. S5 ), indicating highly similar structures; poor expression and solubility of the Mut-Mut variant precluded it from NMR analysis. The 2D NMR spectra of WT-WT dTRAP recorded in the presence of excess Trp showed large chemical shift perturbations, consistent with Trp binding and induced structural changes. By contrast, spectra of WT-Mut and Mut-WT dTRAP were largely unperturbed under equivalent Trp concentrations indicating a Trp binding defect. The Mut-WT variant failed to bind Trp as assayed by other metrics ( SI Appendix , Fig. S5 ), suggesting that the location of the interprotomer linker does affect Trp binding in this context. Nevertheless, without identifying the cause of that effect, we proceeded with thermodynamic analysis of two other mutants, WT-Mut dTRAP, which, when assembled into rings, should be capable of Trp binding at every other site, and the Mut-Mut construct, which lacks native Trp binding sites ( Fig. 4 B – D ). dTRAP variants remain functional in Trp-activated RNA binding. To test for unintended consequences from introduction of the linker and Thr/Ala mutations, we examined Trp-dependent RNA binding by dTRAP variants to (GAGUU) 11 RNA repeats with a filter binding assay ( Fig. 4 B ). In the presence of a high excess of Trp (1 mM), WT-WT, WT-Mut, and Mut-WT dTRAP each exhibits RNA binding capacity. Expected differences in Trp-dependent RNA binding could not be discerned under the conditions of these experiments, with each variant showing similar affinities to that exhibited by the WT protein ( K D,app = 20 ± 5 nM). Interestingly, although as mentioned above, Mut-WT dTRAP failed to bind Trp on its own, it does exhibit Trp-dependent RNA binding with a similar apparent affinity ( SI Appendix , Fig. S6 ). These results indicate that the (G 4 S) 2 linker is not strongly perturbing of dTRAP structure and ligand binding. In addition, the Thr/Ala mutations at every other site do not significantly diminish the protein’s ability to bind RNA. Conversely, dTRAP Mut-Mut appears incapable of RNA binding, presumably due to its inability to bind Trp ( Fig. 4 B ). One hallmark of cooperative ligand binding is biphasic thermograms in ITC experiments ( 46 ). ITC measurement of Trp titrations reveals a biphasic thermograms for dTRAP consistent with cooperative Trp binding and an apparent maximal enthalpy change of −13 kcal/mol ( Fig. 4 C , SI Appendix , Fig. S7 ). Under comparable binding site concentrations of WT-Mut dTRAP (~ twice to account for WT binding sites per chain), the thermograms for titrating Trp into WT-Mut and Mut-Mut, exhibit a smaller binding ΔH of −4 kcal/mol and reduced biphasic character, whereas no measurable heat of binding was detected at that protein concentration for Mut-Mut dTRAP. Although the biphasic character of the thermograms was much reduced, they were reproducibly biphasic, indicating that despite deficient Trp binding to Mut sites, WT-Mut dTRAP retains some modest cooperativity. Nevertheless, these data are consistent with a dominant role of NN contributions on cooperativity and overall Trp binding affinity. Because nMS can better describe the distribution of Trp–TRAP states than can other bulk measures of ligand binding ( 11 , 16 , 47 ), we used nMS to compare Trp binding to dTRAP and WT-Mut dTRAP ( Fig. 4 D and SI Appendix , Fig. S8 ). Under conditions of approximately half maximal saturation for dTRAP at 12 µM binding sites, the mass spectrum is dominated by signals from the Trp-free apo protein and from the fully Trp-loaded holo dTRAP ring (expected: 112,805 Da, observed: 112,832 Da). By comparison, WT-Mut dTRAP exhibits a strong Trp binding defect. In the absence of Trp, we observe the expected major signal corresponding to the apo WT-Mut oligomer (109,993 Da expected, 110,029 Da observed), while in the presence of a 10-fold excess of Trp (12 µM WT sites, 128 µM Trp), not only are the fully Trp-loaded rings a minor species, but intermediate species are much more populated, resembling a statistical gaussian-like distribution. Nevertheless, the population distribution of WT-Mut dTRAP rings with zero to six bound Trp was poorly fit with a noncooperative, independent sites model, yielding nonrandom residuals ( SI Appendix , Fig. S10 ). Fitting the WT-Mut dTRAP populations using the NN cooperative model yielded small, near-random residuals and best fit values of 873 ± 90 µM and 5 ± 1 for K 0 and the cooperativity factor α. Thus, cooperativity in WT-Mut dTRAP is down by a factor of ~25 compared to that of WT-WT dTRAP (α = 123). These data support a model in which the strong cooperativity observed in dTRAP arises from favorable cooperative interactions between adjacent binding sites. It also suggests that differences in the structural features of Trp-loaded oligomers composed of dTRAP and WT-Mut dTRAP may reveal insights into the basis for this cooperative effect.
path: Eliminating NN Interactions Impairs Trp Binding.

sections.title: Cryo-EM Single Particle Reconstruction of dTRAP WT-WT and WT-Mut Constructs.
sections.text: Availability of WT-Mut dTRAP, with alternating binding-competent and -impaired sites provides an opportunity to discern the structural basis for the observed nearest-neighbor cooperativity. We sought to obtain these insights by comparing cryo-EM maps from dTRAP in the absence and presence of Trp, and of WT-Mut dTRAP in the presence of Trp; these samples are expected to exhibit characteristics corresponding to the ligand-free apo protein, the fully liganded holo protein, and an intermediate in which every other site is occupied. Cryo-EM grids of dTRAP and its variants yielded well-defined particles with a good distribution of orientations ( SI Appendix , Figs. S 11–S13 ). Single-particle reconstructions of the Cryo-EM data with application of overall six-fold symmetry resulted in distinct electron potential maps for the three samples ( Fig. 5 ); although each of the unsymmetrized maps yielded slightly higher scores for C12 symmetry ( 48 ), because of the linkers C6 refinement was applied during map and model refinement. Local resolution differences reveal a progressive increase in order from the unbound apo dTRAP protein, to the partially bound WT-Mut protein and finally the fully bound holo dTRAP. Application of six-fold symmetry is justified by the linker connecting the two protomers in dTRAP, reducing overall symmetry from twelve-fold in TRAP to six-fold in dTRAP. Nevertheless, potential map refinement using C1 symmetry resulted in maps with distinct but low overall resolution, as well as visually inequivalent maps for alternating sites in Trp-loaded WT-Mut dTRAP ( SI Appendix , Figs. S14–S16 ); imposition of C6 symmetry following homogeneous C1 refinement increased the WT-Mut map resolution from 5.3 to 4.4 Å. Use of these C6-refined maps in particle reclassification, followed by two more rounds of homogenous and nonhomogeneous refinement resulted in a map with a resolution of 4.1 Å for WT-Mut dTRAP. Similar workflows for apo and holo dTRAP yielded maps with a global resolution of 4.2 Å and 3.6 Å, respectively (gold standard FSC cutoff of 0.143; Fig. 5 , SI Appendix , Figs. S11–S13 and Table S1 ). The ring shape of dTRAP oligomers is clearly established by the density maps, and the highest local resolution is obtained for the β-strands forming the base and the core of each ring. The lowest local resolution is observed for regions that correspond to the Trp binding loops. No density could be assigned to the flexible linker connecting the two TRAP protomers. The C6-refined potential maps are consistent with ligand-dependent local ordering. For the holo protein, maps corresponding to adjacent binding sites were highly congruent despite C6 refinement ( Figs. 5 , 6 and SI Appendix , Fig. S13 ). This finding is consistent with the similarity in the NMR spectra of Trp-loaded TRAP and dTRAP ( Fig. 3 A ), which indicates that the Trp-bound sites are isomorphous in the Trp-bound state. Similarity between the NMR spectra of TRAP and dTRAP in the absence of Trp ( Fig. 3 A ) also suggests that sites in apo dTRAP should be congruent. However, maps for adjacent protomers are visually different at a contour level of 0.135. This apparent asymmetry could be a consequence of the lower resolution of the apo maps, particularly given that the loops are expected to be dynamically disordered ( 4 , 27 , 49 ), due to the effect of the linker on particle alignment, or because the interprotomer linker has a measurable effect on the proximal Trp binding sites. The lower resolution of the map for apo dTRAP, and unexpected asymmetry, gives us less confidence in interpreting this asymmetry. The electron potential map for Trp-bound WT-Mut dTRAP exhibits intermediate resolution between that observed for apo and holo dTRAP and the greatest structural difference between adjacent binding sites ( Figs. 5 and 6 ).
path: Cryo-EM Single Particle Reconstruction of dTRAP WT-WT and WT-Mut Constructs.

sections.title: Map Differences Correspond Primarily to the Trp Binding Loops.
sections.text: To build atomic models into the potential maps for apo and holo dTRAP, and Trp-bound WT-Mut dTRAP, we used Rosetta ( 50 ) to build the (Gly 4 Ser) 2 linkers using the crystal structure of Trp-bound Aha TRAP [PDB ID 3ZZL; ( 28 )] as the template. Model refinement performed in an iterative fashion using Coot, ISOLDE, and PHENIX ( 51 – 54 ) yielded good local agreement between the template and optimized model. Model building into the electron potential map reveals that the largest differences in between the apo, holo, and WT-Mut dTRAP structures are in degree of order of the BC and DE loops ( Fig. 6 ). Of the three samples, the map for holo dTRAP was best defined ( Figs. 5 and 6 ). Backbone density could be resolved for most of the protein chain, with the exception of residues 1-6, which were also not observed in the crystal structure of wild-type Aha TRAP ( 28 ), the Gly-Ser linker, and the C-terminal TEV sequence; density was also weaker for Gly27 and Asp29 in the BC loop. Density corresponding to the bound Trp can be clearly observed between each protomer monomers ( Fig. 6 C and SI Appendix , Fig. S17 ). Overall, there is strong agreement between the location of secondary structural elements and overall geometry of the Trp binding site, although sidechain rotamers cannot clearly be distinguished at this resolution. In comparison to holo dTRAP, in addition to lower overall resolution for apo dTRAP, the most obvious feature is that the density corresponding to the BC and B’C’ loops of apo dTRAP ( Fig. 6 A , middle and right panels) cannot be discerned. This is consistent with the loops being flexible and disordered in the absence of the ligand. The Trp binding sites in apo dTRAP feature only weak density, consistent with the sites being empty ( Fig. 6 A , right panel). Although no clear density could be discerned for the BC and DE loops, they are nevertheless included in the model for guidance, but their position should not be interpreted as defined by the data. The density map for Trp-bound WT-Mut dTRAP showed better overall resolution than that of apo dTRAP ( Figs. 5 and 6 B ), with clearer density for the BC (and B’C’) loops. Defined density assignable to the Trp ligand is observed at alternating binding sites ( Fig. 6 B Middle and Right panels, SI Appendix , Fig. S18 ). However, lesser density is also observed in the Mut sites, which could result from either partial site occupancy under Trp saturating conditions used, buffer atoms or sidechain rearrangement, or partial misalignment of particles during reconstruction; similar weak density is observed in the apo WT-WT dTRAP ligand binding sites, suggesting the latter ( Fig. 6 A ). The higher local resolution indicates a higher degree of order in the Trp binding loops.
path: Map Differences Correspond Primarily to the Trp Binding Loops.

sections.title: Ligand Binding Induces Increased Order at Neighboring Sites.
sections.text: The principal objective of the present cryo-EM studies is to provide insights into the structural basis for ligand binding cooperativity by TRAP. The ligand binding experiments described above demonstrate that WT-Mut dTRAP is strongly deficient in Trp binding, in a way that is consistent with a major role for NN interactions in mediating this effect. One possible mechanism for achieving NN cooperativity would be to induce in neighboring sites a discrete structure that favors ligand binding. In Trp-bound WT-Mut dTRAP, those loops are much less well ordered than in holo dTRAP, indicating that protein rings with ligand bound at alternating sites retain a significant degree of disorder. Nevertheless, the loop disorder is measurably decreased in the Trp-bound WT-Mut protein, compared to the apo protein ( Fig. 6 A and B ). This suggests that NN cooperativity can be explained by a population shift from the wide range of conformations sampled by apo TRAP, to a narrower distribution of states that comparatively favor ligand binding. While this is evident in terms of increased order at the backbone level, it likely also arises from a narrowing of the conformational space sampled by protein side chains in the Trp binding site, and connecting one site to its adjacent sites via strands B,C.
path: Ligand Binding Induces Increased Order at Neighboring Sites.

sections.title: Conclusions
sections.text: Evolutionary pressures have produced in Bacilli a complex network of protein–ligand, protein–RNA, and RNA–RNA interactions as a means of regulating production of the metabolically expensive, but essential amino acid, tryptophan ( 1 ). TRAP, which forms rings of 11 or 12 subunits, depending on species ( 28 ), serves as the intracellular sensor for monitoring changes in intracellular concentrations of Trp and becomes activated to downregulate its production when levels are high. Activation involves the binding of multiple Trp ligands, which induces structural changes in the protein rings, priming them for binding to specific sites in the 5’ leader region of the trp operon. While heterotropic cooperativity between Trp and RNA provides the means for downregulation, homotropic cooperativity between Trp binding events on the homo-oligomeric rings enables fine-tuning of the response. Trp binding to linked dTRAP with alternating mutant and wild-type sites approximates independent site binding. We engineered dTRAP to dissect the intrinsic affinity of Trp for a site, K 0 , from the NN interaction term α that results in higher affinity for binding next to occupied sites ( Figs. 1 and 2 ). Comparison of NMR spectra for Aha TRAP and linked dTRAP, and macroscopic binding metrics ( Fig. 3 ) suggested that the linker introduces only minor perturbations in the structure of the TRAP dodecameric ring and its Trp binding thermodynamics (i.e., a two-fold reduction in the interaction term α). Mutation to Ala of two ligand-coordinating Thr residues in one of the protomers of dTRAP resulted in protein rings with six intact Trp binding sites, but a major defect in Trp binding, with a twenty-five-fold reduction in α ( Fig. 4 ). This is consistent with a dominant effect from NN interactions between sites. Comparing cryo-EM density maps for apo dTRAP, WT-Mut dTRAP, and holo dTRAP, we observe progressive increase in map resolution for the BC and DE loops that gate access to the Trp binding sites ( Fig. 6 ), and also play a role in Trp-activated RNA binding ( 1 , 37 , 55 , 56 ). A plausible mechanism for cooperativity in Aha TRAP, consistent with the presented data, is that binding of Trp to a site rigidifies the BC and DE loops flanking the site, while their proximity and structural coupling to adjacent sites ( Fig. 1 ) likewise results in partial ordering of the adjacent sites. The accompanying shift in the free energy landscape can thus be understood to favor the ligand-bound state, without specifying specifically which conformational states are excluded by rigidification of the adjacent sites ( Fig. 7 ). In this model, ligand binding to neighboring sites changes the free energy landscape such that binding-competent conformations are more populated and thus subsequent ligand binding is favored. A lesser effect from binding at next-nearest-neighbors can also be envisioned as arising from more modest shift in the free energy landscape. The combination of protein engineering with nMS and cryo-EM single-particle reconstruction provided the means to dissect direct and indirect effects of ligand binding on TRAP. nMS provides unmatched detail into the thermodynamics of Trp binding by enabling quantification of states with differing numbers of bound Trp. Construction of the dTRAP-linked variants allows for control over the Trp–TRAP configurations, whereas oligomers with isolated chains would necessarily populate statistical distribution of states, some with bound neighbors, some not. The resulting well-defined configurations provided an opportunity to detail the structural differences between TRAP rings free, fully bound to Trp, and with alternating sites bound. The results strongly support a model in which cooperativity in TRAP is dominated by ligand-mediated ordering of loops that gate Trp binding to individual sites and serve as bridges connecting sites. While the results of the present study strongly support this model, complications limited the precision of the resulting insights. Although introduction of the linkers seemed, based on NMR data and bulk measurements to not perturb the structure and thermodynamics of Trp binding, the linkers had a measurable effect. nMS of Trp binding to WT dTRAP nevertheless showed that ligand binding thermodynamics was slightly perturbed (by - RT ln Δα = −0.69 RT ; Fig. 3 ), and the Mut-WT protein seemed unable to bind Trp at all ( SI Appendix , Fig. S5 ). Although modeling predicts that the linker should not interfere with either Trp or RNA binding ( Fig. 2 and SI Appendix , Fig. S3 ), the observation suggests that coincidence of the linker and the sole WT site could introduce a modest structural defect that interferes with Trp binding in the absence of RNA. In addition, while the flexibility of the linkers was intended to prevent perturbation of the protein fold and thermodynamics, the fact that the linkers are small and disordered rendered them invisible in reconstructed electron density maps. Because of this, it is difficult to assess the extent to which particle misalignment might have contributed to reduced density of the maps, especially for the Trp-loaded WT-Mut protein, wherein asymmetry is expected ( Fig. 5 ). Last, while the data presented strongly support a model in which disorder-order transitions are responsible for the observed Trp–Trp cooperativity, they are insufficient to map out at atomic resolution the conformational ensemble of states present in the Trp-bound and partially loaded TRAP rings. Such atomic-level insights are likely required to enable rational efforts to modulate the thermodynamic response of TRAP and molecules like it for use in diagnostics or synthetic biology applications.

sections.title: Preparation of Linked Aha TRAP Variants (dTRAP).
sections.text: DNA constructs encoding Aha TRAP-(linker)-TRAP-(TEV cleavage site)-His 6 with varying length Gly/Ser linkers were obtained commercially (GenScript, Inc) in a pET21a (Novagen) plasmid; linker sequences were GGGS, GGGSGGG, and GGGGSGGGGS. Proteins were expressed in Escherichia coli BL21(DE3) cells and inducted by adding 0.5 mM IPTG (isopropyl ß-D-1-thiogalactopyranoside) at mid-log phase (OD600 = 0.4 to 0.6) at 37 ˚C. Cells were then harvested through centrifuge and then resuspended in loading buffer (20 mM NaPi, 500 mM NaCl, 100 mM Imidazole, pH = 7.4). The cells were lysed using the French press method at 10,000 psi. The lysate was cleared by centrifugation at 30,000× g for 20 min, and the supernatant was filtrated through 0.45 um cellulose acetate filters (Advantec) using 30 mL syringes (BD). The supernatant was loaded onto 1 mL HisTrap HP column (GE Healthcare) on an AKTA fast protein liquid chromatography. Proteins were then eluted with a gradient of imidazole from 100 mM to 1 M in the buffer of 20 mM NaPi pH 7.4, and 500 mM NaCl. The C-terminal 6xHis-tag was then removed by treatment with TEV protease (in-house produced) at a protease-to-target molar ratio of 1:100 and products were passed through Ni-NTA to remove uncleaved protein. To ensure complete removal of bound Trp, proteins were dialyzed in 3.5 kDa cut-off (Spectrum Labs) dialysis tubing against 3 M Gdn-HCl in buffer A (100 mM NaCl, 50 mM NaPO 4 , pH 8.0 at 25 °C, 0.02% NaN 3 ) for 6 h at room temperature. The samples were then step-down dialyzed against 1.5 M and 0 M Gdn-HCl in buffer A. Refolded proteins were further purified by size-exclusion chromatography using a Hiload 16/600 Superdex 75 column (Sigma-Aldrich) in buffer A. After initial trials for expression, solubility, and Trp- and RNA-binding activity, the construct with the GGGGSGGGGS linker (G 4 S) 2 , was selected for further characterization. The resulting protein has the expected amino acid sequence: MNVGDNSNFF VIKAKENGVN VFGMTRGTDT RFHHSEKLDK GEVM IAQF T E H T SAVKIRGK AIIQTSYGTL DTEKDEGGGG SGGGGSMNVG DNSNFFVIKA KENGVNVFGM TRGTDTRFHH SEKLDKGEVM IAQF T EH T SA VKIRGKAIIQ TSYGTLDTEK DEenlyfq, where the linker is underlined, and the C-terminal TEV protease recognition site is lowercase. With a predicted MW of 18,392.45 Da (ProtParam), fully assembled Trp-free rings have an expected MW of 110,355 Da. To produce dTRAP variants with one or both sites deficient in Trp binding, we used site-directed mutagenesis to generate Ala substitutions of Thr49 and Thr52 (boldface, above) in the N-terminal protomer, the C-terminal protomer, or both protomers to generate dTRAP WT-Mut, dTRAP Mut-WT, and dTRAP Mut-Mut proteins, respectively. Sample preparation steps were as above, except that dialysis in 1 M Gdn-HCl buffer A was enough to deplete the bound Trp. Variants with one pair of Thr/Ala mutants (WT-Mut, Mut-WT) have a predicted MW of 18,332.40 Da, and the double mutant (Mut-Mut) MW is 18,272.35 Da (ProtParam).
path: Preparation of Linked Aha TRAP Variants (dTRAP).

sections.title: Concentration of Components.
sections.text: All dTRAP proteins shared the same predicted extinction coefficient at 280 nm (ε = 4470 M −1 cm −1 ; ProtParam). Protein concentrations were measured using a Nanodrop 2000c spectrophotometer (Thermo Scientific) in droplet mode. Unless otherwise specified, TRAP concentrations refer to the concentration of the TRAP 12-mer ring, not the protomer concentration. Ring concentration is 1/12th the promoter concentration for WT TRAP; it is 1/6th the protomer concentration for dTRAP and its variants. The binding site concentration equals the promoter concentration for WT TRAP, it is twice the concentration for WT-WT dTRAP, and it equals the promoter concentration for Mut-WT and WT-Mut dTRAP. Trp concentration was determined by UV absorbance at 280 nm with the extinction coefficient ε = 5540 M −1 cm −1 using a Nanodrop 2000c spectrophotometer (Thermo Scientific) in droplet mode.

sections.title: CD.
sections.text: Trp binding to dTRAP variants was assayed by CD spectropolarimetry using a JASCO model J-715 instrument and a 1 mm pathlength at 37 °C. The data were recorded between 226 nm to 230 nm using 2 µM TRAP in 50 µM sodium phosphate solution (pH = 8.0) with the Trp concentrations ranging from 0 µM to 300 µM.( 16 , 57 ) The CD signal at 228 nm was used to quantify tryptophan binding ( 13 , 23 ). The fractional change in CD signal Y was fit with the single-site mass-balance binding model, with parameters describing total protein and ligand concentrations, [ P tot ], [ L tot ], and apparent dissociation constant, K D : [EQ:EQ3]

sections.title: ITC.
sections.text: ITC isotherms were recorded on the MicroCal VP-ITC instrument (Malvern) at temperatures of 35 and 40 ˚C. HPLC-purified, refolded, and SEC S75 column-purified TRAP was dialyzed against buffer A (100 mM NaCl, 50 mM NaPO 4 , pH 8.0, 0.02% NaN 3 ). Tryptophan (Trp) stock solution was prepared by dissolving L-Trp powder (Sigma-Aldrich) in the TRAP-dialysate. At 35 ˚C, 293 µM Trp was titrated into 1.9 µM WT TRAP; 512 µM Trp was titrated into 3.4 µM dTRAP WT-WT. At 40 ˚C, ITC thermograms of Trp into dTRAP variants were recorded at 40 ˚C at concentrations of 435 µM Trp into 3.4 µM WT-WT, 500 µM Trp to 8.3 µM WT-Mut and Mut-WT, and 530 µM Trp to 8.3 µM Mut-Mut. Baseline correction and integration of ITC thermograms were performed using NITPIC ( 58 ). Processed data were then fit with one-site phenomenological binding model via itcsimlib ( 10 ). CI in fitted parameters were estimated from 200 bootstrapped samples.

sections.title: TROSY-HSQC NMR Spectra of Aha TRAP and dTRAP Variants.
sections.text: Purified [U- 15 N]-TRAP samples were dialyzed against buffer A (100 mM NaCl, 50 mM NaPO 4 , pH 8.0, 0.02% NaN 3 ) supplemented with 10% (v/v) D 2 O (99.8 atom %, Sigma-Aldrich) and 0.001% (v/v) DSS (4,4-Dimethyl-4-silapentane-1-sulfonic acid) (Sigma-Aldrich). 2D 1 H- 15 N TROSY-HSQC NMR spectra of TRAP samples loaded in Wilmad ® 5 mm 541-PP NMR tubes (Sigma-Aldrich) were recorded at 55 °C (328 K) on a Bruker Avance III HD Ultrashield 600 MHz NMR spectrometer equipped with a 5 mm triple-resonance inverse (TXI) cryoprobe with z-axis gradients. Spectra included: 500 µL of 62 µM TRAP (744 µM WT Trp binding sites), alone and titrated with 30 µL 11.5 mM Trp ([Trp]/[WT sites] ratio of 0.9). NMR spectra of dTRAP variants (WT-WT, WT-Mut, and Mut-WT) were recorded at 55 °C (328 K) on a Bruker Avance III HD 800 MHz NMR spectrometer equipped with a TXI cryoprobe. The dTRAP NMR spectra were recorded on: a) 600 µL of 145.2 µM dTRAP WT-WT (1.74 mM WT Trp binding sites) alone and after addition of 77 µL of 14.6 mM Trp ([Trp]/[WT sites] ratio of 1.1); b) 555 µL 58 µM WT-Mut dTRAP (348 µM WT Trp binding sites) alone and after addition of 27 µL of 10.7 mM Trp stock ([Trp]/[WT sites] ratio of 1.5); c) 555 µL of 136 µM Mut-WT dTRAP (816 µM Trp WT binding sites) alone and after addition of 54.6 µL of 24 mM Trp ([Trp]/[WT sites] = 2.9).
path: TROSY-HSQC NMR Spectra of Aha TRAP and dTRAP Variants.

sections.title: dTRAP Structure Modeling and Prediction.
sections.text: The starting model of dTRAP WT-WT with (G 4 S) 2 linker and C-terminal TEV ENLYFQ was built using the loop modeling tools in Rosetta3 (RosettaRemodel release r231, 2019.35) ( 50 , 59 ) running on NMRBox ( 60 ), expanded via C6 symmetry and relaxed using built-in scoring functions. The lowest energy of 100 modeled trajectories was used as the starting point for modeling the cryoEM density. The position of the modeled linker extends from the C-terminus of the first protomer up through the center of the TRAP ring to the N-terminus of the second protomer, opposite of the Trp binding pocket and RNA binding interface. An Alphafold2 model of dTRAP WT-WT was generated using Alphafold2 multimer v3 on Colabfold ( 61 ). The hexameric dTRAP WT-WT sequences were aligned using MMseqs2 searching against PDB100 and in unpaired_paired mode. The top hit ranked by the predicted local distance difference test score (pLDDT) was relaxed using the Amber forcefield with the default settings. This model was qualitatively similar to that generated with Rosetta.

sections.title: RNA Filter Binding Assay.
sections.text: To determine binding affinity of protein to RNA, nitrocellulose filter binding was performed in excess tryptophan (1 mM) with protein ring concentrations from 0 nM to 300 nM. A DNA sequence encoding the 55-nucleotide RNA, formed by 11 repeats of the sequence 5’-GAGUU-3’, was cloned into the plasmid pUC118GAGUU which includes a hammerhead ribozyme fused to the 3’-end ( 62 ). The RNA (GAGUU) 11 was generated from in vitro transcription followed by hammerhead ribozyme cleavage as previously described ( 63 ). The RNA was 5’ end-labeled with and purified from 8 M urea gels by the crush and soak method, as described previously ( 62 ). The reactions contained 5 pM RNA and were incubated at 37 °C for 10 min before filtering. The data were fit with a hyperbolic single binding site model, [EQ:EQ4] , where B max is the maximum observed bound fraction, [TRAP] is the total protein concentration, and K D is the apparent equilibrium dissociation constant.

sections.title: Native Mass Spectrometry (nMS).
sections.text: Native mass spectra were recorded on a Q Exactive Ultra-High Mass Range (UHMR) orbitrap mass spectrometer and an Exactive Plus Extended Mass Range (EMR) Orbitrap mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Both instruments were modified with a surface-induced dissociation device, and the EMR with a custom mass selection quadrupole ( 64 ); dissociation methods were used to confirm expected masses and oligomeric states. Trp–TRAP titration spectra were recorded on the UHMR under conditions described previously ( 16 ). Briefly, a series of Trp-TRAP samples was prepared at room temperature in a 400 mM ammonium acetate solution, with approximately 2 µM protein and varying concentration of Trp from 0 to 120 µM. Similarly, parallel samples of 2 µM dTRAP were prepared, mixed with Trp concentrations from 0 to 48 µM. Titration data of WT-WT dTRAP were deconvolved using MetaUniDec V4.4 ( 65 ), and populations of liganded species were quantified from peak intensities. Because of proteoform signal interference, titration data of WT TRAP were deconvolved using DoubleDec, a double deconvolution method that uses a reference apo TRAP spectrum to account for proteoform signals across the titration spectra, producing zero-charge mass spectra corrected for overlaps in proteoform and ligand state ( 64 ). Binding site concentrations were further corrected using mass balance Eq. 1 , resulting in adjustment to 1.70 µM for dTRAP and 5.16 µM for Bha TRAP ( SI Appendix , Fig. S19 ). Samples for titration of Trp into WT-WT dTRAP (2 µM ring), WT-Mut dTRAP (2 µM ring), Mut-WT dTRAP (2 µM ring), and Mut-Mut dTRAP (1 µM ring), were prepared at room temperature (~25 ˚C) in 200 mM ammonium acetate and measured on the EMR by static nanoelectrospray as with the UHMR. The nMS titration of dTRAP WT-WT and Mut-Mut was performed with the protein samples mixed with Trp concentration of 0 µM, 12 µM, and 24 µM. The nMS titration of both dTRAP WT-Mut and dTRAP Mut-WT was performed with the protein samples mixed with Trp concentration of 0 µM, 36 µM, 64 µM, and 128 µM. Binding polynomials were generated in the itcsimlib software by iterating through all possible 2 N Trp–TRAP configurations and assigning an intrinsic binding free energy Δ G 0 to each site, plus a nearest-neighbor interaction free energy term Δ G α for each NN interaction on a lattice with twelve (or six) sites ( SI Appendix , Fig. S9 ) ( 10 , 11 , 16 ). Populations extracted from the nMS data were then globally fit with the resulting binding polynomials in itcsimlib, as previously described ( 11 , 16 ).

sections.title: Cryo-EM Sample Preparation.
sections.text: An aliquot of 10 mg/mL of apo dTRAP was diluted with cryo-EM buffer (20 mM HEPES, 200 mM NaCl, pH 8) supplemented with a 0.6% stock of Triton X-100 to obtain a final sample of 6 mg/mL protein and 0.05% Triton X-100. Holo dTRAP was prepared by diluting an aliquot of 10 mg/mL protein with cryo-EM buffer supplemented with 1 mM Trp and 0.6% of Triton X-100, to obtain a sample at 6 mg/mL with 0.05% Triton X-100 and 600 μM Trp. Inclusion of Trion X-100 was found to be critical for avoiding adherence of TRAP rings to the air–water interface, and overcoming orientation bias ( 66 ). The sample of Trp-bound WT-Mut dTRAP was prepared by diluting 14 mg/mL of WT-Mut dTRAP with 20 mM Trp in cryo-EM buffer and 0.6% Triton X-100 to obtain a final protein concentration of 6 mg/mL with 0.05% Triton X-100 and 1.4 mM Trp. For all samples, Au Quantifoil R1.2/1.3 300 mesh grids were glow discharged (20 mA, 30 sec hold, 1 min glow discharge) using a PELCO easiGlow Discharge System. For all three samples, a volume of 3 μL was applied to the glow-discharged grids and incubated horizontally for 60 s. Grids were then loaded onto a Vitrobot Mark IV and blotted with a blot force of 1 for 4 s at 4 °C and 100% relative humidity before being plunged frozen into liquid ethane.

sections.title: Cryo-EM Data Collection.
sections.text: For each dataset, movies were acquired using a total electron fluence of 60 e - /Å 2 spread over 45 frames on a Thermo Fisher Scientific Krios G3i operating at 300 keV equipped with a Gatan K3 detector and Biocontinuum energy filter; slit widths were 15 eV for apo and holo dTRAP, and a 20 eV for holo WT-Mut dTRAP. All movies were collected in superresolution, counting mode using a nominal magnification of 81,000× (0.899 Å/px nominal resolution). For apo dTRAP, 3753 movies were collected over a defocus range of 0.5 to 0.2 μm. For holo dTRAP, 2,307 movies were collected over a defocus range of 0.5 to 2.5 μm. For holo WT-Mut dTRAP, 1722 movies were collected over a defocus range of 1 to 2.4 μm.

sections.title: Cryo-EM Data Processing.
sections.text: For apo and holo dTRAP WT-WT, we performed data processing using CryoSPARC v2.15.0 ( 67 ). Movies were imported and aligned using patch motion correction with an applied B-factor of 250, a maximum resolution of 3 Å, and subsequently binned by a factor of two. Patch contrast transfer function (CTF) estimation was performed with a maximum resolution of 2.5 Å. Manual curation of micrographs was used to remove micrographs with a CTF estimation >5 Å and total motion >100 Å. For each dataset, initial maps generated from homogeneous refinement were subjected to symmetry analysis using PROSHADE ( 48 ). In each case, the maps yielded the highest score for C12 symmetry, with C6 scoring almost as well. Because the presence of the linkers between every other protomer in the ring necessarily reduces the symmetry two-fold, we proceeded with C6 refinement of the maps and subsequent models. For apo dTRAP, Blob Picking was used with a min/max particle diameter of 85/105 Å to process 100 micrographs. 2D classification was performed with 50 classes using a 130 Å mask to classify the good picks from noise/ice picks resulting in a selection of 15,612 particles to train a TOPAZ model( 3 ). TOPAZ was then used to particle pick 3,753 micrographs, resulting in 1.1 M picked particles. Particles were extracted with a box size of 256 px and binned at 4 pixels. A single round of 2D classification was performed to remove 200 k junk particle picks (overlapping particles, vitreous ice). Three ab initio models were generated and subjected to multiple, iterative rounds of heterogenous refinement, homogeneous refinement, and 2D classification to remove particles that resulted in low-resolution reconstructions. A final set of 91,038 particles were extracted with a box size of 256 pixels, and subjected to homogenous refinement with C6 symmetry, giving way to a map with a resolution of 4.56 Å, and a subsequent nonuniform C6 symmetry refinement that resulted in a map with a global resolution of 4.24 Å ( 68 ). For holo dTRAP, Blob Picking was used with a min/max particle diameter of 90/110 Å to pick 30 micrographs. 2D classification was performed with 50 classes using a 140 Å mask to classify the good picks from noise/ice picks resulting in a selection of 7,849 particles that were used as templates to pick 2.3 M “particles”. Three rounds of 2D classification were used to remove junk particle picks and produce a set of 612,271 particles that were then extracted with a box size of 256 px and binned at 4 pixels. Four ab initio models were generated and subjected to multiple rounds of heterogenous refinement, homogeneous refinement, and 2D classification to remove particles that resulted in low-resolution reconstructions. A final set of 104,714 particles were extracted with a box size of 256 pixels, subjected to homogenous refinement with C6 symmetry giving way to a map with a resolution of 4.30 Å, and a subsequent nonuniform with C6 symmetry refinement that resulted in a map with a global resolution of 3.6 Å ( 68 ) For holo WT-Mut dTRAP, we performed data processing using CryoSPARC v3.2.0 ( 67 ). Movies were imported and aligned using patch motion correction with an applied B-factor of 500, a maximum alignment resolution of 5 Å. Patch CTF estimation was performed with a maximum resolution of 4 Å. Manual curation of micrographs was used to remove any micrographs that had a CTF resolution estimation >5 Å and total motion >100 Å. After curation, Blob Picking was used with a min/max particle diameter of 90/110 Å to pick 2.5 M particles. 2D classifications were performed with 50 classes using a 140 Å mask to classify the good picks from noise/ice picks resulting in a selection of 402 K particles that were used as template to pick 2.7 M particles. Seven rounds of 2D classification were used to remove junk particle picks and produced a set of 182,939 particles that were then extracted with a box size of 256 px and binned at 4 px. Three ab initio models were generated and subjected to multiple rounds of heterogenous refinement and homogenous refinement followed by another three rounds of 2D classification to remove particles that resulted in low-resolution reconstructions. A final set of 46,244 particles were extracted and subjected to multiple rounds of nonuniform refinement and local refinement generating a map with a resolution of 4.14 Å. Reconstructed volumes of each cryoEM maps generated using a nominal pixel size of 0.899 Å were expanded by ~6% in comparison to those expected from the crystal structure of Aha TRAP (PDB ID 3ZZL) ( 28 ), and from the cryo-EM volumes of dodecameric rings in engineered cages (EMD-17195) ( 18 ). Examination of data from an Apoferretin standard resulted in recalibration of the pixel scale 0.858 Å/px. The maps were then rescaled accordingly using ChimeraX ( www.cgl.ucsf.edu/chimerax ).

sections.title: Cryo-EM Model Building.
sections.text: For both apo and holo dTRAP, the Rosetta-designed dTRAP model was used as a starting model. The C6 reconstructed map and initial model were used to refine a linked dTRAP protomer using multiple iterations of Coot, ISOLDE, and PHENIX Real Space Refinement ( 51 – 54 ). Secondary structures were restrained during PHENIX real space refinement automatically using the HELIX/SHEET records from the crystal structure of Aha TRAP (PDB ID 3ZZL). Upon convergence of the model with the map, the map symmetry tool in Phenix was used to determine the NCS operators and to generate the other asymmetric units. For Trp-loaded WT-Mut dTRAP, the Cryo-EM structure of holo dTRAP was used as a starting model. The C6 symmetry reconstructed map and initial model were used to refine a single linked dimer using multiple iterations of ISOLDE and Phenix Real Space Refinement ( 6 – 8 ). The last five rounds of iterations were performed using the full dTRAP ring constructed using the apply NCS operators’ tool by PHENIX so that the interface between the protomers is properly modeled.

Protein Structure & Enzyme Engineering.title: Strategic Optimization of the Middle Domain IIIA in RBP-Albumin IIIA-IB Fusion Protein to Enhance Productivity and Thermostability
Protein Structure & Enzyme Engineering.abstract: The protein therapeutics market, including antibody and fusion proteins, has experienced steady growth over the past decade, underscoring the importance of optimizing amino acid sequences. In our previous study, we developed a fusion protein, R31, which combines retinol-binding protein (RBP) with albumin domains IIIA and IB, linked by a sequence (AAAA), and includes an additional disulfide bond (N227C-V254C) in IIIA. This fusion protein effectively inhibited hepatic stellate cell activation. In this study, we further optimized the sequence. The G176K mutation at the C-terminus of RBP altered the initiation site of the first α-helix in domain IIIA, shifting it from P182 to K176, and promoted polar interactions between K176 and adjacent residues, enhancing the rigidity of the RBP/IIIA interface. The introduction of an additional disulfide bond (V231C/Y250C) connecting helices 3 and 4 in IIIA resulted in a three-fold increase in productivity and a 2 °C improvement in thermal stability compared to R31. Furthermore, combining the G176K mutation with V231C/Y250C further enhanced both productivity and anti-fibrotic activity. These findings suggest that the enhanced stability of domain IIIA, conferred by V231C/Y250C, along with the increased rigidity of the RBP/IIIA interface, optimizes interdomain distance and alignment, facilitating proper protein folding.
