sections.title: Large-Scale Production in Pichia pastoris and Biochemical Characterization
sections.text:
To benchmark the different
variants, we transferred them from E. coli to P. pastoris (recently reclassified
as Komagataella phaffii ). P. pastoris can reach high cell densities in simple
media of up to 130 g L –1 of dry cell weight, favoring
upscale production of enzymes in a fed-batch bioreactor. Moreover,
it can readily perform appropriate post-translational modifications
and it streamlines any downstream processing due to its ability to
secrete heterologous proteins into the culture broth. 24 Accordingly, M-RQW, EvoPROSS, ancestral node 45, and SarLacc
were cloned and overproduced in this yeast. The expression of M-RQW
in E. coli is roughly 10 mg/L but when
we cloned this variant in P. pastoris , its yield increased strikingly up to ∼160 mg/L in shaking
flask production, c.a. 16-fold higher than its expression in bacteria,
whereas the in-flask production of EvoPROSS and ancestral node 45
was 262 and 41 mg/L, respectively. As such, ASR achieved notable levels
of heterologous GOase secretion without the need for a directed evolution
campaign targeting expression. 3 Similarly,
PROSS increased expression ∼1.7-fold through a single shot
of computational mutagenesis. When compared with node 45, the final
SarLacc mutant boosted expression to 173 mg/L, a clear consequence
of introducing the EvoPROSS mutations into the ancestral GOase scaffold
( Table 1 ). To determine whether the P. pastoris variants could be useful for future production
upscaling, we ran
a large fermentation of M-RQW in a 10 L fed-batch bioreactor. Without
any optimization of the fermentation parameters, 0.8 g/L production
was achieved, placing our P. pastoris recombinant GOases in a good position for future industrial purposes
( Figure S4 ). Subsequently, the P. pastoris variants were purified to homogeneity
by IMAC ( Figure S5 ) and their main biochemical
properties were assessed ( Table 1 ). In terms of glycosylation, the M-RQW and EvoPROSS
variants expressed
by P. pastoris showed a similar degree
of glycosylation to that from the original fungus, yet glycosylation
of ancestral node 45 and SarLacc was enhanced to ∼10%. It is
highly likely that new glycosylation sites have been generated among
the common ancestral mutations present in these two mutants. Indeed,
the GlycoEP server predicted three new N -glycosylation
sites in the ASR and SarLacc variants (Asn36, Asn55, and Asn344; https://webs.iiitd.edu.in/raghava/glycoep/index.html ). All in all, the degree of glycosylation remained low, as expected
for recombinant proteins expressed in P. pastoris , which may facilitate future protein crystallization studies. Kinetic thermostability was determined by measuring the T 50 values, defined as the temperature at which
the enzyme retains 50% of its activity after a 10 min incubation ( Table 1 , Figure S6 ). The T 50 values were
node 45 > SarLacc > EvoPROSS, given the 27, 13, and 8 °C
increase
in thermostability relative to M-RQW, respectively. The pH-dependent
stability over the course of 10 days was measured, with all of the
enzymes being stable in the pH range from 5.0 to 9.0 ( Figure S7 ). Initial turnover rates for galactose
and glucose were measured and as seen during the screenings, the ancestral
node had the highest activity on galactose of the entire enzyme panel
(55 U/mg), yet it lacked activity against glucose. By contrast, both
the EvoPROSS and SarLacc mutants had similar turnover rates for galactose
and glucose, the latter 2-fold higher than that of the parental M-RQW
( Table 1 ). When
M-RQW was engineered to unlock its activity on glucose, it
also showed unexpected latent activities for secondary alcohols that
has been the subject of study for years. 5 , 6 Accordingly,
we benchmarked our ensemble of variants against a representative set
of primary and secondary aromatic alcohols with different degrees
of bulkiness. Reactions with benzyl alcohol ( 1 ), 1-phenylethanol
( 2 ), 1-phenylpropanol ( 3 ), 1-phenylbutanol
( 4 ), 1-phenylpentanol ( 5 ), alpha-tetralol
( 6 ), and diphenylmethanol ( 7 ) were carried
out and analyzed by HPLC-MS ( Figure 3 , Table S5 ). Regardless
of the compound tested, the best conversions were produced by SarLacc.
In good agreement with previous M-RQW studies, 4 − 6 reactions with
primary alcohol ( 1 ) achieved up to 94–96% conversion
to benzaldehyde ( Figure 3 , Figure S8 ). There was greater or lesser
latent activity of the mutants when assayed with secondary alcohols
containing different alkyl chains ( 2 ) to ( 5 ). Parental M-RQW converted 13% of ( 2 ) into the corresponding
ketone, with SarLacc achieving conversions up to 82% under the same
reaction conditions ( Figures 3 and S9 ). Conversion became weaker as the
length of the alkyl chain increased
from ( 3 ) through to ( 5 ), yet SarLacc did
show latent activity with conversions ranging from 8 to 2% ( Figures 3 and S10–S12 ). Although cyclization of the
alkane substitution into alpha-tetralol ( 6 ) produced
a bulkier substrate, all four GOase variants were more active on this
compound than on its aliphatic counterpart ( 5 ), with
conversions up to 31% for the SarLacc mutant ( Figure 3 ). With the bulkiest substrate ( 7 ), the mutants showed a similar trend as with ( 6 ) but
offering much lower conversion rates ( Figures 3 , S13, and S14 ). In summary, our results indicate the substrate-binding plasticity
of the GOase variants in terms of accommodation of bulky aromatic
alcohols, although this plasticity does not extend to that of long
aliphatic side chains.

sections.title: Mutational Analysis of GOase Variants
sections.text:
At the structural
level, GOase belongs to the group of β-folded proteins, and
it is composed of three domains. The domain I (residues 1–155)
adopts a β-sandwich structure, also known as the carbohydrate
binding domain (CBD), which is folded by two β-sheets disposed
one over the other one, each of them being formed of four β-strands
connected in antiparallel orientation. The domain I plays a crucial
role not only in facilitating substrate recognition but also in ensuring
the proper folding of domain II, as its removal renders a nonfunctional
enzyme. The domain II (residues 156–532) features a Kelch-like
structural motif folded as a 7-fold β-propeller arrangement
and attaches the cupric ion by three (Y495, H496, and Y272) of the
four coordinating ligands. Finally, the domain III (residues 533–639)
is characterized by an immunoglobulin-like (Ig) module, which carries
the fourth coordinating ligand (H581) in an antiparallel β-ribbon
that pierces domain II for a characteristic copper coordination. 25 With over 25% of substitutions relative to GOase
wt in the entire protein, the mutations in SarLacc are distributed
across the three domains so that any epistatic effect between the
mutations is complicated to interpret ( Table S4 ). We can only speculate that the biochemical properties of our mutants
might be modulated by the structural packaging of the individual domains,
perhaps improving the interactions between each of them to different
extents, influencing expression, stability, and reactivity ( Figure 4 ). For instance, of the 28 mutations from the PROSS campaign, only
6 mutations were located in β-strands, while the remaining substitutions
were situated in disordered loop regions ( Figure S15 ). The mutations that reside in these loop areas could potentially
restructure these disordered fragments, facilitating the overall folding
of the enzyme by enhancing the conformational flexibility. This effect
could explain the strong expression of EvoPROSS in yeast, reaching
secretion levels as high as 262 mg/L in the flask fermentation. By
contrast, 37 of the 151 ancestral mutations in node 45 are located
in β-strands ( Figure S15 ), which
might be responsible for the strong increase in thermostability (27
°C in T 50 ) in our study. Mutations
in β-strands could have a dual effect on thermostability by
(i) reinforcing the intramolecular hydrophobic interactions of the
β-strand and (ii) enhancing intermolecular packaging of close
β-strands. Indeed, the number of hydrophobic residues in the
GOase variants increased from 309 in M-RQW, to 315 in EvoPROSS, 322
in node 45, and 326 in SarLacc. The major effect of increasing the
hydrophobic amino acid content was attributed to the addition of Pro
residues from 41 in M-RQW to 51 in SarLacc, lowering the protein backbone
entropy by restricting the conformations of neighboring residues. 26

sections.title: Conclusions
sections.text:
The stereoselectivity
and promiscuity of the M-RQW GOase variant
reflects its strong potential in green chemistry, as demonstrated
in previous studies assessing the kinetic resolution of benzylic and
alkylic secondary alcohols to the transformation of renewable chemicals. 5 , 6 , 30 M-RQW is a highly versatile enzyme
that can be immobilized onto biosensors in order to monitor glucose
or galactose. This variant has the advantage that it can be switched
on/off given that its active state involves a tyrosyl radical that
can be fully oxidized for functionality or that can be turned off
upon reduction. 29 For all these applications,
thermostable GOases with endurance for longer operations and more
promiscuous activities are needed that can be produced in industrially
relevant hosts. Here, we engineered strongly secreted and thermostable
GOases variants with latent activities by bringing together directed
evolution with PROSS computational mutagenesis and ASR. Stabilizing
mutations from the directed evolution campaign on M-RQW were recombined
into the most stable PROSS design, and in parallel, ASR was performed
to generate functionally expressed ancestral nodes carrying over 100
ancestral mutations. The final convergence of directed evolution,
PROSS, and ASR allowed us to design hybrid GOases, the mutations of
which seem to influence structural packaging of the different protein
domains. From a general perspective, directed enzyme evolution
is, beyond
a doubt, the most successful approach for protein engineering known
to date. We are witnessing the advent of computational methods led
by artificial intelligence, whereby the construction and exploration
of mutant libraries is becoming more and more efficient aimed at achieving
the “holy grail” of enzyme engineers, that is, the function
global fitness optima. 31 Our study sought
to enhance the sequence and functional diversity of GOase by incorporating
in the directed evolution workflow PROSS mutagenesis and ASR. With
this strategy, we generated GOase designs that are readily expressed
by P. pastoris on a g/L scale in a
fed-batch bioreactor, showing an ensemble of biochemical properties,
with good stability at high temperatures and across a range of pHs,
with latent activities, all features that make them useful tools for
organic synthesis and biosensing applications. Indeed, our results
agree well with previous studies, highlighting the significance of
PROSS and ASR to produce suitable candidates with which to start a
directed evolution campaign or to be added to the workflow of a lab
evolution experiment. 10 − 20 , 22 , 23

Cancer Biology & Oncology.title: Multifunctional Nanovaccine Sensitizes Breast Cancer to Immune Checkpoint Therapy
Cancer Biology & Oncology.abstract: AbstractBreast cancer is the primary cause of cancer‐related death in women worldwide. Breast cancer subtypes are characterized by different gene expression patterns, which drive their prognostic factors and therapeutic options. Among them, triple‐negative breast cancer (TNBC) is one of the deadliest due to its aggressiveness, high rate of early recurrence and distant metastases, and limited therapeutic options. Despite the recent approval of monoclonal antibodies targeting programmed cell death protein 1 (PD‐1) or its ligand (PD‐L1) for the treatment of TNBC patients with a locally recurrent unresectable or metastatic tumor expressing PD‐L1, their response rate is very modest. It is reported that polymeric nanoparticle (NP)‐based cancer vaccines, co‐entrapping tumor‐associated antigens, Toll‐like receptor ligands and small interfering RNA (siRNA) targeting the expression of the immunosuppressive cytokine transforming growth factor (TGF)‐β1 by dendritic cells, sensitized TNBC to the agonist immune checkpoint OX40, inhibiting tumor growth and increasing overall survival. This anti‐tumor immune‐mediated effect is also observed in a luminal type of mammary cancer similar to human disease. Therefore, these synergistic anticancer effects of αOX40 and the antigen‐specific adaptive immunity induced by nanovaccine‐mediated TGF‐β silencing may guide the development of novel combination regimens able to improve the response rate to this aggressive tumor.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.text: 1 Breast cancer is a multifactorial disease, which incidence is expected to increase by 40% in 2040. [ 1 ] Among the different breast cancer subtypes, triple‐negative breast cancer (TNBC) is the most aggressive, and accounts for 15% to 20% of all breast cancer cases, being typically observed in young women. [ 2 ] Since TNBC does not express hormone receptors nor the human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2), [ 2 ] the effective therapeutic options available are very limited. Advances in immunotherapy, notably immune checkpoint modulators (ICM), have improved patient prognosis in various cancer types. [ 3 ] Compared to other breast cancer subtypes, TNBC is more susceptible to immunotherapy, as it presents a higher number of tumor‐infiltrating lymphocytes (TIL), as well as higher genomic instability and tumor mutational burden, [ 4 ] which gives rise to a greater number of tumor neoantigens with the potential to trigger stronger and specific anti‐tumor immune responses. [ 5 ] Despite the recent approval of two monoclonal antibodies (mAb) targeting programmed cell death‐1 (PD‐1) (pembrolizumab) and its ligand PD‐L1 (atezolizumab) for the treatment of TNBC patients with locally recurrent unresectable or metastatic tumor expressing PD‐L1, primary resistance (as well as adverse events) occurs in most patients. [ 6 ] Thus, although a durable response has been observed in early‐phase trials in patients treated with mAb targeting PD‐1 or PD‐L1, the response rate of TNBC patients is very modest: only 10% in unselected TNBC patients and 20% to 30% in patients with TNBC expressing PD‐L1 (ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT02447003 , NCT01772004 , NCT01848834 , NCT01375842 ). Luminal B‐like breast cancers are characterized by low TIL and low mutational burden. However, some strategies aiming the T‐cell priming via the activation of antigen‐specific dendritic cells (DC), for example using radiation, are ongoing to improve T‐cells' infiltration and therefore the response to immune checkpoint inhibitors. [ 7 ] Besides the strategy of blocking inhibitory T‐cell pathways, T‐cell co‐stimulation via OX40 has also attracted broad interest as a therapeutic target in TNBC. [ 8 ] This co‐stimulatory receptor is transiently expressed on activated T cells, while its ligand OX40L is expressed on antigen‐presenting cells (APC), endothelial cells (EC), and activated T cells. Upon activation, OX40 promotes T‐cell expansion, trafficking, and survival, and elevated pro‐inflammatory cytokine production. [ 9 ] In addition, OX40‐signaling can also block the inhibitory activity of tumor‐infiltrating regulatory T cells (Treg) by hindering Forkhead box protein P3 (FoxP3), transforming growth factor‐β (TGF‐β) and interleukin (IL)−10 signaling, related to an immunosuppressive tumor milieu. [ 10 ] Moreover, OX40‐stimulated Treg was also reported to present a Th1 effector phenotype through the production of IFN‐ɣ, TNF‐α, and granzyme B. [ 11 ] Despite the initial enthusiasm, agonistic mAb targeting OX40 were later found to be related to conflicting results and controversies between in vitro and in vivo studies. [ 10a ] Moreover, high interpatient variability and immune‐related side effects have been reported in cancer patients, [ 12 ] which have so far limited their approval by regulatory agencies. Nevertheless, combinational strategies with other immunotherapies, such as ICM, [ 13 ] cytokines, [ 14 ] and cancer vaccines, [ 15 ] have been shown to minimize these drawbacks and improve therapeutic outcomes. Preclinical studies in TNBC‐bearing mice report that cancer vaccines sensitized the tumor to the agonist OX40. Malamas and co‐authors reported that the addition of a poxvirus‐based cancer vaccine, incorporating transgenes for the tumor antigen Twist and a triad of costimulatory molecules to an OX40L fusion protein agonist impaired tumor metastasis by inducing T‐cell expansion and memory formation, which improved the overall survival of TNBC 4T1‐bearing mice. [ 16 ] Similar results were reported following the combination of anti‐DEC‐205‐HER2 mAb/Poly(I:C)) with anti‐OX40 (αOX40)/anti‐cytotoxic T lymphocyte‐associated antigen 4 (ɑCTLA‐4). This combinational immunotherapy increased the anti‐tumor CD8 + T‐cell function while reducing Th2 polarization in CD4 + T cells, induced extensive tumor destruction, and improved the overall survival in mice bearing established HER2‐expressing mammary carcinoma. [ 15a ] Cancer vaccines take advantage of the host immune system to induce antigen‐directed cell death while generating a memory response to prevent metastasis and disease progression. Although cancer vaccines have been greatly improved, most of them have failed so far in providing clinical benefits as monotherapy in patients with advanced cancers. This can be explained by several immune escape mechanisms developed by tumors, which include the recruitment of immunosuppressive cells, such as Treg and myeloid‐derived suppressor cells (MDSC), and the overexpression of potent inhibitory molecules, such as the cytokine TGF‐β1 and inhibitory checkpoint molecules, such as CTLA‐4 and PD‐1, leading to an ineffective anti‐tumor immune response. [ 17 ] Considering the multiple immune suppressive mechanisms hindering the efficacy of anti‐tumor approaches, combinational strategies should be devised to take advantage of agents with synergistic mechanisms of action, while avoiding the common increase in adverse effects. Based on these observations, we hypothesized that a nanovaccine able to activate DC through the combined delivery of a breast tumor‐associated antigen (TAA), Toll‐like receptor (TLR), and stimulator of interferon genes (STING) ligands, in addition to silencing TGF‐β1 expression by DC and tumor cells, which are the main producers of this immune suppressive cytokine, could re‐shape the tumor microenvironment (TME), sensitizing TNBC to the agonist immune checkpoint OX40, and thus, improving the overall anti‐tumor immune response. This nano‐immunotherapy combining a nanovaccine with the mAb αOX40 could therefore potentiate key steps in the cancer‐immune cycle by targeting the peripheral and tumor‐infiltrating immune cells. Moreover, the anti‐tumor immune‐mediated effect induced by this combinational nanotechnology‐based immunotherapy could also improve the response of luminal B‐like breast cancer to immunotherapy and thereby provide important insights into the development of this type of cancer treatment in this disease context. Here, we report the preparation and characterization of a biodegradable multifunctional vaccine based on poly(lactic acid) (PLA) nanoparticles (NP) able to co‐deliver in vivo breast cancer‐associated antigens, TLR ligands and small interfering RNA (siRNA) targeting TGF‐β1 (siTGF‐β1). We demonstrate the synergistic anti‐tumor effect of combined αOX40 and this NP‐based vaccine, which halted tumor growth and improved overall survival, in two different mouse models of breast cancer, TNBC and luminal B‐like breast cancer.

sections.title: Multifunctional Poly(Lactic Acid) (PLA)‐Based Nanoparticle (NP) Co‐Entraps Tumor‐Associated Protein or Peptide Antigens and Oligonucleotides
sections.text: 2 The first step in the development of the multifunctional NP consisted of preparing polyplexes to enable the entrapment and subsequent release of the siTGF‐β1. The interaction between the positively charged chitosan backbone and the negatively charged siRNA leads to the spontaneous formation of stable polyplexes in the aqueous milieu. [ 18 ] Accordingly, three different water‐soluble chitosan (Cs) derivatives – glycol chitosan (GCs), glutamate chitosan (GlutCs), and hydrochloride chitosan (HCCs) – were used at two different Cs‐siRNA ratios (5:1 and 15:1 (m/m)) to prepare the polymer‐siTGF‐β1 complexes by electrostatic‐based interactions. Cs‐siTGF‐β1 polyplexes were analyzed by electrophoresis on an electrophoretic mobility shift assay (EMSA) to select the Cs‐siRNA ratio with the highest ability to retard the siTGF‐β1 mobility on the agarose gel, using free siTGF‐β1 as control. While GCs did not complex with the siRNA, GlutCs and HCCs efficiently retained the siRNA with an optimal Cs‐siRNA ratio of 15:1 (m/m) (Figure S1a , Supporting Information). Although both GlutCs and HCCs were found to complex efficiently the oligonucleotides at a Cs‐siRNA of 15:1 (m/m), GlutCs was chosen for nanovaccine preparation since it has been related to a higher post‐transfection gene silencing effect, when compared to HCCs. [ 18 , 19 ] PLA NP was prepared by a double emulsion solvent evaporation method, using block co‐polymer Pluronic F‐127 (PF127) as an external aqueous phase surfactant, in addition to hyaluronic acid (HA) to modify NP surface. NP formulation was optimized to enable the incorporation of combinations of TLR ligands, siTGF‐β1, and antigens with distinct physicochemical properties, namely the proteins Ovalbumin (OVA) (NP1_OVA) and α‐Lactalbumin (NP1_α‐Lac), and the KRAS Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) class II‐restricted peptide antigen (NP1_KRAS) ( Figure 1 a ). While OVA was used as a model antigen, ɑ‐Lac and KRAS peptide were used as TAA. Although α‐Lac is expressed in healthy breast tissue during late pregnancy and lactation, this protein is also expressed at high levels in the vast majority of TNBC cases. [ 20 ] Surprisingly, Tuohy et al. [ 20 ] showed that prophylactic vaccination of adult women against α‐Lac provided a substantial pro‐inflammatory T‐cell response against human α‐Lac, which protected against the development of breast cancer. Moreover, it has also been demonstrated that a history of lactation and breastfeeding had no impact on the α‐Lac‐induced immunity. [ 20 ] In our study, we take advantage of α‐Lac entrapment in a nanosystem to develop an anti‐tumor immune‐mediated therapy for breast cancer. KRAS signaling is related to cancer progression in a variety of cancer entities. [ 21 ] Little is known about its role in breast cancer. Although <2% of breast cancer cases present KRAS mutations, [ 22 ] wild‐type KRAS expression is amplified in over 30% of basal‐like breast cancer/TNBC. [ 23 ] In our study, KRAS is explored as a potential antigen delivered by a nanosystem to modulate host anti‐tumor immunity against breast cancer. NP presented an average hydrodynamic diameter close to 200 nm (185 ± 5 nm to 202 ± 8 nm), with a low polydispersity index (PdI) (0.06 ± 0.02 to 0.17 ± 0.09), and a near‐neutral surface charge (−2.89 ± 0.62 mV to −1.08 ± 0.43) (Table S1 , Supporting Information). NP presenting these average diameters and narrow PdI values are suitable for the trafficking of these nanosystems through the lymphatic drainage directly to the lymphoid organs, [ 24 ] while a surface charge (ZP) close to neutrality prevents their premature extensive phagocytosis by macrophages in circulation. The size, shape, and surface morphology of NP were also assessed by atomic force microscopy (AFM). The section analysis of NP revealed a homogenous spherical shape with a slightly rough surface and a diameter close to 190 nm, which correlates with dynamic light scattering (DLS) measurements (Figure 1b ; Figure S1b , Supporting Information). The stability of NP was inferred considering the changes in the carrier size (mean diameter and PdI) and ZP observed for 84 days following NP resuspension in phosphate‐buffered saline (PBS, pH 7.4) and storage at 4 and 25 °C. During this period, no significant changes were observed for all three parameters, at both storage conditions (Figure S2a , Supporting Information). NP presented high levels of entrapment efficiency (EE) and loading capacity (LC) for all biomolecules (Table S2 ). NP was able to co‐entrap whole proteins (α‐Lac and OVA), peptides (KRAS MHC class II‐restricted), TLR ligands (CpG oligodeoxynucleotides (CpG‐ODN), and Polyinosinic:polycytidylic acid (Poly(I:C)), and siRNA molecules with high EE and LC values. EE values of at least 81.7% ± 5.7% and LC of 40.9 ± 2.9 µg∙mg −1 were obtained for whole proteins (α‐Lac and OVA), whereas EE values of 64.4% ± 1.3% and LC of 32.2 ± 0.6 µg∙mg −1 were obtained for KRAS MHC class II‐restricted peptide. Regarding the entrapment of oligonucleotides, NP presented an EE >91.5% ± 3.7% for siTGF‐β1 (LC values of 0.9 ± 0 µg∙mg −1 ), and 92.1% ± 0.7% for the TLR ligands, CpG‐ODN and Poly(I:C) (LC < 7.9 ± 0 µg∙mg −1 ). NP preparation method did not affect the structure of the protein entrapped, which is fundamental to inducing the specific and desired immune response, as a single band was obtained at a molecular weight similar to the one presented by the protein standard solution (Figure S2b , Supporting Information). NP entrapping Alexa Fluor 647‐OVA showed a sustained antigen release over 22% (m/m), 33% (m/m), and 72% (m/m) released after 1, 3, and 4 weeks of incubation in the medium at 37 °C, under gentle stirring, respectively (Figure S2c , Supporting Information). This prolonged antigen release overtime is highly desired in vaccination since it has been shown to elicit more efficiently antigen‐specific immune responses and activate cytotoxic T lymphocyte cells (CTL) and immune memory cells in vivo, reducing or even eliminating the need for booster immunizations. [ 25 ]

sections.title: Multifunctional Nanovaccines Activate and Improve Dendritic Cell Activation and Maturation
sections.text: 3 An AlamarBlue assay was performed to determine the effect of NP on the viability of DC (murine immature JAWSII cell line and primary murine bone marrow‐derived DC (BMDC)) and mammary carcinoma cell line 4T1. Cells were incubated with increasing concentrations (250 to 1000 µg mL −1 ) of NP, for 48 h. NP did not affect the viability of DC (JAWSII (> 94%), BMDC (> 80%)) nor 4T1 breast cancer cells (> 91%), in the concentration range tested, which supports their physiological biocompatibility (Figure 1c ). NP were extensively internalized by DC (JAWSII and BMDC) (in vitro and ex vivo) and 4T1 breast mammary carcinoma cells (in vitro) as demonstrated by flow cytometric analysis and confocal microscopy. DC and tumor cells were incubated with rhodamine (Rho)‐labeled NP for 3, 12, and 24 h (Figure 1d ). NP highest internalization levels were achieved after 12 h of incubation for JAWSII cell line and 4T1 tumor cells, and after 3 h of incubation for BMDC. When compared with the most used surfactant for NP preparation, [ 26 ] polyvinyl alcohol (PVA), NP stabilized by PF127 showed a higher and faster internalization by DC and tumor cells, than the ones prepared using PVA (Figure S3a , Supporting Information). NP internalization by tumor cells is per Menon et al., [ 27 ] where the authors attest that cancer cells internalized more poly(lactic‐co‐glycolic) acid (PLGA) NP coated with PF127 than the ones coated with PVA. Additionally, despite being the most well‐known and the most used surfactant in the formulation of polymeric NP, [ 26 ] diverse side effects have been reported for PVA, namely hypertension, organ lesions, anemia, and depression of the central nervous system, upon subcutaneous (s.c.) and intravenous administration in vivo. [ 28 ] NP synthesized using PF127 as a surfactant and coated with HA were taken up by DC and breast tumor cells at a higher extent than NP containing only HA ( P = 0.0001 in JAWSII DC and P < 0.0001 in BMDC and 4T1) or PF127 ( P < 0.0001 in BMDC and 4T1) (Figure S3a , Supporting Information). As expected, the modification of the NP surface with HA also improved their ability to be taken up by tumor cells, when compared with the other NP formulations ( P < 0.0001). This can be explained by the fact that HA is a targeting moiety specifically recognized by the receptor CD44, which is overexpressed on several tumor cell surfaces, including breast cancer cell lines, such as 4T1 [ 29 ] and EO771. [ 29 , 30 ] Upon encountering tumor cells, these NP are internalized via HA‐CD44 interaction. We further demonstrated that the formation of the complex GlutCs‐siTGF‐β1 was required to decrease the expression of this cytokine at both mRNA ( P = 0.0439) and protein ( P = 0.0188) levels when compared to NP without previous complexation with GlutCs (NP‐siRNA)) internalized by 4T1 cells (Figure S3b , Supporting Information). The immature DC also internalized NP modified with HA at a higher extent than the other NP ( P < 0.0001). Although there is no evidence in the literature that HA may target DC, Do et al. [ 31 ] revealed that HA induced the activation of DC, markedly enhancing their ability to stimulate allogeneic and antigen‐specific T cells. Therefore, NP synthesized using PF127 as a surfactant and modified with HA were selected for further studies. Cy5‐labeled NP were prepared to assess the internalization pattern of NP by immature JAWSII DC by confocal microscopy. Z ‐stacks and maximum projections showed that the optimized NP were effectively internalized by DC and the internalization levels increased with incubation time until 24 h, being the highest internalization extent obtained after 12 h of incubation (Figure 1e ). These results corroborated the ones obtained by the flow cytometric analysis. To assess the ability of NP (empty or entrapping antigen and/or immune modulators) to induce the maturation of primary BMDC, a flow cytometric analysis of the expression of costimulatory molecules (CD40, CD80, and CD86) in the CD11b + CD11c + MHCII + cell population was performed after 48 h of incubation. PBS and lipopolysaccharide (LPS)‐treated cells were used as negative and positive controls, respectively. Free α‐Lac, and α‐Lac + TLR ligands (CpG‐ODN and Poly(I:C)) were also tested. The highest levels for each surface costimulatory molecule were obtained for primary BMDC treated with NP entrapping α‐Lac and both adjuvants (Figure S3c , Supporting Information). When entrapping the antigen only, NP did not increase costimulatory molecule expression to the same extent (Figure S3c , Supporting Information), pointing out the added value of having both the tumor antigen and the TLR ligands entrapped within the same NP. Chitosan has been reported as a vaccine adjuvant able to induce DC maturation and trigger Th1 responses by engaging the STING pathway. [ 32 ] In addition, CpG‐ODN and Poly(I:C) are TLR ligands, also reported to be potent Th1‐inducing immunoadjuvants. [ 33 ] Recently, Poly(I:C) was shown to stimulate specialized DC subsets that are involved in the cross‐presentation of antigens to CTL precursors in humans, known as BATF3‐dependent, CD141 + DC (known as CD103 + in mice). [ 34 ] CpG‐ODN and Poly(I:C) receptors, TLR9 and TLR3 respectively, are both localized in the endosomal membrane where NP can easily get access, upon internalization by DC. [ 35 ] When both TLR ligands are successfully delivered to the same DC, these biomolecules may present a synergistic effect by potentiating the efficient maturation of these APC toward balanced Th1‐ and Th2‐type immune responses, which have a crucial role in controlling homeostasis within tumor site. [ 36 ] The internalization pattern of NP by immature DC was also assessed in vivo by flow cytometric analysis, following NP hock subcutaneous (s.c.) administration. NP were internalized by APC, especially by macrophages (CD11b + CD11c − ) and DC (CD11c + CD11b + ), 17 h after C57BL/6J mice immunization with Cy5‐labeled NP (Figure 1f ). To assess the ability of NP to induce the maturation of primary APC, a flow cytometric analysis of the expression of costimulatory molecules (CD40, CD80, CD86) in the activated DC population (CD11c + CD11b + MHCII + ) was performed after 17 h of incubation. Lymph node cells collected from animals treated with the NP entrapping KRAS peptide and TLR ligands (CpG and Poly(I:C)) presented higher levels of CD86 titers, when compared with PBS‐treated group and mice treated with the vaccine biomolecules free in solution ( P = 0.0002 and P < 0.0001, respectively) (Figure 1g ). Overall, the co‐entrapment of the antigen and both CpG and Poly(I:C) TLR agonists in a single polymeric matrix showed to be relevant for the efficient activation and maturation of DC since an increase in the stimulatory molecules’ expression was observed, in contrast with their levels upon incubation with the biomolecules free in solution, ex vivo in BMDC or injected subcutaneously in mice. The efficient activation of those APC is crucial for priming naïve T cells, and the consequent induction of tumor‐specific T‐cell responses. [ 37 ] The ex vivo images of dissected organs (liver, spleen, kidneys, heart, lungs, and inguinal lymph nodes) showed a fluorescent signal in the inguinal lymph nodes recovered from the side of mice injected s.c. with Cy5‐labeled NP, in contrast to the one recovered from the side injected with PBS. Moreover, no fluorescent signal was detected in any other organ (Figure S4 , Supporting Information). This data shows that when injected s.c. by hock immunization, the optimized nanosystem remained near the local of injection, which may explain the obtained preferential accumulation of the NP in the lymph nodes, which is critical for the induction of antigen‐specific adaptive immune responses and vaccine efficacy. [ 38 ]
path: Multifunctional Nanovaccines Activate and Improve Dendritic Cell Activation and Maturation

sections.title: Synergistic Anti‐Tumor Effects Between αOX40 and Multifunctional Nanovaccine Targeting TGF‐β
sections.text: 4 To determine the anti‐tumor effect of this multifunctional nano‐based immunotherapy against TNBC, we administered three doses of NP, seven days apart, to a 4T1 TNBC mouse model and tested if the induced immune response would synergize with the agonist mAb αOX40. To test this hypothesis, 4T1‐bearing BALB/c mice were treated according to the dosing schedule described in Figure 2 a . The multifunctional nano‐based system was composed of two NP, one administered s.c. by hock immunization (NP1_ɑ‐Lac) and the other injected intratumorally (NP2). Both polymeric NP entrapped the TLR ligands CpG‐ODN and Poly(I:C), and the siTGF‐β1, with the addition of the TAA α‐Lac in the NP1. NP2 intratumoral (i.t.) injection aimed to modulate locally the function of tumor‐infiltrating immune cell sub‐populations, following the silencing of TGF‐β1 by tumor cells, in addition to T‐cell activation following the release of CpG and Poly(I:C), as previously demonstrated by administering these TLR ligands intratumorally in mice and humans affected with melanoma, [ 39 ] or with colorectal cancer. [ 40 ] Although the use of this administration route has been controversial in immunotherapy due to its limited application to solid accessible tumors, the i.t. administration has numerous advantages. [ 41 ] In our case, we can highlight the proximity of the siRNA molecules to their target to deplete the Treg population within the TME. Additionally, some studies have stated that the i.t. delivery of CpG alters the TME by improving the anti‐tumor activity of both innate and adaptive immune cells. Lou et al. showed that the direct activation of the targeted cells by these immune potentiators within the tumor promotes an extensive infiltration of tumor antigen‐specific T cells and Natural Killer (NK) cells, leading to tumor suppression in vivo. [ 42 ] More recently, Humbert et al. also referred to the inhibition of tumor growth upon i.t. injection of this TLR9 agonist. They also showed the ability of CpG to activate conventional DC, subsequently increasing anti‐tumor T‐cell priming at draining lymph nodes and enhancing the effector T‐cell infiltration within TME. [ 43 ] Poly(I:C) has also been shown to modulate the TME upon i.t. injection. Salmon et al. demonstrated that the i.t. administration of this TLR3 agonist avoids systemic toxicity, but also directly activates tumor‐resident classical DC (cDC)1 in mice. [ 43 ] Interestingly, among many innate immune receptors, TLR3 is expressed almost exclusively by mouse CD8α + cDC and CD103 + cDC [ 43 ] and human CD141 + cDC, [ 34 , 44 ] which excel in the priming and cross‐presentation of cell‐associated antigens to CD8 + T cells. [ 45 ] Hence, by delivering these immune modulators using a NP, we aim to protect them from early degradation and promote their continuous release in vivo. Besides enhancing the immune modulators' internalization by DC, this strategy further contributes to locally improving the expansion of effector T cells, while overcoming Treg‐mediated immunosuppression following the TGF‐β1 silencing. These facts support our interest in delivering these TLR agonists into the TME. A minimal reversible systemic toxicity was observed in the animals treated with the nano‐immunotherapy, reflected by slight body weight changes, which supports vaccine tolerability and safety (Figure S5a , Supporting Information). The tumor volume of the nano‐immunotherapy group (NP1_ɑ‐Lac + NP2 + ɑOX40) was substantially lower than the ones observed in all the other treatment groups ( P ≤ 0.001) (Figure 2b ; Figure S5b , Supporting Information). On day 22 after tumor inoculation, the average tumor volume of mouse groups treated with α‐Lac and immune modulators (siTGF‐β1, CpG‐ODN and Poly(I:C)) free in solution or the NP with siRNA negative control (n.c.) (NP1_ɑ‐Lac + NP2 (siRNA n.c)) were identical to the PBS‐treated group (Figure S5b , Supporting Information). Although mice treated with NP1_ɑ‐Lac and NP2 presented similar average tumor volumes ( P > 0.05), they were slightly lower than the ones obtained by the previously treated groups. Also, αOX40 treatment slightly decreased the average tumor volume when compared with the PBS‐treated group ( P = 0.0254). It is important to highlight that this group presented variable tumor volumes (Figure 2b ). The tumor volume of the animals treated with the NP alone (NP1_ɑ‐Lac + NP2) or combined with αOX40 (NP1_ɑ‐Lac + NP2 + αOX40) was significantly lower compared with the PBS‐treated group ( P = 0.0287 and P < 0.0001, respectively) (Figure S5b , Supporting Information). The tumor volume of the nano‐immunotherapy group (NP1_ɑ‐Lac + NP2 + ɑOX40) was more than fivefold smaller than the one presented by the PBS‐treated animals. Additionally, these immunized animals presented a long‐term survival: 50% (4 out of 8) of the animals treated with NP1_ɑ‐Lac + NP2 + αOX40 remained alive at day 35 after tumor inoculation, compared to the remaining treated groups ( P = 0.0019) (Figure 2c ). On day 19 after tumor inoculation, three animals from each treatment group were sacrificed and the main organs were recovered. The tumor mass from each animal was weighed. The tumor mass of animals treated with the multifunctional NP alone (NP1_ɑ‐Lac + NP2) or in combination with αOX40 (NP1_ɑ‐Lac + NP2 + αOX40) was significantly smaller than those presented by the PBS‐treated group ( P = 0.0322 and P = 0.0009, respectively) (Figure S5c , Supporting Information). Agonistic mAb ɑOX40 are currently being tested in three different clinical trials for the treatment of TNBC, in combination with other immune checkpoint modulators (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT03971409 , NCT02554812 , NCT03241173 ). Although tumor regression was obtained in several preclinical models, conflicting results and controversies between in vitro and in vivo data have been also observed. [ 10a ] Additionally, clinicians have reported some inconsistency in terms of patient response when treated with αOX40, as well as several side effects. [ 12 ] When combined with the nanovaccine, the immune response was not only improved by presenting lower variability in terms of tumor volumes of treated mice but also the αOX40‐related toxicity was reduced. Murine mammary carcinoma 4T1 is known to induce splenomegaly. [ 46 ] For this reason, the spleen was also recovered at day 19 after tumor inoculation from each animal and weighted, revealing a significant decrease in the group treated with NP1_ɑ‐Lac + NP2 + αOX40, when compared to the PBS‐treated group ( P = 0.0228) (Figure S5c , Supporting Information). Tumors recovered from animals also allowed to confirm the ability of the nanovaccine to downregulate TGF‐β1 expression. Both qRT‐PCR and immunoblotting analysis revealed a significant decrease of TGF‐β1 expression in the TME of mice treated with the nanovaccine compared to the PBS‐treated group (2.6‐fold and twofold, respectively) ( P = 0.0287 and P = 0.0008, respectively) (Figure S5d , Supporting Information). When analyzed by flow cytometry, the multifunctional nanovaccine combined with αOX40 stimulated T‐cell infiltration (Figure 2d ) into tumors at an early stage of the treatment (day 19), increasing CD4 + T cells (CD3 + CD4 + cells) (Figure 2e ), with no significant differences in the percentage of Treg (CD3 + CD4 + CD25 + FoxP3 + cells) (Figure S5e , Supporting Information), CD8 + T cells (CD3 + CD8 + cells) (Figure 2f ) expressing tumor necrosis factor (TNF)‐α, interferon (IFN)‐γ and IL‐12 (Figure 2g–i ), and CTL (CD3 + CD8 + CD107b + cells) (Figure 2j ). Additionally, an upregulation of PD‐1 expression in CD8 + T cells was observed in tumors treated with the nanovaccine combined with αOX40 (Figure 2k ). The antigen‐specific nature of the CD8 + T cell‐mediated immune response was also evaluated. Flow cytometric analysis showed that CD8 + T cells recovered from spleens of animals treated with the nanovaccine presented the highest expression of IFN‐γ, IL‐2, and TNF‐α, following their incubation with the specific antigen α‐Lac (Figure S5f , Supporting Information) when compared with the same sample incubated with PBS or with a non‐specific antigen (gp100). We also reported the impressive infiltration of migratory DC (Figure S5g , Supporting Information), monocyte‐derived DC (Figure S5h , Supporting Information), macrophages (Figure S5i , Supporting Information), and specially CD103 + cDC (Figure S5j , Supporting Information). The last excel at cross‐presenting exogenous antigens (e.g., tumor antigens) to CD8 + T cells and are critical for the generation of CTL responses. [ 47 ] However, 4T1‐bearing BALB/c mice also presented levels of tumor‐infiltrating MDSC (CD11b + Gr‐1 + ) (Figure 2l ) higher than those observed in tumors of animals treated with αOX40 alone, NP1_ɑ‐Lac, NP2, and NP1_ɑ‐Lac + NP2. MDSC have emerged as an important contributor to tumor progression, promoting tumor angiogenesis, chemoresistance, and metastasis, [ 48 ] in addition to being correlated with resistance to immunotherapy in different cancer types. [ 49 ] The antigen‐specific nature of the immune response induced by the nanovaccine was also confirmed following the immunization of B16.MO5 melanoma‐bearing mice with OVA‐loaded nanovaccine (NP1_OVA), according to the dosing schedule described in Figure S6a (Supporting Information). In contrast to the remaining treatment groups, the combination of the multifunctional nanovaccine (NP1_OVA + NP2) with αOX40 reduced significantly the average tumor volume ( P = 0.0320), at day 22 after tumor inoculation, when compared with the PBS‐treated group (Figure S6b,c , Supporting Information), with negligible systemic toxicity observed (Figure S6d ). Flow cytometric analysis revealed that mice treated with the nanovaccine (NP1_OVA + NP2) induced the highest expression of activated SIINFEKL (OVA)‐specific CD8 + T cells (Figure S6e , Supporting Information). Germinal center‐dependent antibody responses can be induced by immunization with NP containing TLR agonists [ 50 ] and OX40 activation has been shown to promote T follicular helper (Tfh) cell differentiation [ 51 ] and to impair T follicular regulatory (Tfr) cell function. [ 51 , 52 ] Knowing the role that antibodies may play in the vaccine‐induced anti‐tumor protection, [ 51c ] we decided to evaluate the impact of the different treatments on the development of germinal center reactions in the inguinal draining lymph nodes. The treatment with αOX40 alone and both treatments with the nanovaccine (combined or not with αOX40) induced significantly higher percentages of germinal center B cells (CD19 + GL7 + CD95 + ) compared to the PBS‐treated group (Figure S6f , Supporting Information), and this profile correlated with the induction of germinal center (GC)‐Tfh cells (CD4 + FoxP3 − CD25 − CXCR4 high PD‐1 high ) (Figure S6g , Supporting Information). Moreover, comparing with the other treatments, the combination of the nanovaccine with αOX40 impaired the development of Tfr cells (Figure S6h , Supporting Information), resulting in an especially high GC‐Tfh/Tfr cell ratio (Figure S6i , Supporting Information). Motivated by the results described in Figure 2k,l , two additional combination treatments were performed to understand if the PD‐1 expression and the MDSC infiltration were abrogating the complete remission of 4T1 tumor upon administration of the nanovaccine with αOX40. On the one hand, the dual nano‐immunotherapy (nanovaccine + αOX40) was combined with ibrutinib, according to the dosing schedule described in Figure 3 a , as an attempt to decrease the infiltration of MDSC observed in the 4T1‐bearing animals treated with the nano‐immunotherapy (Figure 2l ). [ 53 ] Ibrutinib is an irreversible inhibitor of Bruton's tyrosine kinase (BTK) and IL‐2‐inducible T‐cell kinase, which was shown to improve DC maturation and migration, inducing T‐cell activation and proliferation in vivo, [ 53 ] in addition to enhancing the efficacy of immune checkpoint modulators. [ 54 ] On the other hand, the nano‐immunotherapy was combined with αPD‐1, according to the dosing schedule described in Figure 4 a , to decrease the immune suppressor‐mediated effect of the PD‐1 expression in CD8 + T cells, previously found in the tumors of nanovaccine + αOX40 treatment group (Figure 2k ).
path: Synergistic Anti‐Tumor Effects Between αOX40 and Multifunctional Nanovaccine Targeting TGF‐β

sections.title: Modulation of MDSC Improved TNBC Growth Control but Did Not Synergize with the Nano‐Immunotherapy
sections.text: 5 Concerning the combination of the nano‐immunotherapy and ibrutinib, the αOX40‐, ibrutinib‐ and PBS‐treated groups showed similar average tumor volume at day 22 after tumor inoculation (Figure 3b ). Moreover, the groups treated with ibrutinib showed variable individual tumor volumes, as found for the animals treated with the αOX40 as monotherapy (Figure S7a , Supporting Information). Although mice treated with the nanovaccine + αOX40 + ibrutinib showed a significantly smaller average tumor volume when compared with the PBS‐treated group (1.8‐fold) ( P = 0.0235) (Figure 3b ; Figure S7a , Supporting Information), with negligible systemic toxicity observed (Figure S7b , Supporting Information), the average tumor volume observed in nanovaccine + αOX40 group was significantly lower than the one presented by animals treated with the nano‐immunotherapy + ibrutinib ( P = 0.0209) (Figure 3b ; Figure S7a , Supporting Information). In addition, the triple combination treatment did not improve the overall animal survival since none of those animals survived after 35 days (Figure 3c ). The analysis of tumor‐infiltrating immune cells by flow cytometry showed that the nanovaccine combined with αOX40 and ibrutinib also improved the infiltration of T cells (Figure S7c , Supporting Information), namely CD4 + (Figure S7d , Supporting Information) with no significant differences in the percentage of Treg (CD3 + CD4 + CD25 + FoxP3 + cells) (Figure S7e , Supporting Information), and activated CD8 + T cells (Figure S7f,g , Supporting Information), into tumors at an early stage of the treatment (day 19), but at a lower extent than nanovaccine + αOX40 group. Also, the expression of PD‐1 in CD8 + T cells decreased in nanovaccine + αOX40 + ibrutinib group, when compared with the nanovaccine + αOX40 group (Figure S7h , Supporting Information). Moreover, the highest expression levels of IFN‐𝛾, IL‐2, and TNF‐α expressed by CD8 + T cells (Figure S7i–k , Supporting Information) ( P < 0.01) were obtained for the nanovaccine combined with αOX40 treatment group. As expected, the nanovaccine combined with αOX40 and ibrutinib reduced significantly the MDSC infiltration into the tumors, when compared with the nanovaccine + αOX40 group ( P < 0.0001) (Figure S7l , Supporting Information). However, the overall immune response (average tumor volume, animal survival, and infiltration of immune cell populations) was not improved. These results suggest that this immature myeloid cell population is not a major contributor to the immune suppressive milieu that prevented total tumor remission, contrary to what was observed in melanoma‐bearing vaccinated animals. [ 10b ] Another important aspect to consider is the non‐specificity of ibrutinib to MDSC, being able to affect other immune cells, such as B cells, T cells, NK cells, macrophages, and neutrophils, [ 55 ] which may counteract the induction of an extensive anti‐tumor immune response. Despite the non‐specificity for MDSC, systemic administration of ibrutinib has been shown to enhance the anti‐tumor immune response induced by the i.t. injection of CpG‐ODN in mouse lymphoma, [ 56 ] which reinforces our interest in combining this agent with the nanovaccine.
path: Modulation of MDSC Improved TNBC Growth Control but Did Not Synergize with the Nano‐Immunotherapy

sections.title: PD‐1 Blockade Did Not Improve the Anti‐Tumor Effect of Nano‐Immunotherapy
sections.text: 6 To revert the immune suppressive effect induced by the overexpression of PD‐1 and the consequent exhaustion of tumor‐specific effector T cells, the dual therapy (nanovaccine + αOX40) was combined with an anti‐PD‐1 mAb (Figure 4a ). The combination of αOX40 and PD‐1 blockade has already been studied in different cancer types, including, melanoma, [ 10b ] ovarian cancer, [ 13a ] lung cancer, [ 15c ] and TNBC. [ 13c ] However, the anti‐tumor immune‐mediated effect of this combination and the interaction of the two molecules on the downstream immune outcome remain unclear. In ovarian cancer and melanoma, the combination of these two immune checkpoint modulators induced a significant increase in CD8 + T cells compared to Treg at the tumor site. [ 10 , 13 ] Interestingly, Messenheimer et al. demonstrated that the combination of αPD‐1 and αOX40 is additive in metastatic breast cancer, but for such effect, they require to be given in the right sequence. [ 13c ] The simultaneous addition of αPD‐1 to αOX40 negated the anti‐tumor effects of αOX40, leading to a lower infiltration of antigen‐specific CD8 + T cells into the tumor, a weak anti‐tumor response, and lower overall survival. [ 13 , 15 ] However, the sequential administration of antibodies targeting OX40 first and then PD‐1, but not vice versa, was effective and additive. [ 13c ] This study corroborates the results obtained by Shrimali et al. who showed that the simultaneous addition of αPD‐1 to αOX40 negated the anti‐tumor effects of OX40 antibody, by inducing T‐cell apoptosis. [ 15c ] As can be seen in ClinicalTrials.gov, some clinical trials have started, and others are being planned to test this combination. However, efficacy results have not yet been reported. The administration of nanovaccines with αOX40 and αPD‐1 decreased significantly the average tumor volume of the animals at day 22 after tumor inoculation, when compared with the PBS‐treated group (2.4‐fold) ( P = 0.0015) (Figure 4b,c ), with negligible systemic toxicity (Figure S8a , Supporting Information). However, the average tumor volume was slightly higher than the one obtained while combining the nanovaccine with αOX40. The control groups (PBS‐, αOX40, and αOX40 + αPD‐1) also presented similar tumor volumes (Figure 4b ). Nevertheless, the group treated with αOX40 alone and combined with αPD‐1 showed variable individual tumor volumes (Figure 4c ). Flow cytometric analysis of the tumor cell suspension of mice treated with the triple combination nanovaccine + αOX40 + αPD‐1 revealed a higher infiltration of T cells (Figure 4d ), namely CD4 + (Figure 4e ) with no significant differences in the percentage of Treg (CD3 + CD4 + CD25 + FoxP3 + cells) (Figure S8b , Supporting Information), and activated CD8 + T cells (Figure 4f,g ), compared to PBS‐treated group, at an early stage of the treatment (day 22). However, the infiltration observed was at a lower extent than the one quantified in animals treated with the nanovaccine + αOX40 group. CD8 + T cells were shown to overexpress TNF‐α and IL‐2, but not IFN‐γ, in contrast to what was observed in mice treated with the nanovaccine + αOX40 (Figure 4h,j ). However, as expected, the expression of PD‐1 by CD8 + T cells decreased in the group treated with the nanovaccine + αOX40 + αPD‐1, when compared with the nanovaccine + αOX40 group (Figure 4k ) ( P = 0.0001). Although this treatment induced the infiltration of monocyte‐derived DC, macrophages, and migratory DC (Figure S8c–e , Supporting Information) into the tumor, the CD103 + DC infiltration was not significant (Figure S8f , Supporting Information). Also, the administration of nanovaccine with αOX40 and αPD‐1 reduced the MDSC infiltration into the tumors, when compared with the nanovaccine + αOX40 group ( P < 0.0001) (Figure 4l ). Different studies have emphasized the dual role of PD‐1 in defining efficient or ineffective immune T‐cell responses. Indeed, although an inhibition signal is triggered upon ligation to PD‐L1, the PD‐1 expression is first a marker of T‐cell activation, allowing the identification of the tumor‐reactive CD8 + T cells, as well as CD8 + T cells with high avidity for specific cancer antigens, [ 57 ] as the level of PD‐1 expression has been related to the strength of TCR signaling. [ 58 ] Thus, PD‐1 expression can also be considered a marker of activated tumor‐reactive T cells.
path: PD‐1 Blockade Did Not Improve the Anti‐Tumor Effect of Nano‐Immunotherapy

sections.title: Nano‐Immunotherapy Controlled Tumor Growth and Prolonged Survival of Luminal B‐Type Breast Cancer Mouse Model
sections.text: 7 We further evaluated the effect of the dual therapy (nanovaccine + αOX40) in a second orthotopic mammary carcinoma model to validate the anti‐tumor immune‐mediated effect in a “cold” luminal B‐type breast cancer (EO771‐bearing C57BL/6J mice). In this study, NP entrapping combinations of the KRAS MHC class II restricted‐peptide antigen, CpG‐ODN, Poly(I:C) and siTGF‐β1 were administered s.c. by hock immunization to EO771‐bearing mice to improve the delivery of antigens to DC (NP1_KRAS (s.c.)), and also intratumorally to trigger the tumor‐infiltrating immune cell activation and expansion (NP1_KRAS (i.t.)) ( Figure 5 a ). Despite controversies, the i.t. administration of bioactive molecules allows close contact with their target cells in the TME. [ 41 ] In our case, these bioactive molecules are co‐entrapped in NP, which in addition allows their protection from premature degradation and their continuous release in situ, promoting a continuous i) decrease of TGF‐β1 levels, and consequent depletion of Treg population within the TME (siTGF‐β1), ii) infiltration of immune cells within the TME due to CpG and Poly(I:C), and iii) stimulation of tumor‐specific CTL, and consequent anti‐tumor immune response due to the proximity of TAA to i.t. or peritumoral DC, which antigen presentation profile is modulated by NP. A previous report demonstrated that upon i.t. injection in OT‐I mice, OVA 257‐264 peptide is recognized by i.t. and peritumoral DC, which further induce antigen‐specific CTL. [ 59 ] Interestingly, it was also demonstrated that i.t. injection of MHC class I‐restricted peptide induced its loading onto the tumor's MHC class I molecules, leading to an increased tumor cell recognition by CTL, and further tumor cell killing. [ 59 ] This supports our interest in administrating vaccine components intratumorally. Although the average tumor volume of mice administered s.c. with NP1_KRAS (NP1_KRAS (s.c.) group) was similar to PBS‐treated mice, its combination with the NP1_KRAS administered i.t. (NP1_KRAS (s.c.) + NP1_KRAS (i.t.) group) decreased the average tumor volume (Figure 5b,c ) and improved the overall survival (Figure 5d ). In fact, comparable anti‐tumor efficacies were also observed for the following treatments: αOX40 alone, NP1_KRAS (s.c.) + αOX40, and with the combination of the biomolecules free in solution with αOX40 (KRAS+siTGF‐β1+Adj + ɑOX40 group) (Figure 5b ). Nonetheless, mice treated with αOX40 alone presented a superior overall survival rate (Figure 5d ). However, similarly to what was observed in the 4T1 mammary carcinoma model, mice treated with the nanovaccine in combination with αOX40 (NP1_KRAS (s.c.) + NP1_KRAS (i.t.) + αOX40 group) presented the lowest average tumor volume (Figure 5b ), with negligible systemic toxicity (Figure S9a , Supporting Information) and low variability (Figure 5c ), which contrasts with the high variability obtained for the remaining groups, namely those treated with the combination of the biomolecules free in solution with αOX40 (KRAS+siTGF‐β1+Adj + ɑOX40 group) (Figure 5c ). Moreover, these animals presented a long‐term survival (Figure 5d ): 100% (6 out of 6) of the animals treated with the nanovaccine (s.c. + i.t.) and with αOX40 remained alive for over 130 days after tumor inoculation, with a residual tumor volume (Figure S9b , Supporting Information), in comparison with the remaining treated groups ( P < 0.0001). This strong outcome can be supported by the anti‐tumor dual boost resultant from the increased tumor cell recognition and killing by the antigen‐specific CTL that were strongly stimulated by the simultaneous combination of the i.t. nanovaccine, which allowed a prolonged and controlled stimulation of peritumoral DC, with αOX40. On day 22 after tumor inoculation, three animals from each treatment group were sacrificed and the main organs were recovered. Tumor‐infiltrating cell populations were analyzed by flow cytometry. Tumors recovered from mice treated with the nano‐immunotherapy (NP1_KRAS (s.c.) + NP1_KRAS (i.t) + αOX40) induced a higher T‐cell infiltration into tumors (Figure 5e ) at an early stage of treatment, resulting in an increase of CD4 + (Figure 5f ) and CD8 + T cells (Figure 5g ), specially of cytotoxic CD8 + T cells (CD8 + CD107b + cells) (Figure 5h ), with no significant differences in the expression of PD‐1 by CD8 + T cells when compared with PBS‐treated group (Figure S9c , Supporting Information). Moreover, a significant decrease of Tregs was observed in mice treated with the nanovaccine and αOX40 when compared with PBS‐treated group (Figure 5i ) ( P <0.0001). It is also important to highlight the increased infiltration of NK cells and NK T cells (NKT) in the TME of mice treated with nanovaccine (s.c. + i.t.) + αOX40 (Figure S9d,e , Supporting Information). These two are important cell subsets of the innate immune system and are dynamically involved in the anti‐tumor immune response, as reported by several preclinical and clinical studies in different cancer types, namely colorectal cancer, [ 60 ] melanoma, [ 61 ] and breast cancer. [ 62 ] Although the role and prognostic value of NKT cells in TNBC are still unclear, NK cell infiltration has been related to improved survival rates in TNBC patients. [ 62a,c ] To further demonstrate that the NP composition was essential to obtain the anti‐tumor effect described above, we have evaluated the tumor‐infiltrating T cells obtained in EO771‐bearing mice treated with αOX40 and with the combination KRAS+siTGF‐β1+Adj entrapped in NP prepared using 1) PVA, 2) PVA + HA, 3) PF127, and 4) PF127 and HA (Figure S10 , Supporting Information). Significant differences were observed in the frequency of CTL and activated CTL within the lymph nodes of animals treated with αOX40 in combination with the antigens and immune modulators entrapped in NP containing the PF127 and HA, compared to the other three types of NP. Following these results, and to better understand the different T‐cell states and activated transcriptional programs following the treatment, we performed single‐cell RNA sequencing on TIL. To infer the dynamic changes of the CD8 T‐cell subsets, we performed a sub‐clustering analysis of the CD8 + T cells ( Figure 6 a ). To define CD8 + T‐cell sub‐clusters, we used the deferentially expressed genes of each cluster and known marker genes, such as IFN‐γ and Perforin1, for effector CD8 + T cells, Ki67 for proliferating cells, Tcf7 and Il7r for naïve/memory cells, and Lag3 and Havcr2 (Tim3) for exhausted CD8 + T cells (Figure 6d ). To determine proportional changes in the sub‐clusters following the treatment, we calculated the normalized cell count for each cluster. This enabled us to compare the dynamics following the treatment within the clusters while regressing our sample sizes. This analysis indicated that among the tumor‐infiltrating CD8 + T cells, “IFN‐γ Signaling” and ‘T effector (Teff)’ clusters were relatively more abundant post‐treatment, while “Teff/Exhausted” CD8 + T cell cluster proportion was reduced (Figure 6c ). To further support these findings, we conducted a signature analysis of two T‐cell states: memory [ 63 ] and exhaustion (Tigit, Tim3, Lag3, Ctla4, Pdcd1, Icos, Entpd1, Tox). We observed downregulation in the exhaustion signature (ANOVA and a Tukey post‐hoc test, P value < 4.76 × 10 −9 ) (Figure 6f,h ) and upregulation in the memory signature following combination treatment (ANOVA and a Tukey post‐hoc test, P value < 4.76 × 10 −9 ) (Figure 6e,g ). This suggested that the combination treatment reduces T‐cell exhaustion and promotes a memory‐like state. Here, we also demonstrated the combination of the nanovaccine + αOX40 with the αPD‐1 mAb (Figure S11 , Supporting Information) in the orthotopic luminal B‐type breast cancer mouse model did not improve the anti‐tumor effect obtained with the dual scheme (nanovaccine + αOX40). At day 22 following tumor inoculation, the average tumor volume of the combinations NP1_KRAS (s.c.) + NP1_KRAS (i.t.) + αOX40 and NP1_KRAS (s.c.) + NP1_KRAS (i.t.) + αOX40 + αPD‐1 were three‐ and 4.5‐fold smaller than those obtained for the monotherapies nanovaccines‐ and PBS‐treated mice ( P < 0.001), respectively (Figure S11a–c , Supporting Information). In addition, a weak and variable anti‐tumor efficacy was also obtained for the administration of nanovaccines in combination with αPD‐1 alone or sequentially administered before αOX40 (Figure S11a–c , Supporting Information). Negligible body weight changes were observed for all treatment groups (Figure S11d , Supporting Information). Despite the similar average tumor volume presented by mice treated with the dual therapy nanovaccine + αOX40 or the triple combination of nanovaccines with the sequential administration of antibodies targeting OX40 first and then PD‐1 (Figure S11a–c , Supporting Information), an increased NK and T‐cell infiltration followed by a minor exhaustion and suppression signature, at both intratumor (Figure S11e–n , Supporting Information) and systemic (Figure S12 , Supporting Information) levels, was only triggered by the NP1_KRAS (s.c.) + NP1_KRAS (i.t.) + αOX40 treatment. These studies also corroborate the results obtained for the TNBC 4T1 model, highlighting the promising efficacy of the nanovaccine in combination with αOX40 (NP1_KRAS (s.c.) + NP1_KRAS (i.t.) + αOX40 group) against breast cancers.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.text: 8 Despite the extensive research in the development of alternative therapeutic strategies, breast cancer remains an unmet medical need. Herein, we show that the combination of a polymeric NP‐based cancer vaccine with the immune checkpoint agonist OX40 leads to a promising anti‐tumor effect in TNBC and luminal B‐like breast cancers. We report the co‐delivery of tumor antigens, TLR ligands, and siRNA molecules to promote DC activation and maturation but also to simultaneously decrease the expression of the immunosuppressive cytokine TGF‐β1, mainly produced by DC and tumor cells. By delivering these biomolecules entrapped in NP, we aimed at protecting them from early degradation and promoting their continuous release in vivo, thus enabling their extensive internalization by DC, in addition to locally improving the expansion of effector T cells, while overcoming Treg‐mediated immunosuppression following the TGF‐β1 silencing. Recently, clinical trials studying the combination of vaccination with TGF‐β blockade have been reported for the treatment of cancer patients. A phase I/II trial ( NCT04574583 ) assessed the immune and clinical activity of a BN‐CV301 vaccine (a poxviral‐based vaccine containing transgenes encoding TAA MUC1 and carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), as well as costimulatory molecules (B7.1, ICAM‐1, and LFA‐3)), in combination with 1) BinTrafusp Alfa (M7824), a bifunctional fusion protein targeting TGF‐β and PD‐L1); and 2) SX‐682, a CXCR1 and CXCR2 inhibitor that blocks tumor MDSC recruitment and enhances T‐cell activation. The anti‐tumor activity of these combinational immunotherapies is being evaluated in metastatic TNBC or p16‐negative head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC). Unfortunately, this clinical trial stopped as the maximum tolerated dose was reached. The therapeutic efficacy of BN‐CV301 and BinTrafusp Alfa was also assessed in combination with N‐803, which is an IL‐15 superagonist that promotes endogenous NK activation and CD8 + T‐cell proliferation, for the treatment of metastatic, recurrent, or refractory small bowel and colorectal cancers (Phase II trial, NCT04491955 ). Two additional clinical trials are active ( NCT04432597 , NCT04247282 ), and another is not yet recruiting ( NCT05445882 ). These clinical trials demonstrate the clinical relevance of blocking the TGF‐β pathway while boosting host antigen‐specific immune responses by cancer vaccines. The selection of tumor antigens to induce anti‐tumor immune responses is currently considered one of the most important steps in cancer‐vaccine development. [ 5 ] So far, no TNBC‐specific antigen has been validated. Despite the expression of α‐Lac during late pregnancy and lactation, this protein has been shown to be expressed at high levels in 70–80% of TNBC cases. [ 20 ] Recently, α‐Lac has been selected as TAA for a phase I trial ( NCT04674306 ) in non‐metastatic TNBC at high risk of recurrence. This trial will assess the safety and most effective dose of the cancer vaccine composed of α‐Lac and zymosan (free in solution), upon 3 immunizations, given 2 weeks apart. KRAS signaling is related to cancer progression in different cancer types, namely pancreatic, [ 64 ] non‐small cell lung, [ 65 ] and colorectal [ 66 ] cancers. Although little is known about KRAS’ role in breast cancer, over 30% of basal‐like breast cancer/TNBC has been shown to overexpress KRAS. [ 23 ] Herein, we demonstrated the potential of this TAA for the development of a breast cancer vaccine. We demonstrated the potential of these NP as cancer vaccines to sensitize breast cancers to αOX40, as this nano‐immunotherapy stopped tumor growth and improved overall survival. These results were observed in mouse models of TNBC and luminal B‐like breast cancer, proving that the strong anti‐tumor immune‐mediated effect was not specific for each of the 4T1 or EO771 cell lines. The anti‐tumor effect obtained with this nano‐immunotherapy may be explained by the reduced expression of TGF‐β1 by tumor cells, while simultaneously priming antigen‐specific T‐cell responses and blocking the inhibitory activity of tumor‐infiltrating Treg, [ 67 ] which led to an increased T‐cell expansion, trafficking, and survival. [ 9 , 68 ] Importantly, these tumor‐infiltrating T cells presented a downregulated exhaustion signature, while the memory signature was found to be upregulated. Thus, synergistic approaches combining cancer vaccines with TGF‐β1 knockdown and OX40 targeting may be a promising strategy to treat this aggressive cancer.
