sections.title: Preparation of Chitosan‐siRNA Polyplexes
sections.text: Water‐soluble chitosan (Cs) derivative – glycol chitosan (GCs), glutamate chitosan (GlutCs) or hydrochloride chitosan (HCCs) – and siRNA were dissolved in RNase‐free water at 15 and 1 mg mL −1 , respectively. Cs‐siRNA polyplexes were formed by adding the Cs solution dropwise to an equal volume of the siRNA solution (5:1 or 15:1 (m/m) Cs:siRNA ratios) and quickly mixed. This mixture was further incubated at room temperature, under stirring for 1 h.

sections.title: Gel Retardation Assay
sections.text: The ability of chitosan polymers to retard siRNA mobility was determined by 4% (m/v) agarose (low melting point) gel electrophoresis. Two different Cs:siRNA weight ratios (5:1 and 15:1) were loaded (20 µL of the sample containing 0.2 µg of siRNA) in the agarose gel. The 1:6 dilution of loading dye was added to each well and electrophoresis was carried out at a constant voltage of 55 V for 2 h in TAE buffer containing 0.5 µg mL −1 ethidium bromide. The siRNA bands were then visualized under a UV transilluminator, at a wavelength of 365 nm.

sections.title: Preparation of Multifunctional Biodegradable Nanoparticles
sections.text: PLA NP were formulated by the double emulsion (w/o/w) solvent evaporation method. [ 69 ] PLA was dissolved in DCM at 50 mg mL −1 . The aqueous phase containing 500 µg of antigen (model antigen OVA, a tumor‐associated antigen (TAA) α‐Lac or MHCII‐restricted KRAS peptide), the TLR ligands (100 µg of CpG‐ODN and 200 µg of Poly(I:C)) and/or 10 µg of siRNA targeting the TGF‐β1 or negative control) previously complexed with GlutCs, were mixed with an equal volume of 25% PVA (m/v). The aqueous phase was then added to the oil phase, while GlutCs in 12.5% (m/v) PVA aqueous solution was used for the synthesis of empty NP. The mixture was emulsified by sonication for 15 s at 70 W (Sonicator Ultrasonic processor, Misonix, Inc). Then, 5% (m/v) PVA aqueous solution or 5% (m/v) PVA aqueous solution containing 0.05% (m/v) hyaluronic acid (HA) was added and the second emulsion was formed under the same conditions. This double emulsion was added dropwise into 0.125% (m/v) block co‐polymer PF127 aqueous solution and stirred for 1 h at room temperature. NP suspension was collected by centrifugation at 22 000 g for 45 min at 4 °C (Beckman Coulter Allegra 64R High‐Speed Centrifuge). NP were washed twice with ultrapure water, collected by centrifugation, and finally resuspended in PBS 1× (pH 7.4). Cy5‐labeled NP were prepared by adding 25 and 750 µg cyanine5‐grafted PLGA to the polymer blend for in vitro and in vivo assays, respectively, while 250 µg rhodamine‐6G‐grafted PLGA were added to prepare Rho‐labeled NP. All solutions were prepared with ultrapure DNase/RNase‐free water.

sections.title: Size Distribution and ζ‐Potential Measurements
sections.text: NP hydrodynamic mean diameter was measured by Dynamic Light Scattering with Malvern Nano ZS (Malvern Instruments, UK). Z‐average size was determined by cumulative analysis (13‐16 measurements), in triplicate. ζ‐potential of NP was measured by Laser Doppler Velocimetry in combination with Phase Analysis Light Scattering, using the same equipment. NP were diluted in ultrapure water (1 mg mL −1 ) and electrophoretic mobility was determined at 25 °C with the Helmholtz‐von Smoluchowski model, by cumulative analysis (100 measurements), in triplicate.

sections.title: Particle Morphology
sections.text: NP surface morphology was determined using atomic force microscopy (AFM). NP were diluted at 5 mg mL −1 in ultrapure water. A drop of the sample was placed onto freshly cleaved mica for 15 min and dried with pure nitrogen. Samples were analyzed in tapping mode in air at room temperature, using a Nanoscope IIIa Multimode Atomic Force Microscope (Digital Instruments, Veeco), and etched silicon tips (ca. 300 kHz), at a scan rate of ca. 1.6 Hz.

sections.title: NP Physical Stability Assay
sections.text: Empty NP were dispersed in PBS 1× (pH 7.4) and maintained at 25 and 4 °C. After predetermined periods over 3 months, samples were collected and particle size, PdI, and ζ‐potential were analyzed.

sections.title: Entrapment Efficiency and Loading Capacity of Antigens and Immune Potentiators
sections.text: Supernatants collected from centrifugations were used for the indirect quantification of entrapped antigens (OVA, α‐Lac, and KRAS peptide), siRNA (anti‐TGF‐β1 and negative control), and immune potentiators (CpG‐ODN and Poly(I:C)). Entrapment efficiency (EE % (m/m), equation ( 1 )) and loading capacity (LC µg.mg −1 , equation ( 2 )) were calculated as follows: [EQ:EQ3] [EQ:EQ4] The amounts of OVA and MHCII‐restricted KRAS peptide in the supernatants were evaluated using fluorescamine. The fluorescence intensity was measured at 360 nm excitation and 460 nm emission wavelengths using a microplate reader (FLUOstar Omega, BMG Labtech). The amount of α‐Lac was determined by high‐performance liquid chromatography (HPLC). Chromatographic analyses were performed using a Beckman System Gold: UV–vis detector (Beckman 166), Beckman 126 solvent module, and a Midas autosampler. Samples of 20 µL were injected onto a Shodex PROTEIN KW‐803 series (8.0 mm ID × 300 mm, 5 µm particle size, 300 Å pore size) and eluted with 50 m m sodium phosphate buffer (pH 7.0) and 0.3 m NaCl, at a flow rate of 1 mL min −1 with a run time of 20 min at room temperature. α‐Lac elution was monitored at 220 nm by spectrophotometric analysis. The amount of α‐Lac in each sample was calculated using a standard curve generated with known concentrations of the surfactant, which was demonstrated to be linear over the range of 0 to 40 µg mL −1 of α‐Lac, with a correlation coefficient higher than r 2 = 0.99. Loading of siRNA (siTGF‐β1 and negative control) and Poly(I:C) in NP was quantified using the Quant‐iT RiboGreen RNA Assay Kit, following manufacturers’ instructions. Fluorescence generated by the binding of RiboGreen to siRNA or Poly(I:C) was measured using a microplate reader (FLUOstar Omega, BMG Labtech, Durham, NY, USA) at 480 nm excitation and 520 nm emission wavelengths. The amount of CpG‐ODN in the supernatant was determined by the Quant‐iT OliGreen single‐stranded DNA (ssDNA) Assay Kit, following manufacturers’ instructions. The fluorescence generated was measured using the microplate reader (FLUOstar Omega, BMG Labtech, Durham, NY, USA) at 485 nm excitation and 530 nm emission wavelengths.
path: Entrapment Efficiency and Loading Capacity of Antigens and Immune Potentiators

sections.title: Integrity of the Antigen Entrapped in NP
sections.text: After 3 h at 37 °C under continuous stirring, NP suspensions (20 mg mL −1 ) or α‐Lac solution (250 µg mL −1 ), used as control, were mixed with SDS‐containing loading buffer, and digested at 95 °C for 20 min. Samples at room temperature were loaded onto a 12.5% polyacrylamide gel prepared with an acrylamide:bisacrylamide solution 29:1 at 30% (m/v) (Bio‐Rad). Electrophoresis was then performed at a constant voltage of 150 V for 90 min using a Bio‐Rad 300 power pack (Bio‐Rad). Mw marker (6500‐200 000 Da) was used as a control. Gels were further stained with Coomassie Blue G 250 0.025% (m/v) to reveal protein bands.
path: Integrity of the Antigen Entrapped in NP

sections.title: NP Antigen Release
sections.text: Alexa Fluor 647 OVA conjugate‐loaded NP were prepared as described above and dispersed in RPMI medium 1640, with no phenol red. The final NP suspension (5 mg mL −1 ) was divided by Eppendorf tubes of 2 mL, two for each time point (0 h, 6 h, 24 h, 72 h, 1 week, 3 weeks, 4 weeks, and 8 weeks) and incubated at 37 °C, under gentle stirring (150 rpm). At each time point, NP suspensions were centrifuged at 22 000 g for 20 min, at 4 °C. The supernatants were recovered and displayed in a 96 well‐plate. A calibration curve was prepared using Alexa Fluor 647 OVA solution, with concentrations ranging from 0 to 8 µg mL −1 . Fluorescence values were read in a microplate reader (FLUOstar Omega, BMG Labtech) at 480 nm excitation and 560 nm emission wavelengths.

sections.title: Cell Lines
sections.text: Murine bone marrow dendritic cells (DC) JAWSII cell line (ATCC CRL‐11904) were cultured in MEM‐α, nucleosides, with no ascorbic acid, supplemented with 10% (v/v) FBS, 1% (v/v) PEST, 1% (v/v) sodium pyruvate, and 5 ng mL −1 GM‐CSF, in an incubator at 37 °C equilibrated with 5% CO 2 . Murine mammary carcinoma 4T1 cells (ATCC CRL‐2539) and EO771 cells (Tebu‐Bio 2198940001‐A‐T) were cultured in DMEM, high glucose with pyruvate, supplemented with 10% (v/v) FBS, and 1% (v/v) PEST, in an incubator at 37 °C equilibrated with 5% CO 2 . The highly metastatic B16 melanoma cell line transfected with OVA gene (B16.MO5) was cultured in RPMI 1640 with 10% (v/v) heat‐inactivated FBS, 1% (v/v) PEST, 2 mmol.L −1 glutamine, 1% (v/v) sodium pyruvate, 25 mM HEPES, and 1% (v/v) NEAA, in an incubator at 37 °C equilibrated with 5% CO 2 .

sections.title: Animal Studies
sections.text: Female BALB/c mice (8–12‐weeks‐old) and female C57BL/6J mice (10–11 weeks old) were purchased from Charles River (France) and Instituto Gulbenkian Ciência (Portugal), respectively, and housed in the animal facility of the Faculty of Pharmacy, University of Lisbon. All animal procedures were completed in compliance with the Faculty of Pharmacy, University of Lisbon guidelines, and protocols were reviewed and approved by the Direção‐Geral de Alimentação e Veterinária (DGAV, Portugal). Animals were housed under a 12‐h light, 12 h dark cycle, with food and water available ad libitum and handled in compliance with the National Institutes of Health (NIH) guidelines and the European Union (EU) rules for the care and handling of laboratory animals (Directive 2010∖63∖EU). Mouse body weight change was monitored three times a week. Mice were euthanized according to ethical protocol when showing signs of distress or with rapid weight loss (above 10% within a few days or 20% from the initial weight). For tumor‐bearing mice, tumor volume was monitored three times a week. Animals were also euthanized in case the tumor size exceeded 1000 mm 3 or if the tumor was necrotic/ulcerative. Tumor volume (mm 3 ) was determined using a caliper by d 2 × D × 0.5 where d and D are the shortest and longest diameter in mm, respectively.

sections.title: Isolation of Murine Hematopoietic Stem Cells from Bone Marrow and Differentiation into BMDC
sections.text: Immature bone marrow‐derived DC (BMDC) were generated as described by Inaba et al., [ 70 ] with some modifications. Fresh bone marrows flushed from femurs and tibias from female BALB/c mice (8–12‐weeks‐old, purchased from Charles River, France) were depleted of erythrocytes by ACK lysing buffer for 5 min at 37 °C, and cultured for 7 days in RPMI 1640 + Glutamax with 10% (v/v) FBS, 1% (v/v) PEST, 1% (v/v) sodium pyruvate, 1% (v/v) HEPES buffer, 0.1% (v/v) β‐mercaptoethanol, and 20 ng mL −1 murine GM‐CSF, in an incubator at 37 °C equilibrated with 5% CO 2 . On days 3 and 6, plates were gently swirled, and the medium was replaced. On day 7, loosely and non‐adherent cells were harvested for further assays. BMDC purity was assessed by flow cytometric analysis of CD11c‐APC monoclonal antibody‐surface stained cells (Miltenyi Biotec, Cat.# 130‐102‐800, mouse, clone: N418, 1:10 dilution).
path: Isolation of Murine Hematopoietic Stem Cells from Bone Marrow and Differentiation into BMDC

sections.title: In Vitro and Ex Vivo Cell Viability in the Presence of NP
sections.text: Cell viability of JAWSII DC and BMDC was assessed by AlamarBlue assay. Briefly, 1 × 10 4 cells were seeded in 96‐well plates and incubated overnight, at 37 °C and 5% CO 2 . Cells were then treated with different NP concentrations (up to 1 mg mL −1 ) for 48 h, at 37 °C and 5% CO 2 . AlamarBlue reagent was added at 10% (v/v) and incubated for 4 h, at 37 °C and 5% CO 2 . Fluorescence measurements were performed at an excitation wavelength of 570 nm and emission of 600 nm with a FLUOstar Omega microplate reader (BMG Labtech, Ortenberg, Germany). The 0.5% (v/v) triton X‐100 solution and PBS 1× (pH 7.4) were used as negative and positive controls, respectively.
path: In Vitro and Ex Vivo Cell Viability in the Presence of NP

sections.title: In Vitro and Ex Vivo NP Internalization by Targeted Cells
sections.text: For flow cytometric analysis, dendritic cells (JAWSII DC and BMDC, 3 × 10 4 cells well −1 ) or 4T1 breast carcinoma cells (1 × 10 4 cells well −1 ) were seeded in 96‐well plates and incubated overnight, at 37 °C and 5% CO 2 . Cells were then incubated with Rho‐grafted NP (0.5 mg mL −1 , 465 nm excitation, and 559 nm emission wavelengths) for 3, 12, and 24 h, at 37 °C and 5% CO 2 . Cells were then washed with PBS 1× (pH 7.4) and resuspended in a flow cytometry buffer. Non‐treated cells and non‐labeled NP were used as negative controls. The individual fluorescence of 10 000 cells was collected for each sample using an LSR Fortessa cytometer (BD Biosciences) and analyzed with FlowJo software v10 for Microsoft (TreeStar, San Carlos, CA). For microscopic analysis, JAWSII DC (1 × 10 5 cells well −1 ) were seeded in 8‐well Ibidi µ‐Slide microscopy chambers, previously coated with fibronectin (10 µg mL 1 ) and incubated with empty Cy5‐labeled NP at 0.5 mg mL −1 for 3, 12, and 24 h, at 37 °C and 5% CO 2 . Cells were then washed with PBS 1× (pH 7.4) and incubated with a solution containing PFA 4% (m/v), WGA‐Alexa Fluor 488 Conjugate (5 µg mL −1 ) for plasma membrane (PM) staining, and Hoechst 33 342 (2 µg mL −1 ) for nucleus staining, for 20 min at room temperature and protected from light. JAWSII DC were then washed three times with PBS 1× (pH 7.4) and after covered with Fluoromount Aqueous Mounting Medium. Confocal fluorescence microscopy was performed using a Leica TCS SP8 (Leica Microsystems CMS GmbH, Mannheim, Germany) inverted microscope (DMi8) with a 63× oil (1.4 numerical aperture) HC PL APO objective. Excitation of the nucleus‐, PM‐, and NP‐probes was performed using, respectively, the 405, 488, and 638 nm diode lasers. Images were analyzed with ImageJ.
path: In Vitro and Ex Vivo NP Internalization by Targeted Cells

sections.title: Ex Vivo Analysis of NP Effect on DC Activation and Maturation
sections.text: Immature BMDC (1 × 10 5 cells well −1 ) were seeded in 96‐well plates and incubated overnight, at 37 °C and 5% CO 2 . Cells were then incubated with 0.5 mg mL −1 NP (empty or entrapping antigen/adjuvants) for 48 h, at 37 °C and 5% CO 2 . After this period, BMDC were washed with PBS 1× (pH 7.4) and stained with fluorochrome‐labeled antibodies (CD11b‐APC‐Vio770 (Miltenyi Biotec, Cat.# 130‐109‐288, mouse, clone: REA592, 1:10 dilution), CD11c‐APC (Miltenyi Biotec, Cat.# 130‐102‐493, mouse, clone: N418, 1:10 dilution), MHC Class II‐VioBlue (Miltenyi Biotec, Cat.# 130‐102‐145, mouse, clone: M5/114.15.2, 1:10 dilution), CD40‐VioBright FITC (Miltenyi Biotec, Cat.# 130‐105‐109, mouse, clone: FGK45.5, 1:10 dilution), CD80‐PE‐Vio770 (Miltenyi Biotec, Cat.# 130‐116‐462, mouse, clone: REA983, 1:50 dilution), CD86‐PE (Miltenyi Biotec, Cat.# 130‐102‐604, mouse, clone: PO3.3, 1:10 dilution)), following manufacturers’ instructions. Samples were then analyzed using a LSR Fortessa (BD Biosciences) and FlowJo software version 7.6.5 (TreeStar). LPS (100 ng mL −1 ), free antigens (25 µg mL −1 ), and free adjuvants (5 µg mL −1 ) were used as controls.
path: Ex Vivo Analysis of NP Effect on DC Activation and Maturation

sections.title: In Vivo Study of NP Internalization by APC in Draining Lymph Nodes
sections.text: Ten weeks‐old female C57BL/6J mice ( N = 4) were subcutaneously (s.c.) injected at the inguinal site at both right and left flanks with 100 µL (50 µL each side, 30 mg mL −1 ) of Cy5‐labeled NP entrapping MHCI‐restricted KRAS peptide and the TLR ligands, CpG‐ODN and Poly(I:C). Mice treated with PBS or MHCI‐restricted KRAS peptide and the TLR ligands in solution were used as controls. After 17 h, mice were sacrificed, and the inguinal lymph nodes were harvested and homogenized in a single‐cell suspension in cold sterile PBS 1× (pH 7.4). The cell suspension was filtered through a 70 µm filter (BD Biosciences) with cold PBS 1× (pH 7.4) to remove the debris, centrifuged at 300 g for 5 min at 4 °C, and cells were seeded in sterile 96‐well tissue culture plates (2 × 10 6 cells well −1 ). The obtained single‐cell suspension was then stained with fluorochrome‐labeled antibodies, following the manufacturer's protocols, and fixed with 3.7% PFA. Cells were analyzed using an LSR Fortessa (BD Biosciences) and FlowJo software version 7.6.5 (TreeStar). APC panel : CD11b‐VioGreen (Miltenyi Biotec, Cat.# 130‐113‐811, clone: REA592, 1:50 dilution), CD11c‐FITC (Miltenyi Biotec, Cat.# 130‐110‐837, clone: REA754, 1:50 dilution), MHC II‐VioBlue (Miltenyi Biotec, Cat.# 130‐112‐237, clone: REA813, 1:50 dilution), CD40‐APC‐Vio770 (Miltenyi Biotec, Cat.# 130‐116‐113, clone: REA965, 1:50 dilution), CD80‐PE‐Vio770 (Miltenyi Biotec, Cat.# 130‐116‐462, clone: REA983, 1:50 dilution), CD86‐PE (Miltenyi Biotec, Cat.# 130‐122‐129, clone: REA983, 1:50 dilution) and anti‐H‐2Db‐PerCP‐vio700 (Miltenyi Biotec, Cat.# 130‐109‐611, clone: REA619, 1:10 dilution).
path: In Vivo Study of NP Internalization by APC in Draining Lymph Nodes

sections.title: NP In Vivo Biodistribution
sections.text: Female BALB/c mice ( N = 3) were injected subcutaneously with empty Cy5‐grafted NP (20 mg mL −1 ) at the inguinal site on the left flank, and with PBS 1× (pH 7.4) on the right flank, as negative control. After 24 h, the animals were sacrificed and analyzed by fluorescence using an IVIS Lumina imaging system (Xenogen, CA, USA). Major organs (spleen, kidneys, lymph nodes, lungs, liver, and heart) were recovered and analyzed by fluorescence.

sections.title: Intervention Combination Therapies in 4T1 Triple‐Negative Breast Carcinoma
sections.text: On day 0, female BALB/c mice were orthotopically inoculated in the fourth inguinal mammary fat pad with 50 µL of cell suspension, containing 7 × 10 5 4T1 breast carcinoma cells (mycoplasma‐free) in PBS 1× (pH 7.4), as reported by Gregório et al. [ 71 ] On day 5 after tumor inoculation, animals were randomized into different groups ( N = 9–10) according to Table S3 (Supporting Information). Three different intervention combinational studies with distinct treatment schedules (Figures 2 , 3 , and 4a ) were performed by combining nanovaccine (NP1_α‐Lac + NP2) with i) αOX40, ii) αOX40 + ibrutinib, and iii) αOX40 + αPD‐1. Treatments such as PBS and cancer vaccine (antigens and immune modulators in solution or entrapped in NP (NP1_α‐Lac)) were injected by hock immunization, via subcutaneous (s.c.) injection proximal to inguinal lymph nodes (100 µL). Half dose was injected into the right side and the other half into the left side. Cancer vaccine (antigens and immune modulators in solution or NP1_α‐Lac (23.5 mg mL −1 )) contained 100 µg of the TAA α‐Lac, 2 µg of siTGF‐β1 (or siRNA negative control), 20 µg CpG‐ODN and 40 µg Poly(I:C). NP2 were injected directly into the tumor site (i.t.) (50 µL at 47 mg mL −1 ) and did not contain the TAA. αOX40 and αPD‐1 were administered intraperitoneally (i.p.) at 10 mg kg −1 . Ibrutinib (Ib) was also administered i.p. at 6 mg kg −1 . On day 19, three mice from each group were sacrificed and the tumor and spleen were isolated to characterize the tumor‐infiltrating immune population and assess the antigen‐specific nature of the T‐cell response, respectively. The remaining animals were maintained for the survival assay. Mice were sacrificed when the tumor size exceeded 1000 mm 3 .
path: Intervention Combination Therapies in 4T1 Triple‐Negative Breast Carcinoma

sections.title: Intervention Combination Therapies in EO771 Luminal B‐Type Breast Cancer
sections.text: On day 0, female C57BL/6J mice were anesthetized with isoflurane and were orthotopically inoculated in the fourth inguinal mammary fat pad with 50 µL of cell suspension in PBS 1× (pH 7.4) containing 1 × 10 6 EO771 breast carcinoma cells (mycoplasma‐free), which were mixed with growth‐factor reduced Matrigel at a 1:1 ratio, immediately before the injection. On day 10 after tumor inoculation, animals were randomized into different groups ( N = 9–10) according to Table S4 (Supporting Information). Treatments such as PBS and cancer vaccine (antigens and immune modulators in solution or entrapped in NP (NP1_KRAS)) were injected by hock immunization, via s.c. injection proximal to inguinal lymph nodes (100 µL). Half dose was injected into the right side and the other half into the left side. Cancer vaccine (antigens and immune modulators in solution or NP1_KRAS (30.7 mg mL −1 )) contained 100 µg of the TAA MHCII‐restricted KRAS, 2 µg of siTGF‐β1, 20 µg CpG‐ODN and 40 µg Poly(I:C). NP1_KRAS were also injected directly into the tumor site (i.t) (50 µL at 61.4 mg mL −1 ). αOX40 and αPD‐1 were administered intraperitoneally (i.p.) at 10 mg kg −1 . On day 22 after tumor inoculation, three mice from each group were sacrificed and the tumor and spleen were isolated to characterize the tumor‐infiltrating immune population and assess the antigen‐specific nature of the T‐cell response, respectively. The remaining animals were maintained for the survival assay. Mice were sacrificed when the tumor size exceeded 1000 mm 3 .
path: Intervention Combination Therapies in EO771 Luminal B‐Type Breast Cancer

sections.title: Characterization of Tumor‐Infiltrating Immune Populations and Germinal Centers in Inguinal LN by Flow Cytometry
sections.text: Tumors were isolated from three animals per group, directly after euthanasia, and placed in cold sterile PBS 1× (pH 7.4). Tumor single‐cell suspensions were obtained by mechanical disruption of the tissues and enzymatic digestion for 1 h at 37 °C. Enzymatic digestion solution was prepared in RPMI medium with 0.5% (m/v) BSA, 0.1% (m/v) collagenase type II, 0.1% (m/v) dispase, and DNAse. After digestion, the cell suspension was filtered through a 70 µm filter (BD Biosciences) with cold PBS 1× (pH 7.4) to remove the debris. The cell suspension was centrifuged at 300 g for 5 min at 4 °C and washed with cold PBS 1× (pH 7.4). The centrifugation was repeated, and the cell pellet was resuspended in cold PBS 1× (pH 7.4) and seeded in PBS 1× (pH 7.4) in sterile 96‐well tissue culture plates (1 × 10 6 cells per well). The obtained single‐cell suspension was then stained with fluorochrome‐labeled antibodies for surface markers, fixed with 3.7% PFA solution, and stained with fluorochrome‐labeled antibodies for intracellular markers (Inside stain kit, Miltenyi Biotec), following the manufacturer's protocols. Splenocytes recovered from EO771 tumor‐bearing mice were first stained with the LIVE/DEAD Fixable Yellow Dead Cell Stain Kit (Thermo Fischer Scientific). Single‐cell suspensions obtained from draining lymph nodes were blocked with anti‐CD16/CD32 antibodies and normal rat serum for 15 min at room temperature. An anti‐CXCR5 biotinylated antibody was then added and incubated for 15 min at 37 °C plus 15 min at room temperature. After washing, fluorochrome‐conjugated streptavidin and antibodies targeting surface molecules were added and incubated for 20 min at 4 °C. The cells were then fixed and permeabilized using the Foxp3/Transcription Factor Staining Buffer Set following the manufacturer's instructions. Finally, after an additional blocking step, the cells were incubated with a fluorochrome‐conjugated antibody for intracellular staining of the FoxP3 transcription factor. Cells were analyzed using an LSR Fortessa (BD Biosciences) and FlowJo software version 7.6.5 (TreeStar).
path: Characterization of Tumor‐Infiltrating Immune Populations and Germinal Centers in Inguinal LN by Flow Cytometry

sections.title: Assessment of TGF‐β1 Expression in Tumors
sections.text: 4T1 tumors were isolated from three animals of groups 1 and 6 (treated with PBS and NP1_α‐Lac + NP2, respectively), directly after euthanasia to quantify TGF‐β1 expression at both mRNA and protein levels. Quantitative RT‐PCR : Total RNA was extracted from 4T1 tumor samples using the TRIzol reagent, according to the manufacturer's instructions, and quantified in a Qubit 2.0 fluorometer (Invitrogen, Thermo Fisher Scientific). Total RNA (1.5 µg) was converted into cDNA using NZY First‐Strand cDNA Synthesis Kit (Bioline, Meridian Bioscience, Inc.), according to the manufacturer's instructions. Quantitative real‐time PCR (qRT‐PCR) was performed in 5 µL triplicate reactions on a 384‐well QuantStudio 7 Flex Real‐Time PCR System (Applied Biosystems, Thermo Fisher Scientific), using the 2× SensiFAST SYBR Hi‐ROX kit, following manufacturer's protocol. The following primer sequences were used: for Tgf‐β1 gene 5′ CTG CTG ACC CCC ACT GAT AC 3`(forward) and 5′ GTG AGC GCT GAA TCG AAA GC 3′ (reverse); for the glyceraldehyde‐3‐phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH) gene 5′ ATT CAA CGG CAC AGT CAA GG 3′(forward) and 5′ TGG ATG CAG GGA TGA TGT TC 3′ (reverse). Three independent reactions for each primer set were assessed in a total volume of 5 µL containing 2× SensiFAST SYBR Hi‐ROX kit and 0.6 µM (each) primer. The relative amount of Tgf‐β was calculated based on the standard curve and was normalized to the level of GAPDH, being expressed as fold change from PBS controls. Protein extraction and immunoblotting : For isolation of total protein extracts, tumor pieces were homogenized using a motor‐driven grinder on ice‐cold lysis buffer (10 m m Tris‐HCl, pH 7.6, 5 m m MgCl 2 , 1.5 m m potassium acetate, 1% Nonidet P‐40, 2 m m dithiothreitol) and 1× Halt Protease and Phosphatase Inhibitor Cocktail (Pierce, Thermo Fisher Scientific). The lysate was sonicated at 80% power for 10 s and centrifuged at 10 000 g for 10 min at 4 °C. The supernatants were recovered and stored at −80 °C. Protein concentrations were determined using the Bio‐Rad protein assay kit (Bio‐Rad Laboratories), according to the manufacturer's specifications. Briefly, 40 µg of total protein extracts were separated on a 10% SDS‐PAGE. Following electrophoretic transfer onto nitrocellulose membranes and blocked with 5% (m/v) milk solution, blots were incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary rabbit polyclonal antibodies against TGF‐β1 (Abcam: Cat. # ab92486, rabbit, 1:1000 dilution) or β‐actin (Merck; Cat. #A5541, mouse, 1:40 000 dilution). Then, membranes were incubated with a secondary antibody conjugated with HRP diluted 1:5000 (Bio‐Rad Laboratories) in a blocking solution for 2 h at room temperature and processed for protein detection by chemiluminescence using Immobilon Western Chemiluminescent HRP Substrate (Merck) on a ChemiDoc XRS+ imaging system (Bio‐Rad Laboratories). The relative intensities of protein bands were analyzed using the Image Lab densitometric analysis program (version 5.1; Bio‐Rad Laboratories, Hercules, CA, USA).
path: Assessment of TGF‐β1 Expression in Tumors

sections.title: Functional assessment of T cells
sections.text: Spleens from 4T1 tumor‐bearing BALB/c treated with NP1_α‐Lac + NP2 (group 8) were collected from three animals, 23 days after tumor inoculation, and placed in cold sterile PBS 1× (pH 7.4). Splenocyte suspensions were obtained by mechanical disruption of the tissues and filtered through a 70 µm filter (BD Biosciences) in cold PBS 1× (pH 7.4) to remove the debris. Suspensions were depleted of erythrocytes by ACK lysing buffer for 5 min at 37 °C, and cultured for 5 days in RPMI 1640 + Glutamax with 10% (v/v) FBS, 1% (v/v) PEST, 1% (v/v) sodium pyruvate, 1% (v/v) HEPES buffer, 0.1% (v/v) β‐mercaptoethanol containing PBS 1× (pH 7.4), 100 µg mL −1 of α‐Lac aqueous solution or 100 µg mL −1 of gp100, in an incubator at 37 °C equilibrated with 5% CO 2 . After 5 days, splenocytes were recovered and stained with fluorochrome‐labeled antibodies for surface markers, fixed with 3.7% PFA solution, and stained with fluorochrome‐labeled antibodies for intracellular markers (Inside stain kit, Miltenyi Biotec), following manufacturer's protocols. Splenocytes were then analyzed using an LSR Fortessa (BD Biosciences) and FlowJo software version 7.6.5 (TreeStar, San Carlos, CA). Panel : CD45‐VioBlue (Miltenyi Biotec, Cat.# 130‐110‐663, mouse, clone: REA737, 1:50 dilution), CD3‐PerCP‐Vio700 (Miltenyi Biotec, Cat.# 130‐109‐841, mouse, clone: REA641, 1:10 dilution), CD8a‐APC‐Vio770 (Miltenyi Biotec, Cat.# 130‐109‐328, mouse, clone: REA601, 1:10 dilution), IL‐2‐PE (Miltenyi Biotec, Cat.# 130‐110‐154, mouse, clone: REA638, 1:10 dilution), TNF‐α‐APC (Miltenyi Biotec, Cat.# 130‐109‐767, mouse, clone: REA636, 1:10 dilution), IFN‐γ‐FITC (Miltenyi Biotec, Cat.# 130‐109‐768, mouse, clone: REA665, 1:10 dilution).

sections.title: Intervention Combination Therapies in B16.MO5 Murine Model
sections.text: The efficacy and specificity of the NP vaccine – NP1, using OVA as antigen (NP1_OVA), and NP2, combined with αOX40 was confirmed in a B16.MO5 melanoma murine model. On day 0, all female C57BL/6J mice were anesthetized with isoflurane, and the right dorsal area was treated with depilatory cream before the s.c. injection of 50 µL of cell suspension, containing 2 × 10 5 B16.MO5 melanoma cells (mycoplasma‐free) in PBS 1× (pH 7.4). On day 10 after tumor inoculation, mice were randomized into one of the following groups ( N = 5) (Table S5 , Supporting Information) and started to be treated (Figure S6a , Supporting Information). Treatments such as PBS and cancer vaccine (either free in solution or entrapped in NP1_OVA) were injected by hock immunization, via s.c. injection into inguinal areas, twice (once a week) with 100 µL. Half dose was injected into the right side and the other half into the left side. The cancer vaccine (either free in solution or entrapped in NP1_OVA (23.5 mg mL −1 )) contained 100 µg of OVA, 2 µg of siTGF‐β1, 20 µg CpG‐ODN and 40 µg Poly(I:C). In contrast to NP1_OVA, NP2 were injected directly into the tumor site (50 µL at 47 mg mL −1 ) and did not contain the antigen. The αOX40 was administered i.p. at 10 mg kg −1 , twice (once a week).

sections.title: Functional Assessment of T Cells Using Tetramer Staining
sections.text: For the assessment of T‐cell specificity using tetramer staining, spleens were harvested 7 days after the second injection, homogenized in a single‐cell suspension, and plated in a 96‐well plate for staining. First, the peptide–MHC tetramer tagged with PE (H‐2Kb‐restricted SIINFEKL PE‐labeled Class I Tetramer (NIH Tetramer Facility at Emory, Atlanta, USA)) was added to the single‐cell suspension, including FcR blocking, following the supplier instructions. After 30 min of incubation at 4 °C, the cells were washed to remove unbound tetramers and centrifuged at 300 g for 10 min at 4 °C. The cell population was enriched using anti‐PE‐conjugated magnetic microbeads and passed over a magnetized column. Cell samples were eluted and centrifuged at 300 g for 10 min at 4 °C. The cells were resuspended in an ice‐cold flow cytometry buffer and plated in 96‐well plates. After adding a mix of the antibodies (LIVE/DEAD Fixable Yellow Dead Cell Stain (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Cat.# L34967 , 1:7500 dilution), CD19‐APC (Miltenyi Biotec, Cat.# 130‐112‐036, mouse, clone: REA749, 1:50 dilution), CD3‐APC‐Vio770 (Miltenyi Biotec, Cat.# 130‐119‐793, mouse, clone: REA641, 1:50 dilution) and CD8α‐Vio770 (Miltenyi Biotec, Cat.# 130‐119‐123, mouse, clone: REA601, 1:50 dilution), the cells were incubated for 10 min at 4 °C, protected from light. Cells were then washed, centrifuged, and resuspended in 200 µL of ice‐cold flow cytometry buffer to determine the specificity of CD3 + CD8α + T cells, by flow cytometry. The absolute number of OVA‐specific T cells within each sample was determined as described by Moon et al. (2009). [ 72 ]

sections.title: In Vivo Assessment of the NP Composition Effect
sections.text: On day 0, female C57BL/6J mice were anesthetized with isoflurane and were orthotopically inoculated in the fourth inguinal mammary fat pad with 50 µL of cell suspension in PBS containing 1 × 10 6 EO771 breast carcinoma cells (mycoplasma‐free), which were mixed with growth‐factor reduced Matrigel at a 1:1 ratio, immediately prior to the injection. On day 10 after tumor inoculation, animals were randomized into four different groups ( N = 6), treated with two doses of αOX40 and the combination KRAS+siTGF‐β1+Adj entrapped in NP prepared using 1) PVA, 2) PVA + HA, 3) PF127 and 4) PF127 and HA, seven days apart, as described in Figure S10a (Supporting Information). On day 24 after tumor inoculation, animals were sacrificed, and the inguinal lymph nodes were harvested and homogenized in a single‐cell suspension in cold sterile PBS 1× (pH 7.4). The cell suspension was filtered through a 70 µm filter (BD Biosciences) with cold PBS 1× (pH 7.4) to remove the debris, centrifuged at 300 g for 5 min at 4 °C, and cells were seeded in sterile 96‐well tissue culture plates (2 × 10 6 cells/well). The obtained single‐cell suspension was first stained with the LIVE/DEAD TM Fixable Yellow Dead Cell Stain (Thermo Fischer Scientific), then with fluorochrome‐labeled antibodies following the manufacturer's protocols, and finally fixed with 3.7% of PFA solution. Cells were analyzed using an LSR Fortessa (BD Biosciences) and FlowJo software version 7.6.5 (TreeStar). Panel : CD4‐PB (BioLegend, Cat.# 100 531, 1:50 dilution), CD19‐Brilliant Violet 650 (BioLegend, Cat.# 115 541, 1:30 dilution), CD44‐Brilliant Violet 711 (BioLegend, Cat.# 103 057, 1:80 dilution), CD8α‐FITC (BioLegend, Cat.# 100 706, 1:50 dilution), CD45‐PerCP (BioLegend, Cat.# 103 130, 1:80 dilution), CD279(PD1)‐PE (BioLegend, Cat.# 135 206, 1:20 dilution), CD25‐PE‐Cy5 (BioLegend, Cat.# 102 010, 1:80 dilution), CD107b‐AlexaFluor647 (BioLegend, Cat.# 108 512, 1:200 dilution), CD127‐AlexaFluor700 (Invitrogen, Cat.# 56‐1271‐82, 1:30 dilution), CD3‐APC‐Cy7 (BioLegend, Cat.# 100 222, 1:80 dilution).

sections.title: Droplet‐Based Single‐Cell RNA‐Seq Data Processing
sections.text: FASTQ files were created using CellRanger mkfastq function (v7 10×Genomics). [ 73 ] Gene counts were obtained by aligning reads to the mm10 genome using CellRanger count function. To remove doublets and poor‐quality cells, cells were excluded that contained: >13% mitochondrially‐derived transcripts; <200 or >7000 genes detected; <200 or >40 000 detected molecules. The filtering process yielded 33703 cells. The four experiment groups COM, NP, OX40, and PBS were merged, and transcript counts were normalized and scaled using the NormalizeData ScaleData functions in Seurat 3.1.4 [ 74 ] R package, which normalizes scales, and centers features in the dataset. The normalized and scaled expression matrix were used for principal component analysis (PCA) and clustering. The top 11 PCs were selected for subsequent tSNE analysis, determined by a drop in the proportion of variance explained by subsequent PCs.

sections.title: Single‐Cell RNA‐seq Clustering
sections.text: The FindClusters Seurat function was used to identify clusters of cells by a shared nearest neighbor (SNN) modularity optimization‐based clustering algorithm. First, the k‐nearest neighbors were calculated and the SNN graph was constructed, and then the RunTSNE Seurat function was used to visualize said clusters (elaborated in the “Visualization of single‐cell data” section below).

sections.title: Genes Differentially Expressed Between Clusters
sections.text: The FindAllMarkers Seurat function was used to find marker genes that were differentially expressed between clusters. This function identifies differentially expressed genes between two groups of cells using a Wilcoxon Rank Sum test with limit testing chosen to detect genes that display an average of at least 0.25‐fold difference (log‐scale) between the two groups of cells and genes that are detected in a minimum fraction of 0.25 cells in either of the two populations.

sections.title: Visualization of Single‐Cell Data
sections.text: To generate tSNE plots, the scores along the 11 significant PCs described above were used as input for the R implementation of tSNE, by the RunTSNE Seurat function. Specific gene expressions were visualized over the tSNE using FeaturePlot Seurat function.

sections.title: Single‐Cell Gene Signature Scoring
sections.text: Single‐cell gene signature scoring was done as described previously. [ 75 ] Briefly, to remove the bias toward highly expressed genes the data were scaled using a z‐score across each gene. For a given gene signature, a score was calculated for each individual cell, using two sub‐scores. One sub‐score was computed by sorting the normalized scaled gene expression values for each cell. The second sub‐score was calculated by summing up the indices (ranks) of the signature genes. Finally, to get to the final score, the two sub‐scores values were scaled and averaged.

sections.title: Statistical Methods
sections.text: Data were presented as mean ± standard deviation (s.d.) for in vitro and ex vivo studies, and as mean ± standard error of the mean (s.e.m.) for in vivo studies. Statistical analyses were performed with Student's t ‐test, one‐way and two‐way analysis of variance (ANOVA), followed by Bonferroni or Tukey post‐hoc tests, and Log‐Rank test was performed to demonstrate statistical differences ( P < 0.05), using the software GraphPad Prism version 7 (GraphPad Software.Inc, CA, USA).

sections.title: Ethics Approval Statement
sections.text: All animal procedures were completed in compliance with the Faculty of Pharmacy, University of Lisbon guidelines, and protocols were reviewed and approved by the Direção‐Geral de Alimentação e Veterinária (DGAV, Portugal). Animals were housed under a 12 h light, 12 h dark cycle, with food and water available ad libitum and handled in compliance with the National Institutes of Health (NIH) guidelines and the European Union (EU) rules for the care and handling of laboratory animals (Directive 2010∖63∖EU).

Cancer Biology & Oncology.title: Long-term Survival Outcomes of Surgical Resection for Lung Adenocarcinoma with Intraoperatively Diagnosed Pleural Metastasis: Target Treatment Era
Cancer Biology & Oncology.abstract: PurposeThis study aimed to evaluate the clinical impact of main tumor resection on long-term survival compared with pleural biopsy alone in patients with lung adenocarcinoma who were intraoperatively diagnosed with pleural metastasis.Materials and MethodsA total of 176 patients with adenocarcinoma who had unexpected pleural metastasis detected during surgery from 2002 to 2021 were retrospectively analyzed. Each surgeon decided whether to perform main tumor resection or pleural biopsy alone.ResultsThe patients were grouped based on the surgical approaches: main tumor resection (resection group; n=83) and pleural biopsy only (O&C group; n=93). The resection group had better overall survival (OS; 10-year survival, 27.9% vs. 9.4%; median survival, 68.3 vs. 36.6 months; p < 0.01) and locoregional progression-free survival (10-year survival, 12.5% vs. 7.1%; median survival, 19.6 vs. 10.6 months; p < 0.01) than the O&C group. Similar results were found for OS in patients who received tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) as first-line therapy (10-year survival, 49.2% vs. 15.0%; median survival, 72.2 vs. 45.4 months; p=0.03), patients who did not undergo TKIs treatment (10-year survival, 29.4% vs. 9.2%; median survival, 82.4 vs. 23.8 months; p < 0.01), and patients with positive target gene mutation (10-year survival, 31.7% vs. 10.1%; median survival, 72.2 vs. 33.7 months; p < 0.01). In multivariate analysis, pleural biopsy only (hazard ratio, 1.73; p=0.04) was a significant predictor of OS.ConclusionMain tumor resection can improve survival in patients with lung adenocarcinoma who had unexpected pleural metastasis during operation.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.text: The 8th TNM staging system classifies non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) with pleural metastasis as stage IV-M1a, which has a 2- and 5-year survival of 23% and 10%, respectively [ 1 ]. In this stage, patients are considered to have systemic disease, and surgical resection is not recommended. Despite advancements in diagnostic accuracy, unexpected pleural seeding during surgery poses a challenge, which often leads to the termination of the procedure with pleural biopsy alone. In such instances, the clinical implications of primary tumor resection, particularly in cases of localized pleural seeding, remain unknown. Recently, several studies have reported the clinical outcomes of patients with NSCLC who were intraoperatively diagnosed with pleural seeding [ 2 - 4 ]. Patients with unforeseen pleural metastasis presented better survival than those with clinical pleural metastasis. Moreover, main tumor resection could improve survival. However, most studies presented short-term or intermediate outcomes, which may not accurately reflect long-term survival. Therefore, the present study aimed to investigate the clinical impact of main tumor resection compared with pleural biopsy alone in patients with lung adenocarcinoma who were intraoperatively diagnosed with pleural metastasis, focusing on long-term survival.

sections.title: 1. Patients
sections.text: This study included patients who were intraoperatively diagnosed with pleural metastasis of lung adenocarcinoma between July 2002 and October 2021. Before operation, the patients were clinical stage M0. All data were obtained from the medical records.

sections.title: 2. Preoperative evaluation and operation
sections.text: The diagnostic, staging, and surgical resection procedures employed in this study adhered to well-established protocols, as detailed elsewhere [ 5 ]. Preoperative staging assessments encompassed a comprehensive array of modalities, including chest radiograph, blood laboratory analysis, brain computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), chest and abdominal CT, positron emission tomography (PET) scan, and pulmonary function tests. In cases where clinical N2 disease was suspected, mediastinal lymph node biopsy was conducted under the guidance of endobronchial ultrasonography or endoscopic ultrasonography. Moreover, chest MRI was used to assess resectability for cases with suspected invasion of adjacent structures. All patients included in this study cohort were confirmed to be resectable. Pleural seeding was pathologically confirmed by intraoperative frozen section biopsy. After confirmation of pleural seeding, the surgeon decided whether to terminate the surgery (O&C group) or to resect the main lesion (resection group). Generally, pleural biopsy only was performed in cases where pleural seeding presented as diffuse (which is considered as unresectable). However, if pleural metastasis was limited to a few nodules and pulmonary function was satisfactory, primary tumor resection with clear margins was undertaken.

sections.title: 3. Tyrosine kinase inhibitor treatment
sections.text: All patients were recommended to undergo testing for epidermal growth factor receptor ( EGFR ) mutation or anaplastic lymphoma kinase ( ALK ) rearrangement. Since 2008, tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) have been used in patients. However, they were primarily administered upon recurrence following first-line platinum-based chemotherapy. TKIs were selectively used as first-line treatment in a subset of patients enrolled in clinical trials in 2005-2006. Since 2010, they have been available as first-line treatment for stage IV NSCLC patients with EGFR mutations or ALK rearrangement. If patients had positive EGFR mutation or ALK rearrangement, the corresponding targeted drugs were recommended for first-line treatment. However, platinum-based chemotherapy was recommended for patients who did not harbor these gene mutations or did not opt for TKI treatment because of various reasons, including cost, allergies, adverse effects, or other factors.

sections.title: 4. Follow-up
sections.text: Postoperative surveillance was performed with a chest CT scan every 6 months for 5 years after operation. In case of any suspicious lesions or symptoms, a PET-CT scan, brain MRI, or bone scan was performed. Based on previous studies, “local progression” was defined as the enlargement of the primary lesion or recurrence at the resection site. “Regional progression” was defined as increasing pleural effusion, pleural nodules, lung lesions, or ipsilateral lymph node recurrence and enlargement. “Distant metastasis” was defined as new lesions in the contralateral lung or any other organ other than the lung (brain, bone, etc.). Vital status was checked through the institutional medical records and the National Population Registry of the Korea National Statistical Office.

sections.title: 5. Statistical analysis
sections.text: Variables are presented as mean±standard deviation or number (percentage). The characteristics of patients between the two groups were compared using Student’s t test and Pearson’s chi-square tests. Statistical significance was considered at p < 0.05. Overall survival (OS) was defined as the time from surgery to death or the last follow-up. OS was tested using Kaplan-Meier survival plots and analyzed with log-rank tests. The Cox proportional hazards model was fitted and adjusted for several parameters associated with survival. The results are presented as the hazard ratio (HR) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). All tests were two-sided, and all analyses were conducted using R software ver. 4.2.2 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing).

sections.title: 1. Patient
sections.text: Our institution performed surgery for lung cancer on 12,772 consecutive patients between July 2002 and October 2021. Among them, we identified 176 patients (mean age, 61.0±10.6 years, 84 females) who were intraoperatively diagnosed with pleural metastasis of lung adenocarcinoma. These patients were divided into two groups based on the extent of surgical intervention: resection group (n=83), which underwent main tumor resection, and O&C group (n=93), which underwent pleural biopsy only. Table 1 shows the baseline characteristics of patients, including age, sex, comorbidities, and pulmonary function. No significant differences were observed in age, sex, comorbidities, pulmonary function, or malignant pleural effusion between the two groups. The clinical T category was higher in the O&C group (p < 0.01) than in the resection group. Moreover, the clinical N state appeared to be higher in the O&C group; however, the difference was not statistically significant (p=0.06).

sections.title: 2. Treatments
sections.text: Patients’ treatment details data are summarized in Table 2 . In the resection group, 27 patients (32.5%) underwent sublobar resection (segmentectomy, n=3; wedge resection, n=24), 38 patients (45.8%) underwent lobectomy, two patients (2.4%) underwent bilobectomy, and three patients (3.6%) underwent pneumonectomy. Macroscopic complete resection (R0/R1) of the primary tumor was possible in 81 patients (81/83, 97.6%). EGFR or ALK TKIs were used to treat 57 (68.7%) and 60 (64.5%) patients in the resection and O&C groups, respectively (p=0.67). Among them, 34 (41.0%) and 28 (30.1%) patients in the resection and O&C groups received EGFR or ALK TKIs as first-line treatment, respectively. Meanwhile, 23 (27.7%) and 32 (34.4%) patients in the resection and O&C groups received EGFR or ALK TKIs as salvage treatment, respectively, when platinum-based chemotherapy failed. Eight patients underwent neoadjuvant chemotherapy: six (7.2%) patients in the resection group and two patients (2.2%) in the O&C group (p=0.21). Postoperative chemotherapy was performed in 65 (78.3%) patients in the resection group and 76 (81.7%) patients in the O&C group. The remaining patients did not undergo postoperative chemotherapy because of old age and poor general condition with patient refusal. Twenty patients received postoperative immunotherapy: nine (10.8%) patients in the resection group and 11 patients (11.8%) in the O&C group. Ten patients received adjuvant radiotherapy for control of local progression or distant metastasis. The treatment plans were established by a multidisciplinary lung cancer team.

sections.title: 3. Clinical outcomes
sections.text: The median follow-up was 44.4 months. The 5- and 10-year OS of the study population was 40.7% (34.0-49.0) and 17.5% (11.7-26.2), respectively. The resection group had better OS (10-year survival, 27.9% vs. 9.4%; median survival, 68.3 vs. 36.6 months; p < 0.01) ( Fig. 1 ) and locoregional progression-free survival (PFS; 10-year survival, 12.5% vs. 7.1%; median survival, 19.6 vs. 10.6 months; p < 0.01) ( Fig. 2A ) and tended to have a higher distant PFS compared with the O&C group (10-year survival, 14.2% vs. 5.2%; median survival, 36.2 vs. 27.5 months; p=0.06) ( Fig. 2B ). Patients who received TKI treatment as first-line therapy presented better OS than those who received TKIs as salvage treatment or those who did not undergo TKI treatment (median survival, 56.3 vs. 41.8 vs. 40.3 months) ( Fig. 3 ). When analyzed according to TKI treatment, similar results were found for OS in patients who received TKIs as first-line therapy (10-year survival, 49.2% vs. 15.0%; median survival, 72.2 vs. 45.4 months; p=0.03) ( Fig. 4A ) and in patients who did not undergo TKI treatment (10-year survival, 29.4% vs. 9.2%; median survival, 82.4 vs. 23.8 months; p < 0.01) ( Fig. 4C ), but not in patients who received TKIs as salvage treatment (10-year survival: 6.8% vs. 7.5%; median survival: 45.0 vs. 36.6 months; p=0.90) ( Fig. 4B ). In patients with positive EGFR or ALK gene mutation, the resection group showed higher OS than the O&C group (10-year survival, 31.7% vs. 10.1%; median survival, 72.2 vs. 33.7 months; p < 0.01) ( Fig. 4D ). In patients who underwent TKI treatment regardless timing, there was no statistically significant survival difference (median survival, 4.64 [3.75-8.28] vs. 3.76 [2.79-5.00] years; p=0.10) ( S1 Fig. ). No significant differences were observed for OS regarding the clinical N status (p=0.88) ( S2 Fig. ).

sections.title: 4. Prognostic factors
sections.text: In the univariable analysis, age (HR, 1.02; 95% CI, 1.01 to 1.04; p=0.01) and pleural biopsy only (HR, 1.95; 95% CI, 1.33 to 2.86; p < 0.01) were significant predictors of OS ( Table 3 ). In the multivariate analysis, the two factors remained statistically significant (age: HR, 1.02; 95% CI, 1.00 to 1.04; p=0.02; pleural biopsy only: HR, 1.73; 95% CI, 1.01 to 2.96; p=0.04).

sections.title: Discussion
sections.text: In this study cohort, patients with lung adenocarcinoma who were intraoperatively diagnosed with pleural metastasis during operation presented better OS than those with IVA NSCLC TNM stage group from International Association for the Study of Lung Cancer 8th (5-year OS, 40.7% vs. 10%) [ 1 ]. Patients who underwent main tumor resection presented better OS and PFS, which was consistent with the findings of previous studies, [ 3 , 4 , 6 ] despite the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guideline recommending only systemic treatments for NSCLC with pleural metastasis [ 7 ]. In their meta-analysis, Deng et al. [ 3 ] evaluated whether surgical resection of the primary tumor was superior to exploratory thoracotomy in patients who were intraoperatively diagnosed with unexpected pleural metastasis. Most of the included studies found that primary tumor resection yielded better outcomes over exploration only [ 3 ]. Given that most of these studies reported the 3-year (28.8%-82.9% vs. 10.9%-38.5%) or 5-year OS rate (14.9%-42.7% vs. 0%-19.5%, surgical resection vs. pleural biopsy only), the 10-year OS of the present study showed long-term outcomes with favorable results (10-year survival, 27.9% vs. 9.4%). Although surgical resection could not achieve complete resection of malignancy in patients with pleural metastasis, the cytoreductive effect of primary tumor resection, along with the rapid development of systemic therapy, would contribute to the outcomes. In this study, pleural biopsy alone was generally performed in cases where pleural seeding presented as diffuse, which is considered as unresectable. Consequently, the O&C group might have included patients with more advanced pleural metastasis, although the prevalence of malignant pleural effusion did not differ significantly between the groups (p=0.83). Several studies have categorized pleural metastasis as either localized or diffuse [ 4 , 8 ]. These studies reported that the extent of pleural metastasis was not a significant factor for survival. However, Li et al. [ 8 ] found that malignant pleural effusion was a significant factor in univariate survival analysis, a finding that contrasts with our results (p=0.07). Notably, all patients with localized pleural metastasis in these studies underwent primary tumor resection [ 4 , 8 ]. TKI treatment has improved the survival outcomes of patients with lung adenocarcinoma and has become the first-line treatment recommendation according to the NCCN guidelines for advanced NSCLC with EGFR mutation or ALK rearrangement [ 7 ]. Several studies have reported that primary tumor resection did not improve survival in patients with pleural metastasis who received targeted therapy [ 6 , 8 , 9 ]. Similar findings were obtained in the present study in patients who underwent TKI treatment regardless timing ( S1 Fig. ). There were no significant intergroup baseline differences ( S3 Table ). However, when patients who received TKI treatment were subdivided into two groups (receiving TKIs as first-line therapy or salvage treatment), there were significant differences between them ( Fig. 3 ). Patients who received TKI treatment after platinum-based chemotherapy failed had higher risk of worse prognosis. Therefore, the mixed oncologic characteristics of the population might have confounded the results. Moreover, this study provided the OS depending on driver gene mutation regardless of the use of TKI treatment, which might offset the confounding effects of different timing of TKI treatment. In NSCLC, salvage surgery may be a viable option for selected patients with locally persistent, progressive tumors or locoregional recurrence after definitive nonoperative therapy. The advent of TKI treatment and immune checkpoint inhibitors has significantly expanded the possibilities of survival improvement in patients with advanced stage and unresectable tumors. Antonoff et al. [ 10 ] have reported the feasibility of surgical resection after TKI therapy, even in stage IV NSCLC, marking a substantial advancement in the approach to advanced disease. This underscores the potential role of salvage operations, particularly after PACIFIC-type regimens, which may become more prevalent than after concurrent chemoradiation [ 11 ]. This evolving trend suggests a shift toward actively addressing the primary tumor lesion in patients diagnosed with pleural metastasis intraoperatively. Previous studies exploring similar subjects identified surgical resection of the main tumor as a prognostic factor for PFS and OS [ 2 , 4 , 6 , 8 , 9 ]. In the present study, multivariate analysis also showed that surgical resection was a significant prognostic factor, suggesting the importance of main tumor resection even on long-term outcomes in patients with intraoperatively diagnosed stage IV-M1a lung adenocarcinoma. The present study has several limitations. Although the data used in this study were collected prospectively, this study was a retrospective study, with inherent shortcomings. Because there was no established protocol to decide surgical extent in intraoperatively diagnosed pleural seeding, primary tumor resection was decided by the surgeon, which could lead to selection bias. A higher clinical T and N category might be associated with a surgeon’s tendency to select pleural biopsy alone. Moreover, patients were included from 2002 covering the beginning era of TKI therapy to maximize the number of the study population, which could increase the risk of time-trend bias. Further studies showing the effects of new-generation TKIs or immunotherapy are needed to validate the results. In patients with lung adenocarcinoma who were intraoperatively diagnosed with unexpected pleural metastasis, surgical resection of the main tumor may improve long-term survival compared with pleural biopsy alone.

Cancer Biology & Oncology.title: Isoliquiritigenin: A natural compound with a promising role in inhibiting breast cancer lung metastasis
Cancer Biology & Oncology.abstract: Background and aimIsoliquiritigenin (ISL) is a dietary bioactive compound that is derived from the roots of licorice and various other plants. Accumulating evidence suggests that ISL has noteworthy anticancer activity in a variety of cancer cells, but it is currently unknown how ISL affects the invasion and migration of breast cancer (BC) cells. Hence, the purpose of this study to determine the inhibitory effect of ISL on cell invasion, migration, and metastasis of BC cells in 4T1-treated lung metastatic animal models.Experimental procedureISL was found to inhibit BC lung metastasis, as confirmed by MTT assay, clonogenic assay, wound healing assay, transwell assay, histological analysis, Western blot and bioluminescence assay in the xenograft model.Results and conclusionThe in vitro studies revealed that ISL treatment significantly prevented BC cell invasion and migration for 24 h. ISL decreased the protein expressions of PI3K, Akt, p-Akt, mTOR, p-mTOR, matrix metalloproteinase (MMP)-2, MMP-9, and N-cadherin, thereby inhibiting BC cell invasion. In addition, ISL decreased MMP-2/9 and N-cadherin expression in lung tissues and reduced mouse 4T1 BC cell lung metastasis. Based on these findings, it suggests that ISL inhibits cell migration and invasion in BC cells by inhibiting the PI3K/Akt signaling pathway and decreasing the activation of MMP-2 and MMP-9 expression. Therefore, ISL may be useful in managing BC invasion and metastasis.
