sections.title: Introduction
sections.text: 1 Globally, breast cancer (BC) is the most common cancer among women, approximately 1.6 million patients diagnosed each year, leading to over 450,000 deaths. 1 A subtype of BC known as triple-negative phenotype (TNBC) lacks estrogen and progesterone receptors, or has an amplification of epidermal growth factor receptors, and is found in 10–20 % of BC cases. 2 TNBC is more common in premenopausal women, African-American women, and those with BRCA gene mutations. 3 Due to its aggressive nature and increased risk of metastasis, the survival rate for TNBC of patients is extremely poor, with an advanced stage at early detection, an earlier reappearance with extensive metastatic spread, and a lower overall survival rate. 4 The development of biomarkers and direct agents with high protection of BC treatment is a major global concern. Metastasis, the process by which cancer cells separate from the primary tumor, involves migrating into the bloodstream, adhering to one another, and invading the lymphatic system. 3 Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) are crucial enzymes that allow cancer cells to reach the target tissue by breaking down type IV collagen. Overexpression of MMP-2 and MMP-9 in BC cells is linked to poor prognosis. 5 Thus, targeting MMPs can effectively reduce BC migration and invasion, and inhibiting them may have significant therapeutic benefits for cancer. 6 One of the most critical steps in BC treatment is the discovery of new, low-toxicity compounds for cancer prevention or treatment. Dietary compounds have gained interest in BC prevention due to their widespread availability, low toxicity, and high acceptance. 2 , 7 Several natural dietary compounds, such as epigallocatechin-3-gallate, ellagic acid, resveratrol, and formononetin, have been found to inhibit BC growth and limit metastasis. 2 , 8 However, the underlying molecular mechanisms and role of these compounds in BC prevention are still unclear. Isoliquiritigenin (2′,4′, 4-trihydroxy chalcone, ISL) is a bioactive compound derived licorice roots and other plants. It has been demonstrated anti-cancer activity through various mechanisms, including inhibition of cell cycle, angiogenesis, proliferation, metastasis, and induction of apoptosis. 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 Recent studies have reported that licorice intake may help mitigate the side effects of radiotherapy and chemotherapy in cancer patients. 13 , 14 , 15 Numerous in vitro and in vivo studies have shown that ISL inhibits the growth of various cancer types. Our laboratory has previously investigated the molecular mechanisms underlying ISL's anti-cancer properties. 16 , 17 , 18 Similarly, our lab has found that fabricated electrospun ISL-nanofiber scaffolds (ISL-NF) has also the potential to inhibit the proliferation and migratory capacity of BC cells in vitro and in vivo. 19 However, there is currently no clear evidence to suggest that ISL effectively inhibits BC cell metastasis. The MDA-MB-231 cell line, derived from a metastatic pleural tumor, is commonly used to study BC metastasis, particularly in TNBC. 20 Additionally, the 4T1 BC cells found in BALB/c and C3H mice exhibit high metastatic potential. When these cells are transplanted into the mammary pads of BALB/c mice, they spontaneously metastasize to the lungs, bones, and liver. This model provides an excellent opportunity to investigate the mechanisms of BC metastasis. 21 , 22 Therefore, the purpose of the study was to examine the inhibitory effect of ISL on cell invasion, migration, and metastasis in BC cells and in an animal model of 4T1-induced lung metastasis.

sections.title: Cell culture
sections.text: 2.1 The MDA-MB-231 and 4T1 cell lines were obtained from the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC, Manassas, VA, USA). The 4T1 cell line was genetically modified to express the firefly luciferase gene (Luc2) and was cultured in DMEM medium supplemented with fetal bovine serum (10 %), penicillin (100 IU/mL), and streptomycin (100 g/mL). The cells were grown at 37 °C in a humidified incubator with 5 % CO2.

sections.title: MTT and colony formation assay
sections.text: 2.2 To compare the anti-cell proliferation efficacy of ISL with that of Doxorubicin (DOX), which was acquired from Sigma-Aldrich (St. Louis, MO, USA), the MTT assay (Sigma-Aldrich) was used to determine the cell viability. The cells were seeded into 96-well plates and allowed to grow for 24 h. The MTT solution was added to the culture at a concentration of 0.5 mg/mL and incubated for 2 h. The purple crystals were then dissolved in DMSO, and the absorbance at 570 nm was measured for calibration. A value of 1 was used to calculate cell viability for the blank groups, and the % of absorbance was used to determine the cell viability. In the colony formation assay, cells were seeded onto a 6-well plate, and treated with different concentrations of ISL for 24 h before being given fresh medium for an additional seven days. The cells were stained with crystal violet (Sigma-Aldrich) for 15 min, and fixed with methanol at room temperature for 15 min.

sections.title: Wound healing assay
sections.text: 2.3 To evaluate the impact of ISL on cell motility, a wound-healing assay was conducted. 4T1 and MDA-MB-231 cells were seeded in 12-well plates and allowed to reach 90%–100 % confluency. A white pipette tip was used to create a straight scratch on the cell monolayer. The detached cells were then washed off with PBS, and a serum-free medium containing various concentrations of ISL was added. After 24 h, photographs of the scratched area were captured using a microscope equipped with 10× objectives (Leica, Wetzlar, Germany). This allowed for the assessment of cell migration and closure of the scratch over time.

sections.title: Transwell migration assay
sections.text: 2.4 To further investigate the effect of ISL on BC cell migration, a transwell migration assay was performed. A total of 1 x 10 5 BC cells were seeded on to the upper chamber of transwell inserts containing with 200 μL of a serum-free medium in the upper transwell chambers and given varying concentrations of free ISL. About 600 μL of medium containing 10 % FBS was used to fill the lower chambers. After 24 h of incubation, a cotton swab was used to remove non-migratory cells from the surface of upper chamber. The migratory cells were then fixed in 4 % PFA and exposed to crystal violet.

sections.title: Western blot
sections.text: 2.5 The cell lysates were analyzed using SDS-PAGE wto determine the expression of various proteins. After transferring the target proteins to membranes, the membranes were incubated overnight at 4 °C with anti-MMP-9 (Abclonal, Woburn, MA, USA), anti-MMP-2 (Abclonal), anti- N-cadherin (Abclonal), anti-mTOR (Abclonal), anti-P-mTOR (Abclonal), anti-GAPDH (Abclonal), anti-P-PI3K (Abclonal), and anti-P-AKT (Abclonal). The membranes were washed five times with Tris-buffered saline containing Tween-20 (TBST), and then immersed in TBST with the suitable secondary antibody at room temperature for 3 h. The immune complexes were observed using the enhanced chemiluminescence (ECL) method. Band intensities were calculated and analyzed using Image J.

sections.title: Animals
sections.text: 2.6 Nude female BALB/C mice, aged 5–6 weeks and weighing 14–16 g, were provided by the Laboratory Animal Unit of the University of Hong Kong. The mice were kept in pathogen-free conditions at 22 °C + 2 °C, 70 % relative humidity, and a 12-h light/dark cycle. Each mouse was subcutaneously injected with 4T1 cells at a density of 105 cells per milliliter into its flank. After, ten days, palpable and quantifiable tumors were observed, and the animals were divided into four treatment groups: (i) vehicle control receiving saline; (ii) the positive control group receiving DOX (0.5 mg/kg/p.o, every two days); (iii) the ISL-L group receiving ISL (20 mg/kg/p.o, every two days); and (iv) the ISL-H group (40 mg/kg/p.o, every two days). All animal experiments were conducted in accordance with the "Principles of Laboratory Animal Care" and were approved by the Committee on the Use of Live Animals in Teaching and Research (CULATR 5872-21). After 14 days of treatment, the mice were euthanized, and their organs and tumors were dissected for analysis.

sections.title: Bioluminescence assay in the xenograft model
sections.text: 2.7 Isoflurane was used to induce anesthesia before injecting 100 μL of D-luciferin (Glod Biotechnology Inc., St. Louis, MO, USA). After 30 s of bioluminescence imaging, the animals were euthanized for further research. Pictures were taken using the IVIS® Spectrum imaging system (PerkinElmer, Alameda, CA), and the fluorescence was analyzed using Living Image software (also from PerkinElmer).
path: Bioluminescence assay in the xenograft model

sections.title: Histology analysis
sections.text: 2.8 The lung, heart, liver, and kidney tissues were collected from a mouse and washed with PBS. The tissues were then fixed in 4 % PFA, dehydrated in ethanol, and embedded in paraffin wax. Paraffin slices were prepared using a sliced machine, followed by staining.

sections.title: Statistical analysis
sections.text: 2.9 The Bio-Bradford Rad protein assay dye (Bio-Rad Laboratories, Hercules, CA, USA) and BSA (as standards) were used to estimate protein concentrations. The data from at least three separate experiments were presented as the mean and standard deviation. Statistical analysis was performed using Bonferroni's post-hoc test and one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA). Groups with significant differences were denoted as follows: ∗P < 0.05 ; ∗∗P < 0.01; and ∗∗∗P < 0.001.

sections.title: ISL's cytotoxicity toward MDA-MB-231 and 4T1-luc cells
sections.text: 3.1 The aim of this experiment was to determine the cytotoxicity of ISL towards two BC cell lines. The MTT assay was used to assess cell viability of MDA-MB-231 and 4T1-luc cells treated with different concentrations of ISL (0–80 μM) for 24 h. Colony formation assays were also conducted to evaluate the effect of ISL on the colony-forming efficacy of both BC cell lines. The results were compared to those of DOX, a known chemotherapeutic drug. The results, as shown in Fig. 1 A and B, indicated that the viability of MDA-MB-231 and 4T1 cells was significantly inhibited when treated with 40–80 μM ISL. However, treatment with 5 and 10 μM ISL did not significantly reduce BC cell viability. Thus, 20 μM (ISL-L) and 40 μM (ISL-H) were chosen for subsequent experiments. The colony formation assays ( Fig. 1 C and D) showed similar trends, with ISL-L and ISL-H significantly decreasing the colony-forming efficacy of both BC cell types compared to untreated cells. Furthermore, the comparison with DOX demonstrated that ISL exhibits strong anti-breast cancer activity against both BC cell lines. The results of the MTT assay and colony formation assay suggest that ISL has cytotoxic effects towards MDA-MB-231 and 4T1-luc cells, with the greatest efficacy observed at concentrations of 20–80 μM. These findings indicate that ISL has potential as a therapeutic agent for BC treatment.
path: ISL's cytotoxicity toward MDA-MB-231 and 4T1-luc cells

sections.title: Effects of ISL on invasion and migration of MDA-MB-231 and 4T1 BC cells
sections.text: 3.2 The aim of this experiment was to investigate the effects of ISL on the invasion and migration of MDA-MB-231 and 4T1 cells. Wound healing assays were used to assess the effects of ISL on the migration of MDA-MB-231 and 4T1 cells. The cells were treated with ISL-L, ISL-H and DOX for 24 h. Transwell Matrigel invasion assays were also conducted to evaluate the effect of ISL on cell invasion of both BC cell lines. The results of the wound healing assays, as shown in Fig. 2 A and B, demonstrated that treatment with ISL-L and ISL-H and DOX significantly inhibited the migration of MDA-MB-231 and 4T1 cells compared to control. The results of the Transwell Matrigel invasion assays ( Fig. 2 C and D) showed that ISL-H and DOX significantly inhibited cell invasion in both MDA-MB-231 and 4T1 cells compared to control. The results of the wound healing and Transwell Matrigel invasion assays suggest that ISL significantly inhibits the migration and invasion of MDA-MB-231 and 4T1 cells. These findings indicate that ISL has potential as a therapeutic agent for BC treatment by targeting the invasive and migratory properties of BC cells.
path: Effects of ISL on invasion and migration of MDA-MB-231 and 4T1 BC cells

sections.title: In vitro effects of ISL on MMP-2/9 expression
sections.text: 3.3 The aim of this experiment was to investigate the effects of ISL on the expression of MMP-2/9 and N-cadherin in two BC cell lines. Western blotting was used to examine the effects of ISL on MMP-2/9 and N-cadherin expression in both BC cells. The cells were treated with DOX, ISL-L and ISL-H for 24 h. The results, as shown in Fig. 3 A and B, demonstrated that treatment with DOX, ISL-L and ISL-H significantly reduced MMP-2/9 and N-cadherin expression compared to the control. These findings suggest that ISL may have anti-metastatic properties by inhibiting the activity of MMP-2/9, which is known to play a crucial role in BC cell invasion and metastasis.
path: In vitro effects of ISL on MMP-2/9 expression

sections.title: ISL suppresses tumor growth of BC cells through the reduces the expression of PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathways
sections.text: 3.4 The aim of this experiment was to investigate the effects of ISL on the PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling pathway in two breast cancer cell lines. Western blot analyses were conducted to determine the impact of ISL on PI3K/Akt signaling. The cells were treated with ISL-L, ISL-H and DOX for 24 h. The results, as shown in Fig. 3 C and D, demonstrated that treatment with ISL-L, ISL-H, and DOX significantly inhibited the expression of PI3K, AKT, p-AKT, mTOR, and p-mTOR. These findings suggest that ISL inhibits the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway in BC cells. These findings support the hypothesis that 10.13039/501100003387 ISL suppresses tumor growth of BCcells through the reduction of expression of PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathways. This inhibition of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway by ISL may contribute to the reduced expression of MMP-2/9 observed in earlier experiments, as previous studies have suggested that this pathway plays a crucial role in regulating MMP-2/9 expression.
path: ISL suppresses tumor growth of BC cells through the reduces the expression of PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathways

sections.title: ISL prevents BC lung metastasis in the 4T1-luc xenograft model
sections.text: 3.5 The aim of this experiment was to investigate the effect of ISL on the prevention of BC lung metastasis in a mouse tumor metastasis model using 4T1-luc cells. A mouse tumor metastasis model was used to evaluate the effect of ISL on 4T1-luc metastasis. 4T1-luc cells were administered to each mouse's flank via subcutaneous injection, and the mice were treated with vehicle control (saline), DOX (0.5 mg/kg b.w. every two days), or ISL-L or ISL-H. Earlier researchers have also used similar dosages for their different rodent studies 23 , 24 , 25 Treatment was continued for 14 days, and the effects of ISL and DOX were assessed by imaging bioluminescence. Tumor size, lung metastases, and body weight were also measured, and H&E staining was performed to assess the development of metastatic lung nodules. The results, as shown in Fig. 4 A and B, demonstrated that ISL significantly reduced tumor size and lung metastases in a dose-dependent manner, as analyzed by the intensity of the bioluminescence. ISL-H decreased the development of metastatic lung nodules compared to the control groups, as presented in Fig. 4 C. H&E staining results showed that ISL-H decreased metastatic nodules in the lungs of mice compared to the control and DOX-treated groups ( Fig. 4 D). Moreover, ISL-L and ISL-H markedly improved body weight compared to the control group ( Fig. 5 A). However, DOX treatment significantly reduced body weight compared to that in the ISL-treated and control groups. Furthermore, dose-dependent treatment with ISL-L and ISL-H markedly reduced tumor volume and weight in 4T1 xenograft mice compared to the control group ( Fig. 5 B–D). Overall, these findings suggest that ISL has the potential to be developed as a therapeutic agent for breast cancer treatment to prevent metastasis.
path: ISL prevents BC lung metastasis in the 4T1-luc xenograft model

sections.title: ISL suppresses migration and invasion through the expression of MMP2/9 and N-cadherin in 4T1-luc xenograft mice
sections.text: 3.6 The aim of this experiment was to investigate the effects of ISL on the expression of MMP-2/9 and N-cadherin in metastatic lung tissues of 4T1-luc xenograft mice. Western blotting analysis was performed on metastatic lung tissues of 4T1-luc xenograft mice to investigate the effects of ISL on MMP-2/9 and N-cadherin expression and their effects on invasion and migration. The mice were treated with DOX and ISL, and the expression of MMP-2/9 and N-cadherin was analyzed. The results, as shown in Fig. 5 E and F, demonstrated that treatment with DOX and ISL significantly reduced MMP-2/9 and N-cadherin expression in metastatic lung tissues compared to the control. These results are consistent with the in vitro analysis. These findings support the hypothesis that 10.13039/501100003387 ISL has anti-metastatic properties and may be an effective therapeutic agent for breast cancer treatment.
path: ISL suppresses migration and invasion through the expression of MMP2/9 and N-cadherin in 4T1-luc xenograft mice

sections.title: ISL suppresses tumor growth of BC cells through the expression of PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathways
sections.text: 3.7 The aim of this experiment was to investigate the effects of ISL on the PI3K/Akt/mTOR signaling pathway in metastatic lung tissues of 4T1-luc xenograft mice. Western blot analysis was conducted to determine the impact of ISL on PI3K/Akt signaling in metastatic lung tissues of 4T1-luc xenograft mice. The mice were treated with ISL-L and ISL-H, and the expression of PI3K, Akt, p-Akt, mTOR, and p-mTOR proteins was analyzed. The results, as shown in Fig. 6 A and B, demonstrated that treatment with ISL-L and ISL-H significantly inhibited the expression of PI3K, Akt, p-Akt, mTOR, and p-mTOR proteins in metastatic lung tissues of 4T1-luc xenograft mice. These findings suggest that ISL may prevent cell invasion and migration by inhibiting the PI3K/Akt signaling pathway. The inhibition of the PI3K/Akt/mTOR pathway by ISL may contribute to the reduced expression of MMP-2/9 observed in earlier experiments, as previous studies have suggested that this pathway plays a crucial role in regulating MMP-2/9 expression. These findings suggest that ISL has the potential to be developed as a therapeutic agent for breast cancer treatment to prevent metastasis by inhibiting the PI3K/Akt/mTOR signaling pathway.
path: ISL suppresses tumor growth of BC cells through the expression of PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathways

sections.title: ISL prevents organ toxicity in vivo
sections.text: 3.8 The aim of this experiment was to investigate the potential organ toxicity of ISL in vivo in comparison to DOX treatment. H&E staining was performed on the heart, liver, and kidney tissues of control and ISL-treated experimental mice and compared to DOX-treated mice. The results, as shown in Fig. 6 C, demonstrated that there were no significant differences in H&E staining of the heart, liver, and kidney of control and ISL-treated experimental mice, indicating that ISL treatment had no discernible side effects or toxicity in any organ. However, the hearts, livers, and kidneys showed obvious morphological changes as a result of the DOX treatment (yellow arrow). The results of the H&E staining suggest that ISL treatment may be a safer alternative to DOX, which is known to cause toxic side effects in various organs. The absence of organ toxicity observed in ISL-treated mice indicates that ISL may have fewer side effects compared to DOX, making it a more desirable option for breast cancer treatment. Overall, these findings further support the potential of ISL as a therapeutic agent for breast cancer treatment.
path: ISL prevents organ toxicity in vivo

sections.title: Discussion
sections.text: 4 BC is the most common cancer in women globally, accounting for approximately 26 % of all BC cases diagnosed in 2022. It is the most common type of cancer, has the worst prognosis, and is responsible for approximately 7.6 million deaths annually worldwide. 26 Due to lymph node metastasis and organ invasion, BC treatment is ineffective. Despite remarkable advancement in BC diagnosis and treatment, the prognosis and 5-year survival rate of patients with BC are still not optimal. 27 BC lung metastasis is a multi-step process involving cell migration, adhesion, and invasion and proteolytic degradation of the extracellular matrix (ECM) and has a high mortality rate. 28 Our study has shown that both MDA-MB-231 and 4T1 BC cells have potent migration and invasion abilities which were significantly inhibited by ISL at 5–80 μM in vitro. The inhibition was caused by a decreased rate cell proliferation as shown in Fig. 1 B and C. These findings suggest that ISL may have potential as a therapeutic agent for the treatment for BC lung metastasis. ISL is a naturally occurring flavonoid that has been shown to possess a wide spectrum of anti-tumorigenic effects, including cell proliferation inhibition, induction of cell cycle arrest, and apoptosis in the lung, skin, cervix, ovary, breast, and glioma. 17 , 29 , 30 However, to the best of our knowledge, no previous studies have investigated the potential of ISL to inhibit BC lung metastasis, which accounts for 90 % of human cancer-associated mortality and remains a significant negative predictor of BC prognosis. 31 , 32 Although no research has been conducted to determine whether ISL inhibits BC lung metastasis. ISL and its cytotoxic effects are responsible for inhibiting the growth, migration, invasion, and metastasis of BC. In addition, ISL has been found to prolong the duration of animal survival and inhibit BC cell metastasis in vivo. These effects were associated with the downregulation of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling pathway. These findings suggest that ISL has a positive effect on preventing BC metastasis. Similarly, the previous study adds to the existing literature by exploring the potential of ISL-NF as a novel approach to delivering ISL as an anti-cancer agent. 19 We found that ISL-NF inhibited the expression of genes involved in cancer cell proliferation and migration, including, MMP-2, and MMP-9. This suggests that ISL-NF may exert its anti-cancer effects by regulating key signaling pathways involved in cancer cell growth and metastasis. 19 Moreover, our lab previously reported that ISL did not cause any toxicity to normal cells, which was confirmed in MCF-10A and rodent model studies. 25 , 30 , 33 , 34 Therefore, these data were not included in the present study. The mechanism of action of ISL in breast cancer cells appears to be unique compared to other herbal remedies. Specifically, ISL targets the PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling pathway, which is an important pathway for cell survival, growth, and proliferation. Previous studies have demonstrated that ISL can also target other molecular pathways involved in cancer development and progression, such as the MAPK, GSK3β, and NF-κB signaling pathways. 33 , 35 , 36 ISL has also been investigated for its anti-cancer effects in other cancer types, such as lung cancer, liver cancer, and colon cancer. The molecular mechanisms underlying the effects of ISL in different cancer types may differ. 37 , 38 , 39 , 40 , 41 , 42 , 43 , 44 In addition, ISL can be compared to other traditional herbal remedies that have been reported to have anti-cancer effects. For instance, curcumin and resveratrol are other natural compounds that have been shown to have anti-cancer effects in various cancer models. 45 , 46 , 47 , 48 , 49 , 50 While these compounds have similar effects on cancer cells, their mechanisms of action may differ from that of ISL. Furthermore, ISL appears to have a relatively low toxicity profile compared to other herbal remedies. Cancer metastasis is caused by the proteolytic cleavage of the ECM by proteolytic enzymes like MMPs. 51 MMPs are a group of endopeptidases, and in aggressive BC, MMP-2, and MMP-9 are highly expressed and are linked to poor clinical outcomes. 49 MMPs break down the basement membrane and ECM, 52 which are necessary for cancer cell proliferation, invasion, migration, and metastasis. Moreover, cancer cell metastasis is functionally linked to elevated MMP levels. However, inhibiting MMP2 and MMP9 expression is a crucial step in preventing cancer metastasis. 53 In the current study, mice given ISL had significantly reduced expression of MMP-2/9 in their lung tissues ( Fig. 5 E). These findings indicate that the downregulation of MMP-9 activity and expression is responsible for ISL's suppressive effects on BC cancer migration and invasiveness. Recent studies have directly linked epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) to tumor invasion and metastasis. Growth factors have been shown to induce morphological changes in cells, such as the up-regulating mesenchymal markers and down-regulating epithelial markers, which are characteristics of the EMT phenotype. 49 EMT is typically identified by a decrease in the expression of N-cadherin, a well-known epithelial marker. 49 In the present study, ISL treatment was found to decrease N-cadherin expression. The PI3K/AKT and MEK/ERK signaling pathways are well known activated EMT signaling pathways. 54 Several researchers have reported that MMP-2/9 expression is mediated by the PI3K/Akt pathway. 2 , 55 , 56 Through the activation of AKT, PI3K controls a number of cellular processes, leading to cancer invasion and metastasis by releasing MMPs. 55 , 57 Various plant-derived bioactive compounds have been found to inhibit cancer cell migration and invasion by reducing MMP expression via the PI3K/Akt signaling pathway. 58 , 59 , 60 Previous studies have shown that ISL reduces the expression of PI3K/Akt pathway proteins, limiting the proliferation of A549 lung cells. 61 In this study, we found that ISL treatment inhibited the PI3K/Akt signaling pathway and significantly reduced the phosphorylation of PI3K and Akt both in vivo and in vitro. Tian et al. 61 reported findings in agreement with ours, stating that ISL treatment decreased the activity of MMP-2/9 in lung cancer cells and decreased Akt phosphorylation. 61 Based on these results, we hypothesize that ISL blocks BC cell invasion and migration by reducing MMP-2 and MMP-9 expression, blocking the PI3K and Akt downstream signaling pathways. Thus, ISL-mediated inhibition of cell migration and invasion in MDA-MB-231 and 4T1 cells is largely mediated by PI3K/Akt signaling pathway. Metastasis is the primary cause of mortality in BC patients, as cancer cells can spread to other tissues through blood or lymphatic vessels. 62 To determine whether ISL influences BC cell metastasis, an experimental lung metastasis mouse model was used. According to previous studies 4T1 cells have the high degree of invasion and can metastasize to the lungs and other organs. 63 The study's findings showed that ISL-treated mice had significantly fewer metastatic nodules in lung tissue sections stained with H&E than the control group. These outcomes were consistent with the in vitro inhibition of cell migration and invasion by ISL. Based on these findings, ISL appears to have a significant protective effect against experimental lung metastasis. It is important to note that in this study, metastasis of 4T1 cells was only performed in the lung tissues of a mouse model. It is possible that ISL treatment could also prevent the metastasis of 4T1 cells to other organs such as the liver, bone, spleen, and kidney. Therefore, further research is needed to investigate this possibility in more detail.

sections.title: Limitations of the study
sections.text: 4.1 Although this study provides valuable insights into the potential anti-cancer properties of ISL, there are several limitations that should be considered. Firstly, the study was limited to in vitro and in vivo experiments, and further studies are needed to determine the safety and efficacy of ISL in human subjects. Moreover, the long-term effects of ISL treatment on breast cancer cells were not investigated, and further studies are required to determine if prolonged exposure to ISL could lead to the development of drug resistance or other adverse effects. Secondly, the optimal dose and duration of ISL treatment for breast cancer were not investigated, and additional research is needed to determine the most effective therapeutic regimen. Thirdly, the study was conducted using a mouse model, and further studies are required to determine if the findings can be extrapolated to human subjects. Lastly, the study did not explore the potential interactions between ISL and other medications or supplements that breast cancer patients may be taking, which is an important consideration when developing potential therapeutic regimens.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.text: 5 This study confirmed that ISL prevented lung metastasis by preventing MMP-2/9 expression, which in turn prevented MDA-MB-231 and 4T1 BC cell migration and invasion. The inactivation of the PI3K/Akt pathway, which prevents BC proliferation, maybe responsible for this effect of ISL. These findings provide new insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying the anti-invasive capabilities of ISL in BC cells. Based on these results, ISL may be an effective anti-invasive agent against BC metastasis.

Cancer Biology & Oncology.title: Post-Lobectomy Tracheal Metastasis of Stage Ib Lung Cancer
Cancer Biology & Oncology.abstract: ABSTRACTBackground:Endotracheal/endobronchial metastases represent an extremely rare category of diseases, lacking population-based incidence studies. These metastases are generally classified into two types: pulmonary and nonpulmonary. Pulmonary metastases are considerably rarer than their nonpulmonary counterparts.Case Report:We present a rare case of tracheal metastasis, diagnosed during a follow-up two years after the anatomical resection of early-stage lung cancer. This case was successfully treated.Conclusion:Tracheal metastases after lung cancer surgery are exceedingly rare. Patients often exhibit radiological findings before becoming symptomatic. Therefore, bronchoscopic evaluation is recommended when radiological and clinical suspicions arise.
Cancer Biology & Oncology.journal: Journal of Clinical Practice and Research

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.text: Endobronchial/endotracheal metastases (EEMs) are bronchoscopically visible tumors in segmental or more central airways, exhibiting histopathological characteristics identical to the primary cancer. EEMs, which are quite rare, result from either pulmonary or nonpulmonary malignancies. 1 Metastases of pulmonary origin are less common. In contrast, nonpulmonary metastases occur in 2–50% of breast, colon, and kidney cancer cases. Literature on EEMs following primary lung cancer surgery primarily consists of case reports. 2 Due to the limited number of patients and studies, there is insufficient information regarding the clinical management, optimal treatment options, treatment outcomes, and survival rates of these patients.

sections.title: CASE REPORT
sections.text: A 61-year-old Asian male with no known prior diseases presented to our clinic with hemoptysis. He had a 30 pack-year smoking history. Chest tomography revealed a 1.5 cm mass with endobronchial extension at the junction between the right lower and middle lobes ( Fig. 1a ). Rigid bronchoscopy identified a lesion originating from the apical segment of the right lower lobe, extending to the right main bronchus. The patient underwent mechanical tumor resection (MTR) with argon plasma coagulation (APC) at a power setting of 60 W in the same session. The procedure was completed without complications. Pathology reported the lesion as squamous cell carcinoma, and the patient was scheduled for surgery. A Positron Emission Tomography-Computed Tomography (PET-CT) showed no involvement except for the 1.5 cm lesion at the same anatomical location (Maximum Standardized Uptake Value (SUV max ): 9.54). A right thoracotomy with inferior bilobectomy and systematic lymph node dissection was performed. No additional chemoradiotherapy was planned, as the final surgical staging was stage Ib. The patient’s follow-up period was three months. The initial controls included bronchoscopy and chest tomography imaging, where the stump location and trachea were evaluated as normal. At the 1-year follow-up, the patient, who had no complaints during this interval, underwent chest tomography. The imaging revealed an appearance with a 2 mm diameter, consistent with secretion in the lower third of the trachea ( Fig. 1b ). The 2-year follow-up chest tomography showed a lesion approximately 2 cm in diameter, obstructing half of the tracheal cross-sectional area at the location previously thought to be secretion ( Fig. 1c ). This lesion, originating from the right lateral trachea, was visualized by flexible bronchoscopy (FOB), and biopsy samples were taken ( Fig. 1d ). The pathology result confirmed squamous cell lung cancer ( Fig. 2a , Fig. 2b ). The patient was referred to the interventional pulmonology clinic. The endotracheal lesion was completely excised during the intervention, which was performed after the patient was evaluated and found eligible for cryotherapy ( Fig. 3a ). No complications were observed following the procedure. The patient was referred to the radiation oncology department and evaluated as suitable for radiotherapy. He received intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT) at a dose of 200 cGy per fraction, totaling 5,000 cGy in 25 fractions. The 3-month post-treatment PET-CT scan revealed no residual tracheal lesion, no involvement of mediastinal lymph nodes, and no signs of metastasis ( Fig. 3b ). Additionally, no endobronchial lesion was visualized in the patient when assessed with FOB. Consequently, tracheal segment resection or any additional intervention was not deemed necessary. The patient, now in the third year of follow-up, remains alive and continues to be monitored every six months.

sections.title: DISCUSSION
sections.text: There is only one population-based incidence study of primary tracheal tumors in the literature, reporting a rate of 2.6 per 1,000,000 people, but no studies exist on EEMs. 3 EEMs are classified into two categories: pulmonary and nonpulmonary metastases, with pulmonary metastases being significantly rarer. The number of patients with EEMs who undergo anatomical resection for lung cancer is even lower, with the largest series in the literature comprising only six patients. 1 Nonpulmonary EEMs are observed in 2–50% of breast, colon, and kidney cancer cases. Only one study reported an EEM incidence of 0.44 in patients with resected lung cancer. Notably, our patient represents a rare case of EEM following stage I lung cancer surgery. 1 This raises the question of whether tracheal metastases are independent of the cancer stage. It is hypothesized that EEMs can develop in four distinct modes: Type I, direct metastasis to the bronchus; Type II, bronchial invasion by a parenchymal lesion; Type III, bronchial invasion by mediastinal or hilar lymph node metastasis; and Type IV, a peripheral lesion extending along the proximal bronchus. We believe that the patient in our case report corresponds to Type I. 4 The clinical course of tracheal metastases varies depending on their location and the extent of obstruction. While cough, dyspnea, and hemoptysis are the main clinical symptoms, 20% of cases can be asymptomatic, as was observed in our patient. 5 Chest X-rays and chest CT scans are basic radiological diagnostic approaches. Endotracheal nodules are often mistaken for endotracheal sputum (phlegm), referred to as mucoid pseudotumor. 6 This can lead to confusion, as it did in the case of our patient. Consequently, Chong et al. 1 have defined criteria that can aid in radiological differentiation. In such cases, bronchoscopy is considered the gold standard for diagnosis, and its use should not be hesitated to confirm the condition. Salud et al. 7 suggested that primary tracheal tumors cannot be histopathologically differentiated from metastases. Although challenging and costly, certain techniques are currently employed for diagnosing this condition. In one case documented in the literature, genetic sequencing was used to confirm metastasis, revealing mutations in the Kirsten Rat Sarcoma Viral Oncogene Homolog (KRAS) and the Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor (EGFR) genes in both the primary and secondary lesions. In our patient’s case, sequencing was not performed due to the associated costs. The recurrence interval for EEMs in nonpulmonary cancers is reported to be 50.4–65.3 months, whereas it is 25.8 months in pulmonary cancers. 4 , 7 , 8 We share Chong et al.’s 1 view regarding the relatively shorter recurrence interval in pulmonary cancers. We believe this is due to the more frequent follow-up of pulmonary cancers, given their aggressive nature. In fact, our patient was diagnosed before becoming symptomatic. There are various treatment options for EEMs, including tracheal resection and reconstruction, debulking surgery, cryotherapy, radiotherapy, and chemotherapy, as utilized in our patient’s case. 9 Each technique has its own advantages and disadvantages. For patients who have previously undergone surgery for lung cancer, making individualized assessments appears to be the most appropriate approach.

sections.title: CONCLUSION
sections.text: In conclusion, careful follow-up is essential after lung cancer surgery. Since tracheal metastases are very rare, they may be overlooked in patient assessments. When evaluating airways, radiological images that could be misinterpreted as secretion should always be confirmed with bronchoscopy. Importantly, patients with EEMs can often be diagnosed radiologically long before they exhibit symptoms.

Cancer Biology & Oncology.title: Gastric Perforation due to Cervical Cancer Metastasis
Cancer Biology & Oncology.abstract: ABSTRACTBackground:Squamous cell carcinoma (SqCC) is the most prevalent subtype of carcinoma of the uterine cervix. It is well-known for its local infiltration and a high frequency of lymphonodal invasion, but distant hematogenous metastases are uncommon.Case Report:This case report highlights the rare occurrence of gastric perforation resulting from metastatic uterine cervical SqCC. A 56-year-old woman, initially treated for cervical cancer, presented with severe abdominal pain and vomiting. Emergency laparotomy revealed a prepyloric stomach perforation. Subsequent subtotal gastrectomy confirmed high-grade malignancy with atypical cells infiltrating the stomach. The literature on gastric metastasis from cervical cancer is limited, making this case noteworthy. Surgical intervention and postoperative therapy were recommended, although the patient’s deteriorating health delayed the planned treatment.Conclusion:While only three similar cases have been reported, emphasizing the need for early radical treatment and postoperative care, this case underlines the complexity and lack of standardized protocols in managing such rare metastatic scenarios.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.text: Squamous cell carcinoma (SqCC) is the most prevalent pathological subtype of cervical carcinoma and the third most common gynecologic cancer. It is one of the main causes of cancer mortality in women globally. Annually, an estimated 500,000 women worldwide are diagnosed with this type of cancer, with nearly half of the cases occurring before the age of 35. 1 The International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) states that cervical cancer remains the only gynecological cancer that is clinically staged. 2 Qin et al., 3 in a study conducted in 2009, concluded that significant discrepancies exist between the clinical stage and pathological results of operable cervical carcinomas ranging from grade IB to IIB. They recommended the use of certain radiological examinations, such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), computed tomography (CT), and positron emission tomography (PET), for more accurate staging of cervical cancer. SqCC is well-known for its local infiltration and a high frequency of lymphonodal invasion. However, distant hematogenous metastases are uncommon and typically affect the lungs and bones. 4 It is extremely rare for solid tumors to metastasize to the stomach, particularly from the cervix. Less than 2% of cervical cancer patients develop gastric lesions, which are typically asymptomatic. 5 , 6

sections.title: CASE REPORT
sections.text: We present the case of a 56-year-old woman. Her initial procedure, a complete hysterectomy with bilateral adnexectomy and pathohistological evaluation, revealed squamous cell carcinoma grade I/II of the cervix ( Fig. 1a ). Following surgery, the patient underwent chemotherapy and radiotherapy, with a favorable prognosis. Regular follow-up examinations showed no local recurrence of carcinoma or distant metastasis. Three years after the initial diagnosis, during a regular oncological follow-up, multi-slice computed tomography (MSCT) of the abdomen revealed a 1.2 cm long nodule in the fat tissue surrounding the stomach’s lesser curvature and a few enlarged lymph nodes (approximately 2.6 x 1.2 centimeters) near the head of the pancreas. The patient was immediately referred to a gastroenterologist after the discovery of the suspicious lesion near the stomach. An esophagogastroduodenoscopy was performed to rule out any intraluminal changes in the stomach and duodenum. Gastroscopy revealed mucosal nodularity with multiple hemorrhagic spots, suggesting an exacerbation of chronic gastritis. A positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) scan was also recommended to evaluate the metabolic activity of the enlarged nodules. The scan showed high metabolic intensity in the ventral wall of the stomach, likely coexisting with the enlarged intraperitoneal lymph nodes previously described in the MSCT scan. The oncology council decided to monitor these lesions and conduct a follow-up MSCT scan in three months. The patient was admitted to the emergency room two months later, complaining of severe abdominal pain that persisted for two days. The pain was localized in the upper abdominal quadrants, and the patient characterized it as unbearable. She also experienced vomiting after a meal earlier that day. The physical examination revealed rebound tenderness and severe pain upon palpation, suggesting a potential acute abdomen. She was normotensive (103/60 mmHg) with a regular heart rate and rhythm (81). An abdominal X-ray revealed subdiaphragmatic free gas, which, in correlation with the previous diagnosis from the gastroenterologist, suggested a possible perforated peptic ulcer. Emergency laparotomy was performed, during which a prepyloric perforation of the stomach was identified, and tissue samples were obtained before repair. The postoperative period was unremarkable, and the patient was discharged on the fifth postoperative day. Pathohistological evaluation revealed atypical epithelial cells infiltrating the desmoplastic stroma, with only a few signet-ring cells described. This case was once again presented to the oncology consilium, and radical surgical treatment was recommended. Subsequently, a subtotal gastrectomy was performed. A resected part of the stomach measuring 11 by 5.5 centimeters, infiltrated with a tumorous mass, was sent for pathohistological analysis. This revealed atypical, poorly differentiated epithelial cells surrounded by abundant desmoplastic stroma and predominantly hyperchromatic, but occasionally also vesicular nuclei with prominent nucleoli. There were numerous necrotic lesions throughout the tumorous masses, where clusters of tumor cells formed palisades. Additionally, without breaching the subserous membrane, the tumor invaded the majority of the layers of the stomach wall (mucosa, submucosa, and muscularis propria). In order to rule out stomach signet-ring cell adenocarcinoma, the tissue was also examined using Periodic Acid-Schiff (PAS)-Alcian Blue staining, and the cells were negative. Surgical margins were clear. All these findings indicated a gastric metastasis of uterine cervical squamous cell carcinoma with high-grade malignancy ( Fig. 1b ). The patient’s deteriorating general health condition necessitated postponing the planned adjuvant post-surgery therapy.

sections.title: DISCUSSION
sections.text: Literature regarding gastric metastasis is extremely limited, with the most frequent primary cancers being squamous cell carcinoma of the esophagus, lung adenocarcinoma, and melanomas. Most patients with primary cervical cancer and simultaneous stomach metastasis also had other organs affected. 7 Since stomach squamous cell carcinoma is relatively uncommon (accounting for less than 0.05% of all gastric cancers), it is typically identified as a metastasis from another primary site when detected in stomach tissue through pathohistological analysis. 8 A gastric lesion in a patient with a history of cervical cancer is usually considered a primary tumor. However, as our case illustrates, metastasis is possible and therefore must be considered. There are three reported cases of sole metastasis to the stomach and five cases of multimetastatic cervical SqCC. In one case of single gastric metastasis from primary cervical SqCC described by Moldovan et al., 5 the patient underwent subtotal gastrectomy along with D2 lymphadenectomy. After the initial surgery, the patient received adjuvant post-surgery therapy, which included radiotherapy to the stomach region and six cycles of Paclitaxel and Carboplatin. Nine months after surgery, the patient was alive and in complete remission. However, the majority of patients with this diagnosis are in poor general health and may not be suitable for post-surgery adjuvant therapy. 9 In both of the remaining case reports on this subject, the patients were not fit for planned surgical treatment and succumbed within a few days and two months, respectively. 9 , 10 Due to their rarity, these conditions lack a standardized protocol for the type of surgery and post-operative chemotherapy or radiotherapy treatment, as well as an estimated life expectancy. Defining such a treatment protocol could benefit these patients by increasing their survival rate.

sections.title: CONCLUSION
sections.text: With this report, we aim to highlight an unusual progression of cervical SqCC with gastric perforation as a complication of metastatic disease. Considering that there have been only three previous case reports of this diagnosis, we advocate for early radical treatment of gastric metastasis combined with suitable post-operative oncological care, which may result in prolonged survival and a higher quality of life. We believe that this report will be beneficial to clinicians and that further, comparable cases will corroborate our findings.

Cancer Biology & Oncology.title: LncRNA H19 Promotes Angiogenesis in Mouse Pulmonary Artery Endothelial Cells by Regulating the HIF-1α/VEGF Signaling Pathway
Cancer Biology & Oncology.abstract: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN) is a syndrome of acute respiratory failure characterized by systemic hypoxemia and elevated pulmonary arterial pressure, which leads to pathological changes in pulmonary vascular remodeling and endothelial cell function. Long non-coding RNA (lncRNA) H19 has been shown to be involved in the regulation of arterial endothelial cell function, but its regulatory role in PPHN is not fully understood. In the present study, mouse pulmonary artery endothelial cells (MPAECs) were cultured in a hypoxic conditions. Subsequently, the regulatory function of lncRNA H19 on MPAECs was explored by constructing adenoviruses knocking down and overexpressing lncRNA H19. The results revealed that the hypoxic conditions could induce the proliferation and migration of MPAECs, as well as the high expression of lncRNA H19 in MPAECs. Knockdown of lncRNA H19 expression in MPAECs reversed hypoxic environment-induced functional changes in endothelial cells, whereas overexpression of lncRNA H19 further enhanced the proliferation and migration of MPAECs. In addition, lncRNA H19 upregulated the hypoxia-inducible factor-1α (HIF-1α)/vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) pathway through sponge of miNA-20a-5p, which in turn promoted changes in endothelial cell function. LncRNA H19 may interfere with vascular remodeling in hypoxia-induced pulmonary hypertension by upregulating the expression of HIF-1α and VEGF in vascular endothelial cells.Supplementary InformationThe online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1007/s10528-024-10983-3.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.text: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN) is a condition characterized by the failure of pulmonary vascular resistance to decrease at birth, leading to reduced pulmonary blood flow and impaired gas exchange (Fortas et al. 2021 ). Abnormal pulmonary vascular reactivity is the main clinical feature of PPHN (Singh and Lakshminrusimha 2021 ). The primary clinical feature of PPHN is abnormal pulmonary vascular reactivity, which often originates during fetal life and disrupts the normal adaptation of pulmonary circulation at birth. As a result, newborn with PPHN experience significant hypoxemia, increasing the risk of mortality and long-term complications. (Sankaran and Lakshminrusimha 2022 ; Babooa et al. 2017 ). Research suggests that adverse conditions, such as chronic hypoxia during pregnancy, can alter the structure and reactivity of the pulmonary vasculature, preventing the normal dilation of pulmonary vessels at birth (Nair and Lakshminrusimha 2014 ; Wedgwood et al. 2019 ). Hypoxia-inducible factor-1α (HIF-1α), a protein with a basic helix-loop-helix PAS domain, is a key regulator of cellular and developmental responses to low oxygen levels (Rashid et al. 2021 ). HIF-1α influences cellular adaptation to hypoxia by upregulating vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), a crucial transcription factor (Song et al. 2023 ; Lu et al. 2023 ). VEGF is a specific endothelial cell mitogen that regulates endothelial cell differentiation, angiogenesis, and vascular maintenance (Shifren et al. 1994 ). It is essential for early vascular development and serves as a critical regulator of pulmonary vascular growth, development, and maintenance throughout the embryonic, fetal, and postnatal stages (Wiszniak and Schwarz 2021 ). In the human fetal lung, VEGF is primarily localized to alveolar epithelial cells and myocytes (Shifren et al. 1994 ). Studies have shown that VEGF stimulation increases the expression of endothelial nitric oxide synthase, which enhances blood flow in vivo (Kroll and Waltenberger 1998 ; Bauters et al. 1995 ). Chronic intrauterine pulmonary hypertension inhibits vessel growth, potentially due to disruptions in VEGF-NO signaling (Grover et al. 2005 ). Indeed, VEGF expression in the lungs is significantly reduced in chronic intrauterine pulmonary hypertension, suggesting that impaired VEGF signaling could adversely affect vascular function, as well as the growth and structural development of the lung, contributing to the pathogenesis of PPHN (Grover et al. 2003 ). However, increased pulmonary VEGF mRNA expression and its receptor have been observed in patients with severe pulmonary hypertension and in animal models of hypoxia-induced pulmonary hypertension (Voelkel and Gomez-Arroyo 2014 ; Nadeau et al. 2005 ; Tuder et al. 1995 ), indicating that the HIF-1α/VEGF axis may play a role in regulating the development of hypoxia-induced PPHN. Despite these findings, the exact regulatory mechanisms remain poorly understood. Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs), a group of non-coding transcripts ≥ 200 nucleotides in length, are transcribed by RNA polymerase II. LncRNAs have little or no potential to encode proteins (Jathar et al. 2017 ; Zhang et al. 2017 ). With the development of high-throughput sequencing technologies, cumulative evidence suggests that lncRNAs can regulate the expression of protein-coding genes epigenetically, transcriptionally, and post-transcriptionally, thereby affecting a range of biological processes (Ashrafizadeh et al. 2022 ; Bridges et al. 2021 ). LncRNA H19, located on human chromosome 11p15.5, is a well-characterized imprinted gene implicated in multiple diseases, including cancer (Müller et al. 2019 ), diabetes (Li et al. 2020 ), and cardiovascular disorders (Zhang et al. 2018 ). Numerous conditions, such as lung cancer, pulmonary hypertension, and asthma, are increasingly recognized as systemic diseases with significant pulmonary manifestations. Notably, the progression of these diseases has been closely associated with the regulation of lncRNA H19 (Wang, et al. 2019 ; Zhang et al. 2022 ; Chen et al. 2021 ). Specifically, lncRNA H19 promotes lung fibrosis in human lung fibroblasts by inhibiting microRNA (miRNA or miR)−140 expression, resulting in enhanced extracellular matrix deposition (Wang, et al. 2019 ). Furthermore, lncRNA H19 exerts regulatory effects on airway smooth muscle cells, adult myocytes, cardiomyocytes, and both small cell and non-small cell lung cancer cell lines (Sun et al. 2019 ; Tan et al. 2021 ; Xie et al. 2022 ). Recent studies have highlighted the role of lncRNAs in pulmonary vascular remodeling. In particular, lncRNA H19 has been implicated in the remodeling of small pulmonary arteries and the pathogenesis of pulmonary hypertension in adults (Wang et al. 2018 ; Hoffmann et al. 2016 ). Overproliferation of pulmonary artery smooth muscle cells and dysfunction of arterial endothelial cells contribute to vascular remodeling (Kim 2014 ). Studies demonstrate that lncRNA H19 can bind to let-7b as a competitive endogenous RNA, downregulating its expression, upregulating cyclin D1, and promoting vascular smooth muscle proliferation and remodeling (Sun et al. 2019 ). Additionally, by binding and isolating let-7b, lncRNA H19 upregulates angiotensin I receptor-1 (AT1R) expression in platelet-derived growth factor-BB-stimulated rat pulmonary artery smooth muscle cells (Su et al. 2018 ). Nevertheless, the role of lncRNA H19 in the pathogenesis of persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN) remains uncertain. This study aims to develop an in vitro model of pulmonary artery endothelial cell dysfunction to investigate PPHN pathophysiology through hypoxia induction. Following this, the effects of lncRNA H19 knockdown and overexpression will be examined via cell transfection.

sections.title: Cell Culture
sections.text: Mouse pulmonary artery endothelial cells (MPAECs) were purchased from Shanghai Fuheng Biotechnology Co (FH-Y055). Cells were cultured in DMEM (Gibco) containing 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) (Gibco) and 1% penicillin–streptomycin in a 5% CO2 incubator at 37 °C. When the cells reach 80–90% fusion, digested with 0.25% trypsin and passage them. The culture medium was changed every two days. The hypoxic intervention cells were placed in a hypoxic cell culture incubator (3% O 2 ), and the normoxic cells were cultured in normal cell culture incubator (21% O 2 ).

sections.title: Cell Infection and Transfection
sections.text: Adenovirus infection with shRNA-lncRNA H19 was used to inhibit the expression of lncRNA H19 in MPAECs, the insert sequence for shRNA-lncRNA H19 group is 5′-GGTCCTGGGTCCATCAATAAA-3′; the insert sequence for the shRNA-NC group is 5′-CGCTGAGTACTTCGAAATGTC-3′. pDC316-mCMV-ZsGreen was used as a vector to construct adenovirus overexpressing lncRNA H19( NR_130973.1 ). The overexpression and negative control (NC) adenovirus were added directly into the complete medium according to MOI = 100 in hypoxic cell culture incubator. The adenovirus was designed and synthesized by Shenzhen TOP Biotechnology Co., Ltd. For microRNA transfection, MPAECs were seeded in 6-well plates and allowed to adhere for 24 h. According to the manufacturer’s instructions, the cells were transfected at a final concentration of 30 nM siRNA/mimic using Lipofectamine RNAiMAX Reagent (Thermo Fisher, USA). miR-20a-5p mimic was purchased from Guangzhou RiboBio Co., Ltd. (miR10000529-1–5). The siRNA was synthesized by OBiO Technology (Shanghai) Corp.,Ltd and siRNA-miR-20a-5p sense sequence is CAUCUACUGCAUUACGAGCACUUAA, antisense sequence is UUAAGUGCUCGUAAUGCAGUAGAUG, the siRNA-control sense sequence is CAUUCAACGAUUAGCACGUCCUUAA, and antisense sequence is UUAAGGACGUGCUAAUCGUUGAAUG. After 24 h of infection/transfection, the medium was changed to normal complete medium for another 24 h culture. And all the experiments were done in a hypoxic culture incubator.

sections.title: Cell Migration Assay
sections.text: Transwell chambers (8 μm pores, Corning Inc., Corning NY) were pre-coated with matrigel (1.25 mg/mL) and incubated at 37 ℃ for 30 min. Add 200 μl (4 × 10 4 cells) serum-free medium of cell suspension to the upper chamber of the transwell, while 700 μl of complete medium containing 20% FBS was added to the lower chamber of the transwell. The cells were incubated in the incubator for 48 h. The upper layer of liquid was discarded from the transwell and soaked in 4% paraformaldehyde for 15 min. The chambers were washed three times with PBS (each time with slow shaking for 5 min). After staining with 0.1% crystalline violet for 15 min at room temperature, the chambers were washed three times with PBS. Cotton swabs were used to dab off the upper layer of unpenetrated cells from the chambers. Finally, the cells were observed and photographed under a high magnification microscope.

sections.title: Flow Cytometry Analysis
sections.text: In the cell transfection group, adenovirus was added directly to complete medium at a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 100. Flow cytometry was performed 48 h after infection to detect apoptosis or cell cycle. For apoptosis analysis, the apoptosis rate was detected by annexin V and PI double staining (cat. no. 640932; BioLegend, Inc.) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Briefly, cells were collected and washed once with PBS. Next, 100 µl Annexin V Binding Buffer was added to each tube to resuspend the cells. In total, 5 µl Annexin V-APC and 10 µl PI were added to stain the cells at room temperature in the dark for 15 min. Finally, the samples were transferred to flow-through sampling tubes after adding 400 µl buffer. For cell cycle assay, a DNA content assay kit to evaluate the cell cycle (cat. no. CA1510; Beijing Solarbio Science & Technology Co., Ltd.) was used after collection of each group of cells, following the instructions of the kit’s manufacturer. CytoFLEX S flow cytometer (Beckman Coulter, Inc.) was used to perform the assay.

sections.title: Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8) Assay
sections.text: 5 × 10 3 cells per well were seeded in 96-well plates and incubated overnight for adherence. After hypoxic intervention or transfection, CCK-8 assay was carried out at 0, 6, 24, 48, and 72 h. A total of 10 μl CCK-8 solution was added to each well, and the plates were incubated in an incubator for 0.5 h and 450 nm zymography was used to determine the OD value.

sections.title: qPCR Assay
sections.text: Total RNA from MPAECs was extracted according to the RNAiso plus manufacturer’s instructions (Invitrogen). Total RNA was reverse transcribed into cDNA according to the instructions of the reverse transcription kit (cat. no. RR037Q; Takara Biomedical Technology Co., Ltd.) and stored at −20 ℃. The sequence of the primers is as follows: GAPDH, which was used as the internal reference gene (upstream sequence 5′–3′: GGCACAGTCAAGGCTGAGAATG, downstream sequence 5′–3′: ATGGTGGGTGAAGACGCCAGTA); target gene lncRNA H19 gene (upstream sequence 5′–3′: TCGCTCCACTGACCTTCTAAAC, downstream sequence 5′–3′: CCTGCCTTTCTATGTGCCATTC); HIF-1α gene (upstream sequence 5′–3′: CCACCACAACTGCCACCACTG, downstream sequence 5′–3′: TGCCACTGTATGCTGATGCCTTAG). For microRNA, Mir-X miRNA First-Strand Synthesis Kit (Takara, Code No.:638315) was used for reverse transcription. miR-20a-5p gene (upstream sequence 5′–3′: CGGCGCTAAAGTGCTTATAGTGC, downstream sequence was obtained form the Mir-X miRNA First-Strand Synthesis Kit); U6 as the internal reference gene (upstream sequence 5′–3′: CTCGCTTCGGCAGCACA, downstream sequence 5′–3′: AACGCTTCACGAATTTGCGT). qPCR detection was performed using SYBR Green Mixture (cat. no. RR820Q; Takara Biomedical Technology Co., Ltd.). The reaction system and reaction conditions were prepared according to the instructions. There are three samples in each group, and each sample is set with two repetitions holes. The relative expression quantity (RQ) of the target genes was calculated using the ΔΔCq method (23): RQ = 2 −ΔΔCq .

sections.title: Western Blotting
sections.text: RIPA lysis buffer was used to lyse MPAECs at the end of the treatment period and sonication was used to fully lyse the cells. The cells were then centrifuged at 12,000 rpm for 10 min at 4 ℃. Next, the supernatant was separated and analyzed with BCA Protein Quantification Kit (cat. no. P0010S; Shanghai Biyuntian Biotechnology Co., Ltd) to adjust the total cellular protein concentration. Samples were then incubated at 100 ℃ for 5 min after adding 5X SDS-PAGE sample loading buffer. Proteins were separated by SDS-PAGE and then transferred to PVDF membranes, which were then blocked with skimmed milk. After three washes with TBS-Tween 20 (TBST) buffer, the primary antibody was added and incubated overnight on a shaker at 4 ℃, anti-HIF-1α (1:1000; cat. no. PA3-16,521; Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc.), anti-VEGF (1:1000; cat. no. MA5-13,182; Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc.), and anti-β-actin (1:1000; cat. no. AC026; ABclonal Technology Co.Ltd.). After three washes with TBST buffer, the secondary antibody was added and incubated at room temperature for 1–1.5 h. Subsequently, the proteins were visualized using ECL system (cat. no.WBULP; Merck Pty. Ltd.). Finally, ImageJ software (version 2022) was used for semiquantitative analysis of protein expression. β-actin was used as internal reference.

sections.title: Statistical Analysis
sections.text: The experimental data were statistically and analyzed using SPSS 23. 0 software (IBM Corp.). Mean ± standard deviation (Mean ± SD) was used to express the data results. Graphpad software (Version 9.0) was used to graph the statistics. For comparisons between the two groups, independent samples t tests were was performed. P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

sections.title: Hypoxia Induces Dysfunction and Promotes the Expression of lncRNA H19 and Angiogenesis-Related Genes in MPAECs
sections.text: The regulation of endothelial cell migration is fundamental to angiogenesis. Therefore, in this study, MPAECs were cultured in an atmospheric low oxygen workstation (3% O 2 , 5% CO 2 , 94% N 2 , 37 °C) or an atmospheric normoxic incubator (21% O 2 , 5% CO 2 , 74% N 2 , 37 °C) for 48 h, respectively. Transwell results showed that compared with the normoxic culture group, low oxygen treatment with 3% O 2 significantly promoted the migration of MPAECs (Fig. 1 A). As shown in Fig. 1 B, C, hypoxia significantly inhibited the apoptosis of MPAECs. MPAECs proliferation was enhanced under hypoxic conditions (Fig. 1 D). The above results suggest the successful establishment of a hypoxia-induced MPAECs dysfunction mimicking pulmonary hypertension model, which provides a basis for further investigation of the mechanism of vascular remodeling in PPHN. HIF-1α and VEGF are key factors of endothelial cell angiogenesis. In our study, qPCR results showed that hypoxia induction significantly promoted the expression level of lncRNA H19 in MPAECs (Fig. 1 E). In addition, the expression of HIF-1α mRNA was also significantly increased (Fig. 1 F). Further, hypoxia induction significantly upregulated HIF-1α and VEGF protein expression in MPAECs. This suggests that lncRNA H19 may be involved in mediating the potential role of angiogenesis in MPAECs.
path: Hypoxia Induces Dysfunction and Promotes the Expression of lncRNA H19 and Angiogenesis-Related Genes in MPAECs

sections.title: LncRNA H19 Promotes Protein Expression of HIF-1α and VEGF in MPAECs Under Hypoxic Conditions
sections.text: LncRNA H19 knockdown and overexpression cell models were constructed to further clarify the regulatory relationship between lncRNA H19 and HIF-1α/VEGF. The results showed that knockdown of lncRNA H19 significantly reduced the mRNA and protein levels of HIF-1α, as well as the protein expression levels of VEGF, under hypoxic conditions (Fig. 2 A–E). Conversely, the overexpression of lncRNA H19 significantly promote the mRNA and protein expression of HIF-1α, as well as the protein expression levels of VEGF (Fig. 2 F–J). This suggests that lncRNA H19 may play a critical role in hypoxia-induced pulmonary hypertension by regulating the HIF-1α/VEGF signaling pathway.
path: LncRNA H19 Promotes Protein Expression of HIF-1α and VEGF in MPAECs Under Hypoxic Conditions

sections.title: LncRNA H19 Affects Migration and Proliferation of MPAECs Under Hypoxic Conditions
sections.text: The migration and proliferation of MPAECs were detected by transwell and CCK8 assay in vitro. Transwell results showed that knockdown of lncRNA H19 significantly reduced the migration of MPAECs, while overexpression of lncRNA H19 significantly increased the migration of MPAECs (Fig. 3 A, B). In addition, CCK8 results showed that knocking down lncRNA H19 significantly inhibits proliferation of MPAECs, while overexpression of lncRNA H19 promotes proliferation of MPAECs (Fig. 3 C, D).
path: LncRNA H19 Affects Migration and Proliferation of MPAECs Under Hypoxic Conditions

sections.title: LncRNA H19 Affects Apoptosis and Cell Cycle of MPAECs Under Hypoxic Conditions
sections.text: Flow cytometry was used to further observe the effects of knockdown/overexpression of lncRNA H19 in a hypoxic environment on apoptosis in MPAECs. The results showed that the apoptosis of MPAECs was significantly increased after knock down the expression of lncRNA H19 (Fig. 4 A, B). Conversely, after overexpression of lncRNA H19, the anti-apoptotic ability of MPAECs was significantly enhanced (Fig. 4 C, D). The cell cycle includes the G1, S, G2, and M phases. Subsequently, the DNA content of the cells was detected using a flow cytometric sorter, which allowed for the determination of the temporal phase of the cell cycle that the cells were in and the proportion of cells in each phase. We found that the (G2 + S)/(G1 + G2 + S) ratio of endothelial cells was significantly reduced after inhibiting the expression of lncRNA H19 using shRNA, which suggests that the cell proliferation activity was significantly inhibited (Fig. 4 E, F). However, after overexpression of lncRNA H19, the (G2 + S)/(G1 + G2 + S) ratio of MPAECs was significantly increased, which indicated that the cell proliferative activity was increased (Fig. 4 G, H).
path: LncRNA H19 Affects Apoptosis and Cell Cycle of MPAECs Under Hypoxic Conditions

sections.title: miR-20a-5p Alleviates Dysfunction of MPAECs by Regulating the HIF-1α/VEGF Signaling Pathway
sections.text: Previous studies have shown that lncRNA H19 participated in the regulation of myofibroblast fibrosis by directly targeting miR-20a-5p (Lin et al. 2021 ). Our results confirmed that lncRNA H19 negatively regulates the expression of miR-20a-5p (Fig. 5 A, B). However, the effect of miR-20a-5p on MPAECs is unclear. Therefore, siRNA was used to knock down miR-20a-5p in MPAECs to further validate the targeted regulatory role of lncRNA H19. As shown in Fig. 5 C–E, after miR-20a-5p was knocked down in MPAECs, the mRNA and protein expression of HIF-1α were significantly increased. Furthermore, knockdown of miR-20a-5p significantly increased the migration (Fig. 5 H) and decreased the apoptosis (Fig. 5 I, J) of MPAECs.
path: miR-20a-5p Alleviates Dysfunction of MPAECs by Regulating the HIF-1α/VEGF Signaling Pathway

sections.title: lncRNA H19 Influences MPAECs Migration and Apoptosis by Regulating miR-20a-5p
sections.text: Using transwell and flow cytometry to examine the effects of knocking down or adding miR-20a-5p mimics on endothelial cell migration and apoptosis in the context of lncRNA H19 knockdown or overexpression. The results showed that in the case of lncRNA H19 inhibition using shRNA-LncRNA H19, adding siRNA-miR-20a-5p promoted endothelial cell migration and inhibited the apoptosis of MPAECs (Fig. 6 A, C, D). Conversely, in the case of lncRNA H19 overexpression, adding miR-20a-5p mimics inhibited endothelial cell migration and promoted endothelial cell apoptosis (Fig. 6 B, E, F). These findings indicate that lncRNA H19 affects endothelial cell function by regulating the expression of miR-20a-5p.
path: lncRNA H19 Influences MPAECs Migration and Apoptosis by Regulating miR-20a-5p

sections.title: Discussion
sections.text: PPHN is a clinical neonatal critical illness with a relatively high incidence, which may occur in 1–2 per 1,000 newborns (Rubin 2022 ; Kipfmueller, et al. 2022 ). It has become a disease associated with high morbidity, mortality, and disability (Ruoss et al. 2022 ; Chetan et al. 2022 ). Impaired relaxation of the pulmonary vasculature in the early postnatal period leads to pulmonary circulatory resistance exceeding body circulatory resistance, resulting in severe hypoxemia and respiratory distress, and ultimately PPHN (Sankaran and Lakshminrusimha 2022 ). Currently, the clinical treatment strategy for PPHN is focused on mechanical ventilation to maintain systemic circulatory pressure and reduce pulmonary hypertension (Pels et al. 2022 ). Neonatal care, including the use of inhaled NO and other vasodilators, improves the prognosis of infants with PPHN (Ball et al. 2023 ). However, clinical statistics show that ≤ 30% of newborns with PPHN do not respond to this treatment and require invasive life support measures (Nair and Lakshminrusimha 2014 ). Therefore, it is crucial to further explore effective novel treatment strategies for PPHN. The pathophysiology of PPHN is characterized by increased pulmonary vascular resistance, resulting in reduced pulmonary blood flow and, therefore, reduced oxygenated blood volume returning to the left side of the heart, leading to hypoxia, reduced end-organ perfusion, acidosis, and cyanosis. Therefore, hypoxic culture is common used to simulate the pathological state of PPHN in mechanistic studies (Dakshinamurti 2005 ). In the present study, hypoxic treatment with 3% O 2 was used to induce lung endothelial cell dysfunction to establish a PPHN cell model. The results showed that the proliferation and migration of endothelial cells were significantly promoted, while apoptosis was significantly decreased under hypoxic conditions. Previous study has also found that low oxygen environment promotes the vascular remodeling of endothelial cells (Chelladurai, et al. 2022 ), which is consistent with the present findings. LncRNAs are a kind of ncRNA with a length > 200 bp, which is widely involved in the occurrence and development of a variety of diseases, such as cancer and respiratory diseases (Paulin and Michelakis 2014 ). Previous studies have demonstrated that lncRNA H19 regulates endothelial cell function and angiogenesis in a variety of diseases, including glioma (Jia et al. 2016 ), hypoxic-ischemic brain damage (Fang et al. 2021 ), and arteriosclerosis obliterans (Li et al. 2019 ). In the current study, the hypoxic environment effectively promote the expression level of lncRNA H19 in MPAECs, which was accompanied by high expression of HIF-1α and VEGF. HIF-1α is an important transcription factor that regulates the effects of hypoxia. HIF-1α has a broad distribution and role, which can enhance the tolerance of vascular endothelial cell to hypoxia by regulating downstream target genes (Grover et al. 2005 ). It has been shown that increased HIF-1α signaling contributes to pulmonary vascular remodeling in adult pulmonary hypertension (Makker et al. 2019 ). VEGF is an important target gene for HIF-1α, as well as one of the most potent and critical regulators of pulmonary vascular growth, development, and maintenance throughout embryonic, fetal, and postnatal life (Jiang et al. 2015 ; Johns et al. 2016 ). VEGF is strongly expressed in the developing respiratory epithelium from the embryonic stage, and promotes angiogenesis by regulating endothelial cell proliferation, migration, and differentiation (Pugliese et al. 2015 ; Maron et al. 2016 ; Thompson and Lawrie 2017 ). Disruption of VEGF gene expression leads to severe defects in blood vessel formation. Loss of a single VEGF allele results in a notable reduction in endothelial cells, which in turn causes early embryonic mortality (Krishnan and Rosenzweig 2015 ). Previous studies have reported elevated lung VEGF mRNA in chronic hypoxia-induced pulmonary hypertension (Tuder et al. 1995 ; Christou et al. 1998 ). In addition, IL-33 expression is elevated in human pulmonary artery epithelial cells under hypoxic conditions, which may be due to the increased downstream expression of HIF-1α and VEGF. This, in turn, triggers vascular remodeling and leading to hypoxic pulmonary hypertension (Liu et al. 2018 ), which is consistent with the present results. A recent clinical study has also demonstrated  that newborns with PPHN exhibit lower levels of VEGF in their blood (Lassus et al. 2001 ). In addition, another study demonstrated a reduction in pulmonary VEGF due to monocrotaline-mediated pulmonary hypertension (Partovian et al. 1998 ). These studies suggest the involvement of non-hypoxia-dependent mechanisms that may regulate pulmonary VEGF expression, such as altered hemodynamic stress. Therefore, the expression of VEGF and its intrinsic regulatory mechanisms in PPHN models mediated by different mechanisms need to be further explored. The current study focused on lncRNA H19, which is the upstream of the HIF-1α and VEGF genes. It was found that hypoxia induced elevated expression of lncRNA H19 in pulmonary artery epithelial cells of mice, suggesting that lncRNA H19 is involved in mediating angiogenesis in MPAECs. Numerous studies have demonstrated that lncRNAs play powerful regulatory functions in biological processes at the epigenetic, transcriptional, and post-transcriptional levels (Qin, et al. 2021 ; Qin, et al. 2020 ; Boucherat et al. 2017 ). Previous research has revealed that vascular remodeling is the result of pulmonary artery smooth muscle cell over proliferation and arterial endothelial cell dysfunction (Kim 2014 ). LncRNA H19 plays a central role in vascular smooth muscle cell proliferation and myocardial extracellular matrix alteration, suggesting that it may be a potential drug target in pulmonary arterial hypertension. In addition, it has been shown that patients with end-stage pulmonary arterial hypertension have significantly increased levels of lncRNA H19 in their blood, which is positively correlated with the degree of right ventricular hypertrophy (Su et al. 2018 ). The lncRNA H19/let-7b axis was reported to be involved in PDGF-BB-stimulated pulmonary artery vascular remodeling (Sun et al. 2019 ). Similarly, Wang et al. (Wang et al. 2018 ) reported an upregulation of lncRNA H19 in a melatonin-mediated rat model of pulmonary hypertension. Targeted modulation of the lncRNA H19/miR-200a/PDCD4 axis exerts therapeutic effects in pulmonary arterial hypertension in rats. The above results suggest that lncRNA H19 may play a critical role in the pathological progression of PPHN. In the present study, the anti-apoptotic ability of MPAECs was impaired after lncRNA H19 was knocked down. Conversely, overexpression of lncRNA H19 significantly enhanced the anti-apoptotic ability of MPAECs, which is consistent with previous findings. It has been reported that miR-20a-5p is a target of lncRNA H19 (Lin et al. 2021 ), and the current results also found that lncRNA H19 could negatively regulate the expression of miR-20a-5p. However, it is not yet known whether lncRNA H19 affects endothelial cell function through regulating miR-20a-5p under hypoxic conditions. Therefore, miR-20a-5p siRNA or mimics were added while knocking down or overexpressing lncRNA H19. The results showed that this effectively reversed the effects of lncRNA H19 on endothelial cell migration and apoptosis, which indicates that lncRNA H19 may be involved in regulating the HIF-1α/VEGF signaling pathway by targeting miR-20a-5p to promote the improvement of pulmonary artery endothelial cell function. Thus, the present results suggest that the lncRNA H19/miR-20a-5p/HIF-1α/VEGF regulatory axis may play an important role in the pathological regulatory process of PPHN. Notably, the current PPHN cell model exposure factor was a hypoxic environment. Combined with the results of previous studies, it was found that different environmental and temporal exposure factors may lead to different results. Therefore, further studies are still needed to investigate and validate the PPHN regulatory mechanisms in different models. Although our results revealed that lncRNA H19 may interfere with vascular remodeling in hypoxia-induced pulmonary hypertension by upregulating the expression of HIF-1α and VEGF in MPAECs, and the lncRNA H19/miR-20a-5p/HIF-1α/VEGF regulatory axis may play a key regulatory role in the PPHN process, there are still several limitations in the present study. Firstly, our study focuses on cell experiments and did not investigate the function of lncRNA H19 in animal model. Therefore, whether lncRNA H19 can be used as a therapeutic target for PPHN still needs further investigation. Secondly, the target of lncRNA H19 is based on others’ research, and new targets will be sought through high-throughput sequencing in subsequent studies.
