Cancer Biology & Oncology.title: Optimization of the formulation of Tubiechong gel plaster and its effect on fracture healing by promoting angiogenesis in a rat model
Cancer Biology & Oncology.abstract: Background and aimTransdermal drug delivery has been used in traditional Chinese medicine for thousands of years and is worth further developing. The purpose of this study was to investigate the preparation method of Tubiechong gel plaster (TGP) and evaluate its activity to promote fracture healing.Experimental procedureUsing rat skin as a barrier, and the human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) proliferation promotion rate of the receiving solution as the evaluation index, the in vitro permeability of the plaster was studied by Franz diffusion cell method. A modified Einhorn method was used to model rat tibia fractures. The bone healing process was monitored by radiography. Bone development and angiogenesis were assessed by Safranin O Fast Green staining and CD31 immunohistochemistry, respectively. Serum bone metabolites and VEGF levels were determined by ELISA method.Results and conclusionThe optimal dose of azone for TGP is 2 %. The transdermal penetration equation for this plaster is consistent with the Ritger-Peppas equation. The prepared plaster was stable for at least 3 months. X-ray images showed that the fracture healing was promoted by TGP in a dose-related form at all periods. Serum BALP, OC, CTX-I, and VEGF levels also indicated better fracture healing after treatment. TGP significantly stimulated angiogenesis and bone growth at the fracture site on days 7,14 and 21, and the effect of promoting bone growth was shown on the third day. These data prove that the prepared Tubiechong gel plasters can promote fracture healing by promoting angiogenesis.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.text: 1 Due to its multifaceted advantages: no liver first-pass effect, high safety, easy to use, long-lasting drug effect, etc., transdermal delivered medicines have a large market space. It is estimated that the global market of transdermal drug delivery systems (TDDS) will reach 9.6 billion US dollars by 2027. 1 More than 30 years have passed since the FDA approved the first transdermal patch, scopolamine transdermal patch, in 1979. 2 Due to the physiological barrier of the epidermis, there are only a limited number of drugs suitable for patch preparations, and only more than 30 drugs have been developed and marketed transdermal preparations, mainly including anti-inflammatory, analgesic, psychotropical, and hormonal drugs. 3 However, transdermal administration has been used in traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) for thousands of years, and various diseases can be treated percutaneously, such as trauma, dermatology, gynecology, pediatrics, and visceral diseases. 4 Developing modern transdermal agents from topical traditional Chinese medicine is one of the paths with great development potential. Tubiechong is a commonly used Chinese medicine in clinical practice, included in more than 200 kinds of Chinese patent medicines. It is the dried body of the female worm of the Steleophaga plancyi (Boleny) or Eupolyphaga sinensis Walker. Tubiechong has a long history of clinical application, and it was recorded in the book “Shen Nong Ben Cao Jing” (Shennong's herbal classic) as early as the first century BC, that is, the Qin and Han dynasties. Clinically, topical use of Tubiechong is very common. There are 138 topical agents in the 2020 edition of the Chinese Pharmacopoeia 5 ; of which 5 contain Tubiechong and another 2 Chinese patent medicines containing Tubiechong can be used externally or orally. As a TCM for blood activation and stasis, it is clinically used in the treatment of a variety of diseases, such as: traumatic injury, low back pain, cardiovascular disease, tumors or mass and nodule, cervical spondylopathy, osteoarthritis and psoriasis. 6 Therefore, developing topical preparations of Tubiechong has high potential value and low risk. Promoting fracture healing is one of the most important clinical treatments of Tubiechong. In folk clinical practice, oral or topical use of Tubiechong can promote fracture healing, and modern research also proved that Tubiechong could facilitate the recovery of animal models of fractures. 7 The formulas containing Tubiechong are also commonly used in the treatment of bone diseases. For example, the Chinese Pharmacopoeia (2020 Edition) includes 34 kinds of Chinese patent medicines containing Tubiechong, 16 of which are used to treat bruises or trauma. Fractures are a common orthopedic disease in clinical practice. Although fractures can heal on their own, about 2–20 % of fractures do not heal properly, 8 and there is still a lack of ideal drugs. New safe and effective drugs are expected. The existing drugs are mainly administered orally. Preclinical and clinical trials have shown that TDDS-administered bone diseases are safer and more effective than oral administration for bone diseases., and TDDS is considered to be a promising tool for the treatment of various bone diseases. 9 Therefore, in this study, the fracture-promoting activity of the Tubiechong gel plaster (TGP) was selected for evaluation. Gel plaster is a kind of external dosage form with water-soluble polymer as matrix and skeleton material, which is very suitable for TCM. TCM is mostly a mixture of multiple ingredients, the amount of medicine is large, generally extracted and refined into a certain concentration of extract, prepared into the patch. The large loading of gel plaster meets this requirement well. 10 In addition, compared with TCM transdermal dosage form black plaster and modern rubber ointment, gel plaster contains excellent characteristics such as moisturizing, good air permeability, anti-aging, non-irritating and allergic, and comfortable to adhere, making it an ideal dosage form for TCM transdermal preparations. 11 At present, there are 9 TCM gel plasters on the market, and more are in the research stage. It has been reported that 181 traditional Chinese medicines were used in the development of gel plasters. 12 In this paper, the preparation method of Tubiechong gel plaster was studied, and the optimal addition amount of azone (1-Dodecylhexahydro-2H-azepin-2-one), a penetration enhancer, was determined according to the activity evaluation, and the performance of the prepared gel plaster was evaluated. Since the topical use of Tubiechong is more frequent in the treatment of bruises, this paper evaluated its activity in promoting fracture healing with animal experiments, and preliminarily explored its mechanism of action. This study would provide a reference for the development of gel plasters related to Tubiechong.

sections.title: Preparation of Tubiechong gel plasters
sections.text: 2.2 The Tubiechong decoction lyophilizate (TDL) was prepared following the method previously established in our laboratory. 13

sections.title: Preparation of gel plasters with different azone content
sections.text: 2.2.1 The prescribed amount of tartaric acid, distilled water, and TDL is stirred evenly as phase A; and glycerin, sodium polyacrylate NP-700 (Showa Denko, Tokyo, Japan), aluminum glycyrrhizinate and kaolin in the prescribed amount are stirred evenly as phase B. A certain amount of azone was added to the B phase to stir, so that the mass concentration of azone was finally 0 %, 1 %, 2, 3 %, 4 % and 5 %, respectively. Phase A is added into phase B while stirring at a speed of about 60 rpm/min, and stirred evenly. It is then coated on a non-woven fabric, covered with anti-mucous film, and left at room temperature for 3 days. 14
path: Preparation of gel plasters with different azone content

sections.title: Preparation of gel plasters for animal experiment
sections.text: 2.2.2 Gel plasters with azone content of 2 % and TDL content of 0, 2.45 %, 4.9 % and 9.8 % were prepared for animal experiments according to the experimental method in 2.1.1 above. The formulation of the gel plaster is shown in Table 1 . The prepared gel plaster was cut into discs with a diameter of 1 cm, and the amount of TDL per disc in the negative control (NC), low (TL), medium (TM) and high (TH) dose groups was 0, 5.19, 10.37, 20.74 mg, respectively. The positive control (PC) is DiedaZhentong Gao (Guangzhou Baiyunshan Pharmaceutical Group Co., Ltd.with a cream content of 35 mg/cm 2 , lot number: U1045, 27.4 mg/patch).
path: Preparation of gel plasters for animal experiment

sections.title: Organoleptic characteristics of prepared plasters
sections.text: 2.3 The prepared plaster was physically inspected for its appearance, color, uniformity, smoothness thickness, feeling of application, and skin followability. The weight per square centimeter of the plaster is detected. Three plasters (1 cm 2 ) from each group were randomly selected and weighed individually. Then, the average weight and standard deviation were calculated. The thickness of the patches was measured by means of a micrometer screw gauge at the 4 edges and the center of the plaster. The results were expressed as average thickness ± SD.

sections.title: Stability studies
sections.text: 2.4 The prepared final TGP containing 2 % azone was subjected to a 3-month accelerated stability study to evaluate its physical appearance, adhesion properties and changes in the chemical composition of the drug in the formulation. The gel plasters were kept in sealed plastic bags at temperature 25 ± 2 °C and RH (relative humidity) 60 ± 10 % (long-term condition), and 40° ± 2 °C and RH 75 ± 5 % (accelerated condition) separately in the stability chamber. Tacking strength, cohesive strength, peeling strength of samples and changes in chemical composition of in vitro releases was analyzed before and after 3 months. The composition of the in vitro release solution of gel plaster was detected by high performance liquid chromatography (HPLC).

sections.title: Adhesive evaluation
sections.text: 2.5 The adhesive was determined by the method specified in Item 0952, Part IV of Chinese Pharmacopoeia. 5

sections.title: Tacking strength
sections.text: 2.5.1 The tacking strength of the gel plaster was determined using a tacking strength tester (CZY-G, Labthink, Jinan, China) according to the slope rolling ball determination method. The diameter of the largest steel ball that happens to stick to the plaster is taken as a result; the test is repeated three times and averaged.

sections.title: Cohesive strength
sections.text: 2.5.2 The cohesive strength of the gel plaster was measured by CZY-25 cohesive tester (Labthink, Jinan, China). The gel plaster (3cm × 6 cm) was pasted at the central junction of the two stainless steel plates, squeezed back and forth 3 times with a 2 kg pressure roller at its own weight, and then hung on the tester, placed vertically, hung 200 g weight, recorded the time (s) of the steel plate falling, tested twice in parallel, and averaged.

sections.title: Peeling strength
sections.text: 2.5.3 The test was conducted according to the 180° peel strength test method using the BLD-200N electronic peel tester (Labthink, Jinan, China). The test gel plaster was patched on a clean stainless steel plate, squeezed back and forth with a 2 kg pressure roller with its own weight 3 times, placed for 10 min, and then placed in the tester for peeling experiment. It was pulled away from the stainless-steel plate by the dynamometer at a speed of 300 mm/min and made a 180°-fold back, the reading displayed by the dynamometer was recorded. It was tested in parallel 3 times, and the average value was taken.

sections.title: HPLC analysis
sections.text: 2.6 The changes of the components in the TGP release liquid were analyzed by using Shimadzu High performance liquid chromatography (Shimadzu, LC-10AD, Japan) system with LC-10Advp pumps, auto-sampler (SIL-10AD), and UV–Vis detector (Shimadzu, SPD-10AV, Japan). The TGP release liquid was prepared by using Franz-type vertical static diffusion cells. The experimental method is the same as below method 2.8.2, and the barrier is changed from rat skin to 3.5 kD dialysis membrane (Beijing BioDee Biotechnology Co. Ltd., Beijing, China). The HPLC conditions were as follows: stationary phase: C18 (250 mm*4.6 mm, 5 μm); mobile phase: ultrapure water (A) and methanol (B) in gradient: 0–25 min, 95-0% A, 5–100 % B; flow rate: 1.0 mL/min; detective wavelength: 254 nm; column temperature: 30 °C; total injection volume: 10 μL.

sections.title: Animals
sections.text: 2.7 Male Sprague-Dawley (SD) rats (initial weight 250 ± 20 g) were purchased from Speyford Biotechnology Co., Ltd. ((No.: SCXK (Beijing) 2019–0010), Beijing, China) and reared from 6 weeks of age. Each rat was housed individually in an animal care center with a 12-h light/dark cycle and free access to food and water. The room temperature was adjusted to 25 ± 2 °C with a relative humidity of 40–65 %. All animal research was conducted in accordance with the principles and procedures approved by the Animal Resources Committee of Beijing University of Chinese Medicine, which are based on the International Guiding Principles for Biomedical Research Involving Animals (approval number: Kj-dw-18-20141,230-01).

sections.title: Preparation of rat skin in vitro
sections.text: 2.8.1 Male SD rats were killed by necking off. The hair of the abdominal was carefully removed with a hair shaver. The abdominal skin was taken and placed in a watch dish. The subcutaneous fat layer was repeatedly wiped with a cotton ball until it was completely removed. The rat skin was washed several times with PBS, dried with filter paper, cut to a suitable size, wrapped with tin foil, frozen in −20 °C until further use. 15
path: Preparation of rat skin in vitro

sections.title: In vitro permeation tests
sections.text: 2.8.2 The in vitro permeation tests were performed using Franz-type vertical static diffusion cells (TK-20D, Shanghai Kaikai Technology Trade Co., Ltd，Shanghai, China) with an effective diffusion area of 1.76 cm 2 and receptor volume of 8 mL. The skin was equilibrated in phosphate buffer solution (Ph 7.4) for 1 h and horizontally fixed between the receiving chamber and the diffusion chamber, and its cuticle was towards the diffusion chamber. The Franz cell sandwich was maintained at the temperature of 32 ± 0.5 °C with circulator water bath. The receiver medium was continuously stirred (300 rpm) with a small magnetic bar. Each gel plaster prepares 8 samples in parallel. At a predetermined time (1, 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 24 h), all the liquid in the receptor compartment was removed, filtered through a 0.45 μm microporous membrane, lyophilized, and stored. Each experiment was replicated three times. The steady-state transdermal efficiency of the drug was indirectly evaluated by the cell proliferative rate Q (%) of transdermal solution at different times, and the calculation method was Q drug-containing ointment group - Q blank paste group, and J（%/h）, the slope of the linear part obtained by plotting Q vs. Time t, represents the steady-state transdermal rate of the drug.

sections.title: HUVECs proliferation activity assay
sections.text: 2.8.3 HUVECs (originally from Shanghai Cell Biology Institute of Chinese Academy of Sciences (Shanghai, China)) in logarithmic growth phase and in good condition were uniformly seeded in 96-well plates, 100 μL per well, and the number of cells was 2 × 10 3 . After 24 h of culture, they were treated with test solutions, and the control group was cell culture medium DMEM (Gibco, Carlsbad, CA, USA). After 24 h of treatment, cells were incubated with MTT (3-(4,5-dimethylthiazole-2)-2,5-diphenyl tetrazozolium bromide) (Sigma, United States) solution for 4 h, and the product formazan was dissolved in DMSO. The absorbance value of each well was measured at a wavelength of 570 nm using a microplate reader (Model: EPOCH, Serial: #130315 A, BioTek, USA). The cell proliferation rate calculation formula is as follows: [EQ:EQ2]

sections.title: Evaluation of Tubiechong gel plasters in promoting fracture healing in rats
path: Evaluation of Tubiechong gel plasters in promoting fracture healing in rats

sections.title: Design of animal experiments
sections.text: 2.9.1 The 84 rats were divided into 6 groups, including 30 each in the NC and TM groups, and 6 in each of the other 4 groups (BC, TL, TH, PC). The closed tibia fracture rat model was established by a modified Einhorn method (Wei et al., 2022). Patch therapy was started on the day of the fracture, and the duration of therapy is 10 h per day. At 0, 3, 7, 14, and 21 days of treatment, six rats were taken from the TM and NC groups, respectively, for histochemical analysis.
path: Evaluation of Tubiechong gel plasters in promoting fracture healing in rats

sections.title: Radiological analysis
sections.text: 2.9.2 X-rays were taken to record the fracture site at 0, 7, 14, 17 and 21 days after the rat tibia fracture was modeled. After anesthetizing the rats by intraperitoneal injection of 3 % pentobarbital sodium (0.1 ml/100 g), the right tibia was photographed by BLX-5 portable X-ray machine (Zhengzhou Tianjie Electronics Co., Ltd., Zhengzhou, China). The selected exposure time was 1.5 s, and the voltage was 60 kV. Fracture healing was scored according to the previously described radiographic healing score scale for rat fractures. 13
path: Evaluation of Tubiechong gel plasters in promoting fracture healing in rats

sections.title: Detection of bone metabolism indicators
sections.text: 2.9.3 To detect the content of serum markers of bone formation in different treatment groups, serum was collected at sacrifice after 21 days of patching treatment in rats. The amount of bone alkaline phosphatase (BALP) and osteocalcin (OC) and the C-terminal content of type I collagen (CTX-I) in rat serum was measured using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) according to the protocol provided by the manufacturer (Nanjing, Jiancheng Bioengineering, China).
path: Evaluation of Tubiechong gel plasters in promoting fracture healing in rats

sections.title: Immunohistochemical staining and safranin O/fast green staining
sections.text: 2.9.4 Rat tibial samples obtained at 0, 3, 7, 14, and 21 days postoperatively were decalcified and embedded in paraffin, cut into 6 μm thick sections. Immunohistochemical staining was performed as previously described. 13 After dewaxed and dehydrated, the sections were incubated with CD31 primary antibody (CD31, Changzhou, Jiangsu, China) and horseradish peroxidase conjugated secondary antibody (Thermo Fisher, Cambridge, MA, USA), stained with DAB (Solarbio, Beijing, China), and finally counterstained with hematoxylin (Solarbio, Beijing, China). The cross-sectional area of CD31-positive blood vessels in a random area around the fracture scab was measured by ImageJ (National Institutes of Health in Bethesda, Maryland, USA). For safranin O/fast green staining, the slices were stained with fast green stain solution (Servicebio, Wuhan, China) for 3–4 min, then rinsed with water, and then treated with safranin O solution (Servicebio, Wuhan, China) for 15–30 s. The sections were put into three cylinders of anhydrous ethanol for 5 min and xylene for 5 min. Finally, they were mounted with neutral balsam. The normal cartilage appears red, and the collagen fibers appear blue. The images were observed and recorded with a super-resolution microscopic imaging system (Leica Aperio VERSA, Weztlar, German).
path: Evaluation of Tubiechong gel plasters in promoting fracture healing in rats
Immunohistochemical staining and safranin O/fast green staining

sections.title: Statistical analysis
sections.text: 2.10 Data from at least 3 independent experiments are expressed as mean ± standard deviation (SD) and analyzed by SAS software (version 8.0; SAS Institute, Cary, NC, USA). The difference between each group was analyzed by One Way Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) and T-test. In all analyses, P < 0.05 indicates statistical significance.

sections.title: Transdermal penetration of Tubiechong gel plaster
sections.text: 3.1 We have preliminarily studied the basic prescription of the Tubiechong gel plaster. 14 To better penetrate the drug into the skin, the penetration enhancer azone (1-dodecylazacycloheptan-2-one) is tried to be added to the prescription. The Franz diffusion cell method was used to find the best amount of azone added, with the isolated rat abdominal skin as the barrier and the HUVECs proliferation promoting rate of the receiving solution as the evaluation index ( Fig. 1 ). The results showed that the addition of different concentrations of azone significantly increased the promotion rate of TGP permeate on the proliferation of HUVECs. Within 24 h, when the amount of azone added was 2 %, the penetration effect was the best, followed by 5 %. After 6 h of percutaneous treatment, the cell proliferation promotion rate of the 2 % azone group was significantly higher than that of other groups (P < 0.05), and after 24 h of percutaneous treatment, its ability to promote cell proliferation was 4.75 times that of the control group. The relationship between Q and t was fitted with different equations, and the results showed that the transdermal penetration equation of TGP was consistent with the Ritger-Peppas equation and did not fit well for both the zero-order equation and the Higuchi equation ( Table 2 ). Except for the 0 % and 3 % azone groups, the Ritger-Peppas equation release parameters of the other groups were greater than 0.89, which means the mechanism of drugs release involves skeletal dissolution.
path: Transdermal penetration of Tubiechong gel plaster

sections.title: Organoleptic characteristics
sections.text: 3.2 The prepared plaster is shown in Supplementary Fig. S1 . It is brown, has a thickness of 2.92 ± 0.16 mm and a weight of 264.2 ± 13.8 mg/cm 2 . This plaster shows excellent homogeneity, skin adhesive property and skin followability. Its surface is smooth and clump-free, uniform in thickness and color. When the plaster is applied to the outside of the subject's right wrist, the plaster does not fall off after the subject shakes his hand 10 times. There is no residue when the plaster is applied to the back of the hand and then removed, and the surface of the removed plaster remains intact.

sections.title: Stability studies
sections.text: 3.3 The stability results of TGP are shown in Table 3 . The data indicated that there was no significant difference in the physical appearance, tacking strength, cohesive strength, and peeling strength determined at the beginning and at 3 months of the accelerated and long-term stability studies. The chromatographic of the in vitro release solution of gel plaster did not change after 3 months of storage at different temperatures ( Supplementary Fig. S2 .). Therefore, the TGP is stable in terms of physical appearance, adhesive properties, and drug composition for at least 3 months.

sections.title: Radioactivity analysis
sections.text: 3.4 X-ray images ( Fig. 2 ) on the day of modeling clearly showed the broken tibia of the module-making rat, indicating that the modeling was successful. On day 7 of treatment, there was a small amount of callus formation in the TH group treated with TGP. On the 14th day of treatment, the callus at the fracture site in the TH group was almost reconnected, and the callus formation in the PC, TL and TM groups was obvious. On day 17 of treatment, fracture sites in the PC and TH groups had relatively intact callus fillings and a large number of external callus formations, while fracture sites in the NC, TL and TM groups had soft callus fillings. On the 21st day of treatment, the fracture recovery effect was the best in the PC group and the TH group, the fracture site was completely filled with callus, the bone cortex was reconstructed, the diaphysis shape was restored, and the medullary cavity was recanalized. The degree of fracture healing in the TL group and the TM group was not as good as that of the first two groups, but it was also better than that of the NC group, in which the callus was basically filled, while the callus at the fracture site in the NC group was still not filled. Fig. 2 B is the result of the degree of fracture healing quantified by scoring.

sections.title: Differences in serum bone metabolism index and VEGF content
sections.text: 3.5 Biochemical markers of bone turnover have long been used to complement the radiological evaluation of patients with bone disease. Serum levels of markers of bone metabolism differ at different stages of fracture healing. They have been used to evaluate the characteristics of different stages of fracture healing. 16 BALP is often used as an early marker of osteogenic differentiation, and CTX-I can be used as an indicator of bone resorption status. BALP and CTX-I are elevated after fracture, and gradually return to normal after the fracture heals. 17 CTX is elevated in the early stages of fracture, reflecting increased bone resorption. CTX peaks in the middle of a fracture, which may be due to processes such as inflammation and fibrous callus formation leading to substantial bone resorption. When CTX decreases in the later stages of fracture, the rate of bone metabolism is further reduced, close to normal. 18 The serum levels of BALP and CTX-I in the model (NC) group were significantly higher than those in the unfractured (BC) group (P < 0.001) at 21 days after surgery ( Fig. 3 A and B), indicating that the fracture repair was still in the active period. Their contents in the treatment groups and the positive group were lower than those in the model group, which converged with the data of the BC group, indicating that the fractures in these groups were better repaired. The level of OC in serum reflects the activity of newly formed osteoblasts. 19 In the early stages of a fracture, the level of OC may drop because the body needs to mobilize all its resources to repair the damage. As the healing process progresses, the level of OC gradually rises as it is involved in the formation and mineralization of new bone. Its content correlates with how active fracture healing is. 19 The OC content in the Tubiechong-treated group increased in a dose-dependent manner ( Fig. 3 C), indicating that TGP application could promote bone formation rate. There was no significant increase in OC levels in the positive group, possibly because the mechanism by which this positive drug promotes fracture healing is not related to OC. Studies have shown that in the process of fracture healing, the expression of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) in serum shows a regularity of increasing in the early stage and then slowly decreasing. 20 From the results of Fig. 3 D, it can be seen that the model group has the highest VEGF content, indicating that the fracture site was still in the healing process. The VEGF content in the high-dose group was significantly lower than that in other experimental groups (P < 0.01), and there was no significant difference from the BC group, indicating that the new angiogenesis in the high-dose group was nearing the end. These data suggest that TGP treatment could effectively accelerate the progress of angiogenesis, thereby promoting fracture healing.
path: Differences in serum bone metabolism index and VEGF content

sections.title: Safranin O and fast green staining analysis
sections.text: 3.6 The effect of TGP on cartilage formation and ossification process at the tibia fracture site was analyzed by safranin O and fast green staining, as shown in Fig. 4 , the red part was cartilage, and the blue part represented collagen fibers. No chondrocytes were visible one day after surgery; 3 days after the fracture, cells gathered at the fracture site, and some cells began to differentiate into chondrocytes; there was no significant difference between treatment and control groups at these two time points ( Fig. 4 B). The zoomed-in photograph shows that the chondrocytes in both the control and TPG groups began to grow vigorously, and a large number of relatively small chondrocytes with blue nuclei and red cytoplasm can be clearly seen. 7 days after surgery, a large number of cells in Tubiechong-treated group differentiated into chondrocytes, while only some cells in the control group began to differentiate into small pieces of cartilage callus; The data of Image J software analysis showed that the number of chondrocytes in the TGP group was significantly higher than that in the control group (p < 0.01). On day 14, the number of chondrocytes in the TGP group peaked, fibrous callus and cartilaginous callus formation were seen, and new trabecular bone formation was seen. While in the control group, cartilage bone callus began to form. On day 21, most of the cartilage callus in the TGP group had completed endochondral ossification, most of the callus had formed woven bone, lamellar bone formation may be seen locally, while endochondral ossification in the control group was ongoing, and some tissues had formed a small amount of woven bone. This result indicates that the topical application of the TGP can significantly accelerate the cartilage and osteogenesis processes during fracture healing.
path: Safranin O and fast green staining analysis

sections.title: Immunohistochemical expression of CD31 in callus tissue
sections.text: 3.7 H-type blood vessels closely regulate the coupling of angiogenesis and osteogenesis in long bones and are therefore closely related to fracture healing. Strong CD31 positivity is one of its important features, so its immunohistochemical staining can be used to analyze the number and area of H-type blood vessels. It can be seen from Fig. 5 that the number of vessels and vascular area in the Tubiechong-treated group were significantly higher than those in the control group after 7 days of postoperative treatment. Especially on days 7 and 21, macrovascular fusion was more common in the Tubiechong-treated group than in the control group. The results suggested that the TGP treatment enhanced the healing of tibia fractures in rats by promoting the formation of H-type vessels.
path: Immunohistochemical expression of CD31 in callus tissue

sections.title: Discussion and conclusion
sections.text: 4 We have preliminarily determined the basic prescription of the Tubiechong gel plaster. 14 In this study, the optimal dose of the permeabilizing agent azone was evaluated by the proliferative activity of transdermal release solution on HUVECs. Since Tubiechong extract is a mixture with unknown active substance, the permeation efficiency of the active substance can be better reflected using a bioactivity assessment. Our previous experiments found that the fracture-promoting activity of Tubiechong was positively correlated with its HUVECs proliferation-promoting activity in vitro , so we have used the later as an evaluation index. The optimal formulation and preparation process were determined, and finally the Tubiechong gel plaster with excellent viscosity and stability was obtained. Azone is a commonly used and effective chemical penetration promoter that interacts with lipids of stratum corneum and disrupts the lipid accumulation arrangement of the bilayer. 21 Azone has been used to deliver drugs such as levamisole hydrochloride, ketoprofen, dimethyl fumarate, and 5-fluorouracil. 22 This study proved that the optimal dosage of azone for the TGP is 2 %. The optimal prescription for final 100 g TGP is TDL 10 g, tartaric acid 0.36 g, water 26.89 g, azone 2 g, NP-700 11.2 g, aluminum glycinate 0.45 g, kaolin 9 g, glycerin 40.1 g. Azone is a widely used permeabilizer in cosmetics and medicine. The reference dosage of azone in topical preparations is generally between 0.5 % and 2.5 %, which can achieve obvious osmotic effect. 23 According to existing toxicological studies, azone is considered safe because it is virtually non-toxic. However, in the actual use process, it may still cause some side effects. Common side effects include itchy skin, redness, sneezing, coughing, and sore skin. In some special cases, it may cause drowsiness and fatigue, may affect attention and reaction ability, and may be harmful to the safety of activities such as driving and operating machinery. 24 Therefore, it is a safer strategy to minimize the dosage of permeabilizers while ensuring that the drug works effectively. In the previous experiments, we found that the dose of permeabilizer in the plaster had an effect on the treatment effect of fractures, but the dose of TGP had a greater effect on the effect of promoting fracture healing. In general, in patches, the relationship between permeabilization and actual efficacy is more complex due to the effect of sustained-release, and more experiments are required to determine the optimal drug dose and permeabilizer dose ratio. In this study, 1 % and 3 % remained almost equivalent to 5 % after more than 15 h of continuous action, and a 1 % nitrogen ketone dosage may also be appropriate. This is to be tried in the future when further optimization of the prescription is made. Fracture healing is the process of callus formation and transformation, which can be roughly divided into 4 stages. 25 A large hematoma is first formed at the fracture site and a mild inflammatory response is produced to induce fracture repair. After that, the peristeum adjacent to the fracture site germinal layer cells proliferate, the peristeum thickens, the periosteal progenitors differentiate in the direction of cartilage, and the chondroblasts secrete a large amount of extracellular matrix, Cartilage is formed. In the third step, the cartilage tissue is further replaced by bone tissue (woven bone) to repair the fracture through intrachondral osteogenesis. Finally, the bone is remodeled to restore the normal cortical bone structure and the fracture heals. 26 Based on the overall experimental data, we believe that the TGP acts on the cartilage formation link of fracture healing. On the 7th day, the angiogenesis of the TGP group was significantly higher than that of the NC group, which provided sufficient nutrients and oxygen for the growth of cartilage at this stage, and by the 14th day, the growth of cartilage in the TGP group had reached its peak, while the chondrogenesis in the control group continued to increase. X-ray analysis also showed that the degree of fracture healing in the TGP group was much higher than that in the control group at day 14. Therefore, the time point when TGP has a stronger effect may begin around day 7. Fracture healing is a complex process involving many different processes and their coordination with each other, 25 in which angiogenesis plays a very important role. 26 In the process of fracture healing, the newly formed blood vessels not only provide various nutrient molecules for bone metabolism, but also participate in the transport of bone metabolites. In particular, H-type blood vessels play an important role in the process of bone formation, which is characterized by the expression of CD31 and the endomucin Emcn. 27 Our preliminary experiments indicate that Tubiechong decoction could promote tibia fracture healing in rats by regulating angiogenesis. 14 In this research, the extract of the Tubiechong was made into a gel plaster, and its pro-fracture healing activity and pro-angiogenic activity were well preserved. In addition, the immunohistochemistry experiment of CD31 and the Safranin O and fast green staining simultaneously detected the process of angiogenesis and bone formation at 0, 3, 7, 14, and 21 days after fracture, respectively. We found that the TGP was very effective in promoting angiogenesis at the fracture site on day 7, indicating that its effect began earlier than 7 days. However, on the third day, its angiogenic effect was not significant, yet by this time its ability to promote bone formation had been revealed. This suggests that in addition to promoting angiogenesis, the TGP also has other ways of promoting fracture healing. Modern studies have found that in addition to promoting fracture healing, Tubiechong also has a wide range of pharmacological effects such as dissolving thrombi, anticoagulation, antitumor, lowering blood lipids, hypoxia resistance, analgesia, antibacterial, anti-ischemia and hypoxia, and protecting vascular endothelial cells and nerve cells. 6 , 28 In this study, we found that the TGP was able to reverse the increase in serum alkaline phosphatase (ALP), alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and total bilirubin (TBIL) levels caused by fractures (unpublished), indicating that it has a protective effect on the liver. In addition, the Tubiechong gel plaster can reverse the increase of triglyceride (TG), total cholesterol (TC); low density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) in rats caused by fractures, indicating that it has the effect of lowering blood lipids (unpublished). Therefore, the TGP may be able to be applied to other diseases that can be treated by Tubiechong, which needs to be further validated. This study provides a valuable reference for the development and improvement of topical preparations containing Tubiechong.

Cancer Biology & Oncology.title: Developing a Discrete Choice Experiment Instrument for Evaluating Patients’ Preferences in Precision Oncology
Cancer Biology & Oncology.abstract: BackgroundIn addition to clinical and technical considerations, patients’ preferences are essential for evaluating interventions such as precision medicine (PM).ObjectivesThis study aimed to identify and prioritize attributes of precision oncology that are important for patients to develop and validate a standard stated preference instrument.MethodsThe key attributes of precision oncology and their related levels were extracted from the systematic literature review and were presented on a validated 5-point Likert scale questionnaire to experts (n = 35). In two rounds of Delphi, participants scored and prioritized the attributes through this personally administered questionnaire to identify the five most important ones to develop a discrete choice experiment (DCE) instrument. The developed DCE questionnaire was subsequently validated, providing a robust and standard instrument for evaluating patients’ preferences for precision oncology.ResultsBased on the consensus criteria, the final DCE included four attributes and a total of 14 levels, which were access to treatment (easy/not easy), out-of-pocket (OOP) expenditures (four levels according to treatment costs in the country), change in life expectancy (LE, six levels from an average gain of three months to four years), and change in quality of life (QoL, improvement or no change).ConclusionsThe above-mentioned attributes represent patients’ main preferences from the views of the Iranian experts. The developed DCE questionnaire can be used to assess patients’ preferences and willingness to pay (WTP) in precision oncology.

sections.title: 1. Background
sections.text: In recent years, it has been increasingly evident that cancer is a complex disease with varying responses to generic treatments, such as chemotherapy and radiation ( 1 ). The “one size fits all” approach to cancer therapy is too simplistic and often results in ineffective, expensive treatments with unnecessary toxic adverse effects and costs for patients ( 2 ). Oncologists consider not only the genetics and biology of cancer but also the age, medical condition, lifestyle, and goals of each patient when deciding on treatment strategy. The precision medicine (PM) approach, which tailors treatments to the specific tissue, gene mutations, and personal factors relevant to each unique case of cancer, has improved patient health in recent years. For instance, in the case of human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)-positive breast cancer, trastuzumab has emerged as a paradigm-shifting therapeutic agent that illustrates the power of PM in oncology ( 3 ). Patient centricity is characterized by respecting and responding to individual patient preferences, needs, and values to optimize the information and achieve the most beneficial patient outcomes ( 4 ). Patients’ preferences are progressively emerging as essential in health decision-making and drug development, reflecting the shift from a “physician-dominated decision-making” to a more active and decisive role for patients ( 5 ). The valuation of the interventions through patients’ preference data is crucial to facilitate the successful implementation of precision oncology, as acknowledged by organizations such as the European Network for Health Technology Assessment (EUnetHTA) ( 6 ). Such data can help estimate their willingness to pay (WTP) for treatments, predict the market diffusion of various PM outcomes, and determine how demand will be affected by factors such as health technology prices and evolving evidence ( 7 ). Moreover, obtaining consumer-centric information can aid stakeholders in anticipating behaviors regarding implementing new care paradigms, such as PM ( 8 ); nonetheless, no standard instrument to measure it can be found in the literature. Discrete choice experiment (DCE) is one of the widely used instruments for quantifying stated preferences for health. This method is rooted in Random Utility Theory, which assumes that treatments can be described by specific attributes, such as the likelihood of a positive test outcome. Individuals’ preferences are determined based on the levels of these attributes, such as different probabilities. Respondents are presented with hypothetical scenarios that vary these attribute levels and are asked to choose their preferred scenario in each choice task ( 9 ).

sections.title: 2. Objectives
sections.text: This study aimed to seek consensus from experts in Iran regarding the attributes of precision oncology to inform subsequent research and develop a standard and valid DCE instrument to measure patient preferences, as researchers developing a DCE are tasked with creating a limited set of attributes based on a rigorous process, including a literature review and expert opinions to make sure the DCE instrument is standard and not overly complex or burdensome.

sections.title: 3.1. Ethics Statement
sections.text: This study received ethical approval (ID: IR.SBMU.PHARMACY.REC.1400.174 ) from the Research Ethics Committee of the School of Pharmacy at Shahid Beheshti University of Medical Sciences in Tehran, Iran.

sections.title: 3.2. Systematic Search
sections.text: The Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analyses (PRISMA) guideline ( 10 ) was followed to systematically review the studies on patients’ preferences in precision oncology and genetic tests. Search terms were: Patient* preference* OR attribute* OR discrete choice experiment AND precision medicine OR personalized medicine AND cancer OR neoplasm*. Multiple databases were included in the systematic search strategy, namely PubMed, ScienceDirect, and Cochrane Library. The full search strategy for each database is presented in “Appendix 1: Search Strategy”. The references obtained by searching through databases were imported to Mendeley (a reference manager software), and duplicates were removed. Studies were screened for eligibility based on the title and abstract, followed by full-text screening by two researchers. The search was conducted in February 2022 and was restricted to peer-reviewed journals published in English. The included articles’ reference list was checked to find additional relevant publications. No restrictions were placed on the time of publication. Two researchers extracted and summarized the attributes to be presented on a 5-point Likert scale structured questionnaire to experts through a Delphi technique.

sections.title: 3.3. Participants and Recruitment
sections.text: To ensure a diverse range of expertise among the participants, it was aimed to recruit at least 30 experts via maximum variation purposeful and snowball sampling techniques, including clinical oncologists, clinical pharmacists, government officials, healthcare payer specialists, and pharmacoeconomists ( 11 ). The definition of a national expert is an individual who meets the following inclusion criteria: 1- having work experience in a senior professional title and 2- engaging in health decision-making

sections.title: 3.4. Data Collection
sections.text: The Delphi technique is a widely accepted systematic approach in healthcare to establish a consensus from respondents within a specific domain of expertise ( 12 ). The participants responded to the structured, personally administered questionnaires through a modified Delphi approach. One of the modifications was utilizing a structured questionnaire for the rounds, and another was reaching consensus in limited rounds ( Table 1 ). A significant body of research supports both of these modifications ( 13 ). They rated and prioritized the attributes on a 5-point Likert scale. This modified Delphi approach involved two rounds of consensus. In the first round, the panelists received a thorough introduction to state the research inquiry, the study process, definitions of the candidate attributes and their levels, the previous steps taken to extract them from the literature, and the criteria set forth for the inclusion of attributes in subsequent rounds. They were then required to rate their level of agreement with each attribute on a 5-point Likert scale (5 = Definitely include, 4 = Possibly include, 3 = Neutral, 2 = Possibly exclude, 1 = Definitely exclude). In the first round, at the end of the questionnaire, an open question was put for the experts to add if they think of other attributes. To enable a better comprehension of the expert opinion, a five-point scale was implemented instead of a binary response, enabling the participants to express their degree of agreement with the inclusion, whether stronger or weaker ( 14 ).

sections.title: 3.5. Data Analysis
sections.text: Descriptive statistics were used to analyze the results of each round of the modified Delphi method. The goal was to identify the maximum five most important attributes to serve as a limited set of candidate attributes for inclusion in a DCE and prevent complexity and bothersomeness for the participants. The literature emphasizes the significance of defining consensus prior to initiating the first Delphi round. The consensus criteria were defined as a mode value of 5, a standard deviation (SD) of < 1, and an over 85% agreement in the total score of 4 and 5. The study team blindly evaluated the attributes’ scores to reduce the error rate. The mode score, SD, and sum of the agreement scores 4 and 5 were calculated for each attribute. The ones meeting the consensus criteria were included in the next round for further narrowing down and refinement. For the subsequent round of Delphi, all modifications were summarized and presented on a Likert scale, and the experts scored and prioritized the revised attribute list to achieve consensus. Attributes achieving consensus were included in the final DCE instrument. Finally, the face and content validity of the developed DCE instrument was assessed by a group of 12 experts independent of the instrument’s development process, by clarity and ease of understanding, and by calculating the CVI and CVR to develop a standard and validated DCE questionnaire for further research.

sections.title: 4. Results
sections.text: The present systematic review identified 1,156 records. Following the screening and eligibility evaluation, 28 studies were deemed eligible and were subsequently included in the review and attribute extraction ( Figure 1 ). Seven potential attributes extracted from the selected studies included health provider’s recommendation (yes/no), treatment frequency/duration (frequency: Every month/every two weeks, duration: From a few weeks to a few years), predictability and efficacy (high/medium/low), out-of-pocket (OOP) expenditures (four levels based on treatment expenditures), adverse events (the type and severity of adverse effects), change in life expectancy (LE, six levels from an average gain of five months to four years), and change in the quality of life (QoL, improvement/no change) ( Table 2 ). These attributes and their levels were presented on a validated 5-point Likert scale, personally administered structured questionnaire to the experts through a Delphi process for scoring and prioritizing. This questionnaire’s validation process included content validity assessments that were carried out by calculating the CVI and CVR. All the attributes and their levels were deemed acceptable and necessary. Table 3 shows all the attributes, their levels, and a short description that was presented to the participants in the questionnaire in Delphi rounds. A total of 35 national experts who met the eligibility criteria were recruited for the present study, comprising specialists in five different fields related to the study’s aim, including oncologists and clinical pharmacists (n = 10), government officials (n = 8), healthcare payer specialists (n = 6), and pharmacoeconomists (n = 11). The average years of practice were 16 (SD = 6.5). Most experts (n = 31) had senior professional titles and were highly engaged in health management. The median length of the Delphi rounds was about 16 minutes. Anonymity was maintained throughout the Delphi rounds. Figure 2 illustrates a schematic flowchart of the Delphi process. During the first Delphi round, three additional attributes, including reimbursement status (yes/no), familial benefits (yes/no), and access to treatment (easy/not easy), were added by the experts. The experts highlighted the importance of patients’ access to treatment as a critical issue in Iran. According to their experience, sometimes the preferred treatments in the guidelines could not be provided to the patient due to the lack of access due to different causes. Reimbursement status is another important characteristic that the present study’s clinical experts highlighted its importance. A few participants also pointed out the familial benefit, as the genetic test is one of the first steps of precision treatment, which can predict whether the cancer is familial. Therefore, all of the present study’s participants scored these additional attributes at the end of the first Delphi round as a supplementary question on a 5-point Likert scale and in the second round among other attributes. At the end of the first round of the modified Delphi method, four attributes (doctor’s recommendation, predictability and efficacy of the treatment, treatment frequency/duration, and familial benefits) were eliminated based on not meeting the consensus criteria which were agreed upon beforehand as a mode score value of 5, an SD of < 1, and an over 85% agreement in the total scores of 4 and 5. After integrating the results from the initial round into the remaining six attributes, the refined survey questionnaire was administered for a second round. At the end of the second round, two attributes (reimbursement status and adverse events) were removed based on not meeting the consensus criteria. By the end of the second round, the present study’s objective of obtaining consensus about attributes was achieved to develop a standard DCE instrument that is not complex and easy to understand for the patients. Table 4 shows the quantitative results of the Delphi phases. Of all the ten attributes posed, four attributes, including OOP payments of the treatment (four levels based on treatment expenditures), access to treatment (two levels, including easy and not easy), QoL (two levels, including improvement and no change), and LE after treatment (six levels from an average gain of five months to four years), met the consensus criteria and were included in the attributes’ list for developing the DCE instrument. In order to evaluate the DCE instrument, face, and content validity assessments were carried out. The final generated DCE instrument consisted of a list of four attributes and a total of 14 levels. The complete DCE questionnaire was developed via JMP software in four surveys with three choice tasks each and can be found in Appendix 2 ( Table 5 ). Table 6 shows the results of the validity calculations.

sections.title: 5. Discussion
sections.text: Assessing the value of interventions and investigating attributes that influence patients’ preferences toward precision oncology and derived WTP estimates in hypothetical treatment options is important to enabling the effective implementation of precision oncology and ensuring that public health spending is allocated toward the most effective strategies that are preferred by the consumers and can benefit the health of the population as a whole. Although some studies have assessed attributes in oncology, there is a gap in the literature regarding using a standard and validated DCE instrument to evaluate these attributes and patients’ WTP in the context of precision oncology. This gap is significant as precision oncology becomes more widely used in clinical practice, and patient preferences are critical for shared decision-making. Therefore, this study contributes to the literature by developing a DCE instrument explicitly tailored to the attributes of precision oncology treatment concerning the “average” patient with cancer. This instrument can be valuable in measuring patients’ preferences and implementing precision oncology programs that align with patients’ needs, preferences, and WTP. Additionally, since work has yet to be performed on this matter in Iran, patients as one of the stakeholders can be used in pricing, determining the service tariff, and determining the reimbursement program. In the following section, the implications of different attributes employed in this study are discussed. The findings of the present work confirm that in the delivery of healthcare services, change in QoL and future life expectations are key attributes, as is proven in several studies for cancer patients, especially in older patients with naturally limited LE ( 41 - 43 ). It has been revealed in previous studies that patients can have equal preferences for QoL and LE or prefer each of them more, and the preference is associated with different factors, such as age, gender, educational attainment, and the nature of their oncologist communication. The current study’s results revealed that healthcare professionals’ disciplines influence the preferences for change in LE and QoL among patients. Specialists and clinicians value LE more than the QoL; however, healthcare payer (insurance) specialists were more concerned about the QoL than LE. These attributes held significant value and were ultimately incorporated into the final DCE instrument. The results of this study suggest that OOP payments are more important to patients than whether the treatment is covered by insurance (reimbursement status), a finding consistent with several studies of other cancer treatments or diagnoses ( 44 ). However, health providers emphasized that precision treatment must be as insured as conventional treatments, as it is a crucial attribute in their point of view. Still, considering that the financial burden of treatment can be graded according to OOP payments and health insurance status, other professional groups believed that the OOP payments were more important to the patient and reimbursement status does not automatically translate into financial protection from medical-related expenditures. Including the OOP payments attribute in a DCE survey allows an estimation of marginal WTP for each service attribute and its levels. As the cost has been one of the crucial attributes of the treatment for patients and healthcare payers, using precision treatment and performing more tests to diagnose a disease increases healthcare expenditures. However, with the disease’s high psychological burden for the cancer patient, precision treatment can be very beneficial, with maximal response to treatment and minimal adverse events. Therefore, PM will benefit insurance companies in the long term because information about a person’s disease and responsiveness to different interventions and treatments will help develop disease-prevention approaches ( 45 ). Another attribute of PM is clinical consensus (i.e., doctor’s recommendation). Although some studies show that this attribute is critical from the perspective of payers ( 46 ), several studies showed that cancer patients are willing to accept and pay for PM when such treatment has been deemed clinically useful by their healthcare provider ( 47 - 49 ). The current study’s results showed that, on the one hand, for a treatment to be covered by insurance, clinical consensus upon the treatment is necessary. On the other hand, this attribute is critical for cancer patients with PM in their disease trajectory, and PM is not an option for them if their healthcare provider does not recommend it. Additionally, the access to treatment attribute, which holds significant importance in Iran, was introduced as a salient attribute despite its limited consideration in the existing literature. Ensuring access to treatments, especially innovative technologies, is crucial to the implementation and uptake of PM. After introducing treatment to patients, healthcare professionals in the present study attached high importance to this attribute for several reasons. Sanctions have negatively impacted access to medical technologies, such as diagnostic kits, genetic databases, and drugs, particularly those that rely on importing raw materials or finished products ( 50 ); the implementation of PM as an innovative technology could result in unequal access and prevent some patients from experiencing potential benefits ( 15 ). In order to overcome these challenges, policymakers need to adopt a systematic and coordinated strategy to ensure nationwide market accessibility, thereby mitigating the impact of limited access on patients’ ability to obtain recommended treatments ( 51 ). Similarly, access to precision oncology is crucial for improving cancer treatment outcomes and reducing health disparities. Precision oncology, which uses genomic information to guide the selection of targeted therapies for individual patients, has revolutionized cancer diagnosis and treatment. However, access to precision oncology is only sometimes universal. It varies based on socioeconomic status and location, resulting in some patients needing access to the latest treatments and technologies and receiving less effective standard care. Improving access to precision oncology is vital for more accurate diagnoses, personalized and effective treatment plans, and improved patient outcomes. To address these disparities, investment in the development and dissemination of precision oncology tools and technologies, in addition to the education and training of healthcare providers, is necessary to ensure that all patients have access to the most advanced treatments available ( 52 , 53 ). To subsequently discuss the further attributes evaluated in this study, the predictability and efficacy of the treatment are of utmost importance to patients. The advancement of PM is crucial for providing optimal cancer care. By enhancing predictability and efficacy, precision oncology holds the potential to enhance the accuracy of diagnoses, personalize treatment plans, and ultimately improve patient outcomes and QoL. However, significant amounts of data are required to support the estimates of accuracy and clinical utility, as noted in the literature ( 7 ). At the same time, the recommendation for cancer treatment by healthcare providers typically takes into account the stage of the disease, the patient’s health, and the availability of treatments. The present study’s experts believe that a healthcare provider’s recommendation can give patients confidence in prioritizing targeted treatment. Another attribute evaluated in the present study is the adverse effects of the cancer treatment. Garfeld et al. have observed that consumers value PM outcomes more than their adverse effects. In the latter study, most individuals (77%) would prefer a cancer treatment with a higher chance of success, even if it had higher side effect rates, compared to a treatment with a lower chance of success but fewer side effects (23%). Likewise, the experts in the current study determined that this attribute could not be among the most critical attributes from the patient’s perspective ( 8 ). This study has several implications. The viewpoint of both healthcare providers and payers will assist in aligning the development programs of tests and therapeutic products with decision-makers. Furthermore, the differing perspectives on the attributes of PM gathered in this study can guide the creation of value-based evaluations by the industry, payers, and healthcare providers. The present study’s findings could enhance HTA activities by highlighting critical areas for evidence collection, generation, and presentation aligned with patient preference. Experts’ points of view on disease attributes can be used to make predictions about PM uptake, which can be helpful for drug developers concerning market planning, pricing, and evidence generation. Payers can further use them to inform financial planning and future budget impact estimates. In this study, the experts in the health system field were chosen to prioritize precision oncology treatment attributes. Their expertise and objective evaluation of treatment options make their input important in decision-making. This study is relevant to the current trend of a growing demand for patient-centered healthcare services and increased emphasis on patient choice ( 54 , 55 ). Although this study was carefully designed and satisfactory results from validity tests were obtained, it is important to recognize the following limitations of the study. One of the limitations of the Delphi method is that it involves limited statistical analysis; instead, the results are based on the collective judgments and opinions of the participants, which can be influenced by individual biases or preferences. Additionally, the Delphi method is often used in cases where there is limited existing knowledge or data on a topic. Although this can be an advantage, it can also limit the ability to explore the range of possible outcomes or solutions.

sections.title: 5.1. Conclusions
sections.text: In this paper, using a systematic review and the Delphi method to identify and prioritize precision oncology treatment characteristics, a DCE instrument has been developed to measure patient preferences toward precision oncology. The novelty of the work relies on the opinion of experts who objectively assess treatment options. The experts articulate and prioritize the attributes of precision oncology with their comprehensive perspectives; this could indicate further future exploitation of patients’ preferences and lay the foundation for PM in chronic diseases, such as cancer. In this instrument, using the DCE method, four characteristics of access to treatment, OOP payments, QoL, and LE with different levels are included. This has the potential to enhance patient health by addressing some of the obstacles faced by PM use in clinical practice.

Cancer Biology & Oncology.title: Concurrent use of tumor necrosis factor inhibitor and tyrosine kinase inhibitor in ankylosing spondylitis and myeloid neoplasm
Cancer Biology & Oncology.abstract: Biologic disease-modifying agents (bDMARDs) are highly effective in controlling the symptoms of autoimmune rheumatic diseases. The decision on whether to continue bDMARDs following a cancer diagnosis is can be challenging for patients and physicians. Here, we describe a case of a middle-aged male with ankylosing spondylitis wno was controlled on infliximab (IFX) ant found to have a myeloid neoplasm with Platelet-Derived Growth Factor Receptor Beta rearrangement. The Patient was started on a tyrosine kinase inhibitor imatinib. Given its significant positive effect on patient’s quality of life, IFX was continued with a favorable outcome. This case highlights the importance of shared decisionmaking in balancing risks and benefits of immunosuppressants in appropriate cases of hematologic malignancy.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.text: Although biologic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (bDMARDs) are highly effective in autoimmune rheumatic diseases, a concern remains that bDMARDs may interfere with immune system’s response to cancer. 1 The decision whether to continue bDMARDs following a new cancer diagnosis is challenging for physicians and patients. Traditionally, tumor necrosis factor inhibitors (TNFi’s) are discontinued with diagnosis of hematological malignancy. Here, we present a patient with ankylosing spondylitis (AS) who was successfully continued on infliximab (IFX) despite a recent diagnosis of myeloid neoplasm with Platelet-Derived Growth Factor Receptor Beta ( PDGFRB ) rearrangement, which was concurrently treated with imatinib.

sections.title: Case Presentation
sections.text: A 67-yaer-old man was referred to rheumatology in January 2018 with longstanding back pain. He reported peripheral arthritis (knee) and arthralgias (shoulders). He did not have psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease, uveitis, dactylitis, or enthesitis. He previously worked as a mechanic but developed difficulties with activities of daily living. Physical exam was notable for severely limited range of motion at cervical and lumbar spine and chronic warmth and mild joint effusion of the right knee. He had a positive HLA-B27 and elevated C-reactive protein of 36 mg L ~1 . Pelvic X-ray showed fusion of bilateral sacroiliac joints. X-rays of the spine revealed extensive syndesmophytes in cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spine. He was diagnosed with AS. Due to previous gastrointestinal bleeding with NSAIDs, he was initiated on IFX 5 mg kg ~1 every 6 weeks with dramatic symptom improvement and normalization of inflammatory markers. Two years later, the patient was admitted with 2 weeks of fevers and fatigue. Lab tests revealed leukocytosis of 127,800 uL –1 with increased absolute neutrophil count of 52,400 uL –1 , left shift (18% metamyelocytes, 10% myelocytes, and 20% promyelocytes), absolute eosinophilia of 1,300 uL –1 , and monocytosis of 7,700 uL –1 . Platelets and hemoglobin were normal. Peripheral blood smear showed all stages of myeloid maturation. Blood flow cytometry demonstrated a myeloid left shift. Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy (BMB) was notable for hypercellular marrow for age (> 90%) with markedly increased left-shifted myelopoiesis. Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) testing notable for negative BCR-ABL translocation showed a deletion of 5’ PDGFRB gene in 68% of bone marrow cells. Comprehensive genomic profiling showed the presence of TNIP1-PDGFRB fusion and confirmed myeloid neoplasm with PDGFRB rearrangement. Patient was started on a tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) imatinib 400 mg daily, and IFX was discontinued. Leukocytosis normalized within 3 weeks. However, due to IFX discontinuation, he experienced remarkable worsening of spinal pain and stiffness leading the impaired activities of daily living and poor quality of life. After multidisciplinary meeting and shared decision-making, IFX was restarted after missing two infusions. At the third month, repeat BMB revealed hypercellular marrow (70%) with FISH demonstrating residual PDGFRB abnormality in only 2.5% of cells, close to the limit of detection. At 9-month follow-up, the patient continues to do well with no detection of PDGFRB abnormality in peripheral blood flow.

sections.title: Discussion
sections.text: It is difficult to ascertain the link between hematologic malignancy and biologics since autoimmune diseases increase baseline malignancy risk. 1 , 2 For instance, patients with RA have a 10-15% increased risk of cancer, nota bly lymphoma, compared to general population. 1 Using the Taiwan National Health Insurance Database, Chang et al. 3 found that male patients with AS had an increased risk of solid cancers and hematologic malignancy. Interestingly, basic science data suggest that the ability of leukemic stem cells to persist even if there is a response to TKI therapy may be due to the stem cell-specific microenvironment. 4 TNFa levels and those cytokines downstream of TNFa have been shown to be elevated in patients with CML and induced in leukemic stem cells in vitro. 4 , 5 There are data to suggest that targeting TNFa in murine CML stem cell model may enhance TKI-induced reduction of clonogenic activity. 4 It is unclear if the same phenomenon may be observed in humans and may suggest a benefit of concurrent TNFi and TKI therapy that merits further investigation. There is hesitation to continue bDMARD in patients with newly diagnosed malignancy. In a systematic review, Lopez-Olivo et al. 6 found no clear agreement on recommendations for bDMARD use in RA and cancer, which advise caution but not absolute contraindication. The further challenge in our case was that bDMARDs was the only effective treatment option in AS. Our case is unique as it describes using a TKI and TNFa inhibition concurrently in a patient with myeloid neoplasm and AS with a favorable outcome. It demonstrates the importance of team-based care and shared decision-making, and emphasizes that continuation of TNFa inhibition in a carefully selected patient with rheumatic disease and particular types of hematologic neoplasms may be considered on a case-bycase basis.

Cancer Biology & Oncology.title: Anlotinib reverses osimertinib resistance by inhibiting epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and angiogenesis in non-small cell lung cancer
Cancer Biology & Oncology.abstract: In the present study, we aimed to investigate whether anlotinib reverses osimertinib resistance by inhibiting the formation of epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) and angiogenesis. In a clinical case, anlotinib reversed osimertinib resistance in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Therefore, we performed immunohistochemical analyses on tumor tissues from three NSCLC patients with osimertinib resistance to analyze alterations in the expression levels of EMT markers and vascular endothelial growth factor A (VEGFA) before and after the development of osimertinib resistance. The results revealed the downregulation of E-cadherin, coupled with the upregulation of vimentin and VEGFA in tumor tissues of patients exhibiting osimertinib resistance, compared with those in tissues from patients before receiving osimertinib. Subsequently, we established osimertinib-resistant (Osi-R) cell lines and found that the Osi-R cells acquired EMT features. Next, we analyzed the synergistic effects of the combination therapy to verify whether anlotinib could reverse osimertinib resistance by inhibiting EMT. The expression levels of VEGFA and tube formation were analyzed in the combination group in vitro. Finally, we determined the reversal of osimertinib resistance by the combination of osimertinib and anlotinib in vivo using 20 nude mice. The combined treatment of osimertinib and anlotinib effectively prevented the metastasis of Osi-R cells, inhibited tumor growth, exerted antitumor activity, and ultimately reversed osimertinib resistance in mice. The co-administration of osimertinib and anlotinib demonstrated synergistic efficacy in inhibiting EMT and angiogenesis in three NSCLC patients, ultimately reversing osimertinib resistance.
