sections.title: Conclusion and discussion
sections.text: In conclusion, our comprehensive virtual screening study brings insights into ML-led LBVS workflow design and provides experimental evidence of the anti-Mtb bioactivities of two predicted novel compounds, aldoxorubicin and quarfloxin. The overall results could benefit recent studies on computational flow construction and optimization of LBVS for anti-Mtb drug discovery. The initial antimycobacterial bioactivity dataset was organized from the ChEMBL database. Six ML models for anti-Mtb bioactivity prediction were trained and validated, followed with an ensemble approach to integrate the established machine learning techniques. For anti-Mtb drug repurposing, molecules in the DrugBank database were screened and the majority of known anti-Mtb drugs could be predicted with high precision. Then, further drug category filtering and experimental validation resulted two candidates (aldoxorubicin and quarfloxin) with anti-Mtb potentials, and their drug-target binding modes were further verified by molecular dynamics simulation and SPR experiments. Among the predicted two candidates, aldoxorubicin exhibited high antimicrobial activity against Mtb both in vitro and in cell lines. As a prodrug of doxorubicin, aldoxorubicin has been successfully tested against glioblastoma and soft-tissue sarcoma [ 53 , 54 ]. Moreover, in our study, doxorubicin, the active form of aldoxorubicin, also exhibited an MIC (10.78 μM/mL) comparable to that of aldoxorubicin (4.16 μM/mL). Doxorubicin, which has been in clinical use for >2 decades, has a very wide antitumor application spectrum; it has been used against cancers such as breast and ovarian carcinoma, sarcoma, and many other solid tumors [ 55 ]. Previous studies have shown that the Cmax of doxorubicin ranged from 14.66 to 303.46 μM/mL (corresponding to dosages of 20 to 340 mg/m 2 ), which corresponds to 1.4- to 28-fold the MIC of Mtb H37Rv [ 56 ]. Generally, Cmax/MIC is considered an index for the efficacy of drugs in vivo . Thus, the Cmax plus the low MIC values obtained in this study also implies the potential efficacy of doxorubicin in the treatment of tuberculosis. Meanwhile, compared to the known Mtb DNA gyrase binder evybactin, our newly discovered aldoxorubicin demonstrated a competitive binding affinity ( K d = 0.3997 μM vs. IC 50 = 1 μM) for a similar protein pocket, previously identified as an allosteric site on the gyrase protein [ 10 ]. However, despite its potential role as an allosteric inhibitor, aldoxorubicin showed relatively lower anti-Mtb bioactivity compared to evybactin [MIC value: 3.125 μg/mL (4.16 μM/mL) vs. 0.25 μg/mL] [ 10 ]. Given these preliminary findings, it is important to experimentally compare aldoxorubicin with evybactin to further explore aldoxorubicin’s therapeutic potential and underlying mechanisms of action. Quarfloxin is an investigational drug for different malignant tumors; it was originally derived from the fluoroquinolone class of compounds to target G-quadruplex within ribosomal DNA [ 57 , 58 ]. Recent studies showed that some stable G-quadruplexes in the genome of M. tuberculosis were in the promoter region of genes belonging to definite functional categories [ 59 ]. Previous studies showed that the stable G-quadruplex structure could be transformed into its duplex conformation by reverse gyrase; the potential interactions of quarfloxin with DNA gyrase found in this study may help to further explain the anti-Mtb mechanism of this compound. Besides, there are certain limitations in this study. First, although the performances in terms of the enrichment factor and hit rate are moderate, the R 2 , MAE, and MSE values of the LBVS methods on the external validation dataset are weak. These results implied that our trained LBVS models may have a relatively limited adaptive domain and chemical structural preference, this be alleviated by introducing the data from more bioactive anti-Mtb compounds. Second, the repurposing dataset can be further expanded to discover more candidates. Considering sample accessibility and cost, this study focused on only anti-Mtb drug repurposing with approved or investigational drugs. Considering that most of the top predicted compounds in DrugBank were known anti-Mtb drugs, therefore it would be promising to screen more investigational drugs to expand the range of compounds for repurposing. To address this issue, we also used our LBVS methods to predict the anti-Mtb bioactivities of molecules in the Drug Repurposing Hub [ 60 ] to promote the identification of more potential anti-Mtb drugs and enhance the application and precision of machine learning–led anti-Mtb drug virtual screening. Third, further studies are needed to explore and validate potential additional Mtb targets for the identified compounds. This will help deepen our understanding of the pharmacological mechanisms of action for both compounds. Key Points We have created and validated an effective machine learning–enabled virtual screening workflow to repurpose existing drugs with anti-Mtb efficiency. We virtual screened the DrugBank dataset against Mtb and successfully identified two novel drugs (aldoxorubicin and quarfloxin) with significant antibacterial activity against M. tuberculosis H37Rv strain and other multidrug-resistant TB isolates. In our study, molecular docking analysis indicated the direct binding of the two promising compounds with Mtb DNA gyrase, which were then validated by molecular dynamics analysis and the surface plasmon resonance experiments.

figure_captions.label: fig1
figure_captions.caption: Proposed mechanism of antiviral compounds targeting the WSSV VP28 envelope protein to inhibit viral entry into shrimp Penaeus monodon . The virus enters host cells via the interactions between viral envelope proteins and host cell receptors. WSSV internalization within the host cell is prominently clathrin-mediated endocytosis since the WSSV virions bound to the surface of the host cell were engulfed by the coated membrane and then taken up into the coated vesicles. 30 The specificity of these interactions is such that inhibitors designed to block them exhibit potential anti-viral efficacy. In WSSV, VP28 stands out as a major envelope protein recognized as an interacting partner with the host surface protein P. monodon Rab7. 29 The antiviral flavonoid compounds in this study interact with specific residues at the binding interface of VP28, blocking viral VP28-host PmRab7 protein–protein interactions, preventing the virus from entering the host cell and disrupting endocytosis, thereby interfering with the normal infection cycle.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.text: 1 The black tiger shrimp ( Penaeus monodon ) presents a highly nutritious choice for human consumption, renowned for its substantial protein content and abundant supply of vitamins, minerals, unsaturated fatty acids, vital amino acids, and antioxidants. 1 Consequently, the shrimp industry has expanded uninterruptedly, firmly establishing its economic importance in the Blue Revolution. 2 The global commercial production of black tiger shrimp amounted to 4200 million metric tons (mt) in the most recent fiscal year, with an estimated worth of USD 4.8 billion. The high demand in local and international markets has led to the prominence of black tiger prawn farming across the coastal regions of Asia, Australia, and numerous Pacific Island countries. 3 Bangladesh, contributing 2.5% to global shrimp production, generated around USD 300 million as the second largest source of export earnings in the previous economic year by exporting 29,000 mt of black tiger shrimp. 4 In addition, around 1.2 million individuals depend on the P. monodon sector for their source of income in Bangladesh. 3 , 4 , 5 However, the catastrophic effects of various viral diseases have negatively impacted the shrimp industry. The extremely pathogenic White Spot Syndrome Virus (WSSV), which causes White Spot Disease (WSD), has been a major concern for over thirty years. 6 It infects P. monodon at various stages of development, and causes severe disease outbreaks, leading to a mortality rate of up to 100% within 3–10 days. 7 WSD manifests through a range of clinical symptoms, including lethargy, decreased food intake, reduced cleaning behavior, cuticle detachment, and hepatopancreas discoloration. 8 It is a destructive viral infection that can result in the total loss of shrimp production, imposing a significant economic strain on farmers and the entire shrimp industry. 9 Since 1992, the cumulative worldwide economic loss has been estimated to be USD 21 billion, with an annual financial loss approaching USD 1 billion, representing 10% of global production. 10 Unfortunately, there is no known anti-WSSV cure or therapy for shrimp, and limited progress and scientific research have led to its proliferation. 11 In this circumstance, it is inevitable to develop novel treatments to combat the WSSV infection of shrimp. To identify the effective strategy for infection of WSSV, research has been conducted on the entry process, specifically the virus's attachment and recognition to the surface of its host cell. 12 Since entry into the host cell is the first step of viral infection, propagation, and persistence, inhibition of this process by designing anti-viral drugs targeting the envelope proteins is expected to be an effective antiviral strategy. 13 WSSV is a rod-shaped, enveloped, double-stranded DNA virus that contains 184 open reading frames (ORFs) with 22 envelope proteins, including VP28, VP24, VP19, VP26, and VP15. 14 VP28, the most abundant and major surface protein, is among the first molecules to interact with host cell receptors. Moreover, it forms a complex by interacting with VP26 and VP24 and is involved in systemic infection. 15 , 16 VP28 plays a significant role in the “infectome” which is essential for cell recognition, facilitating the attachment and navigation of the virus into the shrimp cell. 17 The VP28 protein has a nine-stranded β-barrel structure and a protruding N-terminal region. This feature allows it to interact with the host receptor PmRab7, a membrane-associated GTP-binding receptor located in the endosome. Additionally, it facilitates fusion with the host cell membrane to make viral particle transfer more efficient. 15 , 18 It has been observed that VP28 naturally assembles into a trimer within the viral envelope, potentially influencing the infective mode of the virus. 19 , 20 Therefore, the VP28 trimer is the optimal target for anti-WSSV drugs. Blocking its interaction in the endocytic pathway could significantly combat the infection. 12 . Several medicinal plants have been discovered to have bioactive compounds that possess antiviral drug properties. 21 Plant-based drugs are widely accessible, cheaper, safe, and effective with very few side effects. 22 Hence, the rational approach would be identifying and developing effective treatments for viral infections in aquaculture by discovering new plant-based compounds and small molecules that selectively interact with viral proteins. 18 , 23 The processes involved in the introduction of new efficient drugs often require significant time, financial resources, and extensive labor. 24 In contrast, the computational methods could potentially reduce the expenses and time in developing a drug candidate. Computer-aided drug design (CADD) exemplifies a sophisticated method for effectively exploring pharmacological libraries to discover potential new therapeutics. The in-silico virtual screening (VS) method enables the rapid and economical identification of drug treatments by generating hits for lead compounds more efficiently. 25 As a result, progress in computational drug design has significantly reduced the time required to conceptualize, develop, and refine a drug. Moreover, employing CADD has facilitated the identification, validation, and exploration of diverse biological and physiological properties of plant bioactive constituents. 26 Figuring out the binding mechanisms may offer significant insights for the development of new anti-WSSV drugs. 27 In earlier in-silico research, it was discovered that withanolide, coagulin Q, and withanolide D from Withania somnifera could help fight the WSSV by targeting the VP26 protein and stopping the formation of mature virion. 18 In another in-silico study, Dinesh et al. identified potential inhibitors of WSSV envelope proteins such as VP26, VP28, and VP110 from Phyllanthus amarus . 20 Despite numerous in silico studies that have explored the efficacy of several medicinal plant compounds on WSSV envelope proteins, none have evaluated the antiviral efficacy of Azadirachta indica and Bacopa monnieri compounds against WSSV . To address this inquiry, we evaluated the compounds obtained from these two plants to determine their potential as new therapeutic candidates against the WSSV VP28 envelope protein. The extracts of A. indica have numerous beneficial properties, such as anti-inflammatory, anti-hyperglycemic, anti-carcinogenic, antioxidant, immune-modulatory, anti-mutagenic, anti-ulcer, and anti-viral effects. 28 Similarly, the methanolic extract of B. monnieri has been shown exhibiting antimicrobial, antifungal, antiviral, and neuroprotective activities, highlighting the extensive historical use of these plants for drug development. 27 This study aims to identify and evaluate bioactive compounds from A. indica and B. monnieri as potential inhibitors of the WSSV VP28 envelope protein. Our objective was to identify potential hit compounds from these plants using a readily available integrated bioinformatics approach. This approach utilized a comprehensive computational methodology encompassing virtual screening, pharmacokinetics and toxicity analysis, molecular dynamics (MD) simulation, and MM-PBSA binding energy estimation. Fig. 1 illustrates the possible mechanism by which these flavonoids interact with VP28, thereby inhibiting the viral entry by binding with the host receptor PmRab7. 29 The findings of this study indicate that these compounds could potentially exhibit antiviral properties against the VP28 envelope protein, which may provide new avenues for antiviral strategies to address WSSV.

sections.title: Protein preparation
sections.text: 2.1 The crystal structure of the WSSV major viral envelope protein, VP28 (PDB ID Code: 2ED6), was acquired from the RCSB Protein Data Bank ( rcsb.org ) 31 repository as a drug target for our study. The structure was resolved using the X-ray diffraction technique at an excellent resolution of 2.00 Å (R-value observed: 0.248, R-value free: 0.281, and R-value work: 0.248), with a molecular weight of 220.67 kDa. The WSSV VP28 envelope protein found in the RCSB PDB database consists of 12 identical chains, designated as A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I, J, K, and L ( Fig. 2 A). The residues were numbered from Thr32 to Thr201 in the RCSB PDB database. Despite the discrepancy in the numbering, each chain still consists of 170 residues. Subsequently, the VP28 protein was processed using Discovery Studio 2024 32 to remove all the extra chains except A, B, and C to assemble a VP28 trimer, which plays a vital role in systemic infection in WSSV ( Fig. 2 B). Furthermore, the VP28 trimeric protein was cleaned by eliminating water molecules and all heteroatoms before adding polar hydrogen atoms. Once the protein structure was cleaned, it was subjected to optimization, validation, and minimization utilizing the GROMOS 43B1 force field of the Swiss PDB Viewer (SPDV) v4.1.0 and stored in PDB format. 33

sections.title: Curation and preparation of compound library
sections.text: 2.2 Phytocompounds are the chemical constituents contributing to the therapeutic effects of certain medicinal plants and formulations used for centuries for curing various diseases and, playing an indispensable role in drug discovery. In this study, we used two curated databases, namely Indian Medicinal Plants, Phytochemistry and Therapeutics 2.0 (IMPPAT 2.0) (Accessed on: May 03, 2024, imppat 2.0 ) 34 and Dr. Duke's Phytochemical and Ethnobotanical Databases (Accessed on: May 03, 2024, phytochem.nal.usda.gov ) 35 , to obtain the phytocompounds of A. indica and B. monnieri for VS. The IMPPAT 2.0 repository contains a non-redundant, stereo-aware collection of 17,967 phytochemicals, which include both 2D and 3D chemical structures that were carefully selected and standardized by manual curation to support the discovery of new physiologically significant molecules. We also conducted a literature search on the PubMed and Google Scholar databases using the keywords “ Azadirachta indica ”, “ Bacopa monnieri ”, “phytochemical constituents”, “bioactive compounds”, and different combinations of these keywords to obtain the compounds. In total, 187 compounds were retrieved, with 170 coming from A. indica and 17 from B. monnieri . Of the compounds for A. indica , 141 were retrieved from the IMPPAT 2.0 database, 7 from Dr. Duke's Phytochemical and Ethnobotanical Databases, and 22 through literature searches. For B. monnieri , 15 compounds were sourced from IMPPAT 2.0 and 2 from Dr. Duke's Phytochemical and Ethnobotanical Databases. The redundant entries were eliminated to ensure the integrity of the data sets. The percentage distributions of compounds discovered from various plant parts of both chosen plants are highlighted in Fig. 3 in the form of pie charts. The 3D structures and details of each ligand were obtained in SDF format from the PubChem database ( pubchem ). 36 The compound library was prepared and optimized using OpenBabel software by energy minimization with the MMFF94 force field and subsequently incorporating polar hydrogen atoms. 37 Finally, the ligands were merged into a single SDF file for ease of entry into the PyRx program. 38
path: Curation and preparation of compound library

sections.title: Protein binding site identification and grid box generation
sections.text: 2.3 The VP28 trimer was analyzed using the CASTp 3.0 ( castp ) server to forecast the locations of binding site residues. 39 The CASTp 3.0 server offers a reliable and comprehensive topological analysis of proteins, allowing for the identification and measurement of residues in the binding site pocket, as well as the determination of volume, cavities, and channels. The server predicted many active pockets, and the first binding site was determined based on its greater surface coverage and volume. To avoid blind docking, we used CASTp-identified binding site residues to set up the grid box for virtual screening around the VP28 trimer. It is imperative to select the correctly predicted amino acid residue to ensure that the grid box in the PyRx software 38 encompasses the binding site of the target protein.
path: Protein binding site identification and grid box generation

sections.title: Virtual screening
sections.text: 2.4 Structure-based virtual screening (VS) is a widely employed computational strategy during the early stages of drug design, discovery, and development, adopted by numerous pharmaceutical companies and various research teams. 40 This technique allows researchers to make predictions about the optimal binding poses of a library of small molecules to specific macromolecules. PyRx 0.8 software is a reliable open-source VS tool that is predominantly used in CADD to screen large libraries of compounds against a specific drug target. 38 In the present study, the AutoDock Vina wizard of PyRx was used on selected compounds (n = 187) to identify antiviral drug candidates with strong activity against the VP28 trimer of WSSV. We converted each ligand into an AutoDock ligand, loaded the prepared protein into PyRx, and subsequently converted it to a dockable PDBQT format. The exhaustiveness parameter was set to default 8. The center coordinates of the grid box were established as x  = 29.37, y = 111.52, and z = 86.10, with dimensions of x  = 41.72, y = 41.15, and z = 42.56 in angstrom (Å) around the VP28 trimer protein. The compound with the highest binding energy (most negative) was identified as having the maximum binding affinity. The top 30 compounds were selected for further pharmacokinetic and toxicity analysis based on their relative binding affinities and optimal docking poses, which specifically interacted with key residues within the target envelope protein's binding site. After performing virtual screening-based molecular docking with PyRx, the compounds exhibiting the highest binding affinities underwent further validation of their docking scores through CB-Dock2 ( CB-Dock2 ). 41 Finally, we manually inspected the binding interactions of top-scoring protein–ligand complexes using Discovery Studio 2024 32 and UCSF Chimera 1.18. 42

sections.title: Pharmacokinetics analysis
sections.text: 2.5 Drug-likeness and pharmacokinetic analyses are critical for assessing the potential of a specific molecule in the context of drug development. Using the SwissADME web server ( swissadme ), we predicted the pharmacokinetic profiles and various physicochemical properties of the top thirty potential VP28 trimer inhibitors. 43 The phytochemicals that were screened were submitted to SwissADME, utilizing their Canonical SMILES identifiers as input. At this stage, the compounds underwent assessment based on various parameters, such as physicochemical properties, lipophilicity, water solubility, and pharmacokinetic properties. Furthermore, drug-likeness assessments were conducted using Lipinski 44 , Ghose 45 , Veber 46 , Egan 47 , and Muegge 48 filters, as well as medicinal chemistry assessments. Based on the results, we inferred whether the targeted ligands or compounds would have the appropriate safety profile for real-time pharmacological formulation.

sections.title: Toxicity analysis
sections.text: 2.6 Toxicity is defined as the extent to which a substance can cause harm to an organism or its components, including cells and organs. Hence, the inspection of the toxicological profile is a crucial step since the failure of drug development in later stages is often attributed to this factor. 49 Chemical toxicity is currently being evaluated utilizing computer-guided in-silico testing, eliminating the requirement of animal trials. The ProTox 3.0 ( tox.charite.de/protox3 ) prediction algorithms were employed to assess the toxicity of the phytocompounds, facilitating the evaluation of parameters such as cytotoxicity, hepatotoxicity, carcinogenicity, mutagenicity, and immunotoxicity of potential antiviral agents. 50 This computational model is advantageous because it takes a 2D chemical structure and provides a comprehensive toxicological profile for each endpoint, along with a confidence score.

sections.title: Molecular dynamics simulation
sections.text: 2.7 Molecular dynamics (MD) simulation is a popular tool in computational research that explores the complex movements of molecules and atoms over time when exposed to dynamic systems. 51 More specifically, protein–ligand complex stability can be effectively monitored for fluctuations and conformational alterations since MD simulation offers valuable insights into crucial physiological processes. 52 In this study, we performed five sets of MD simulations on the apo form of VP28 trimer and four protein–ligand complexes. Each simulation lasted for 100 ns and was run using YASARA (version 24.4.10) dynamics software, which used the Amber 14 force field for all calculations. 53 , 54 The docked complexes, including the hydrogen bond network optimization, were cleaned and optimized early on. A cubic simulation box with periodic boundary conditions was created for placing the complexes at their center, with explicit TIP3P water molecules solvating them. 55 The gap between the cubic box and the protein edge was determined to be 12.5 Å, while the cubic box itself has dimensions of 80 × 80 × 80 Å. The simulation system was adjusted to replicate the physiological settings, with the entire environment set at a temperature of 310 K, pH 7.4, and a NaCl content of 0.9%. To optimize the structures and eliminate any steric clashes, the initial energy minimization was achieved by employing a simulated annealing method with the steepest descent algorithm (5000 cycles). The particle mesh Ewald (PME) technique was employed for calculating the long-range electrostatic interactions. 56 The cutoff radius of 8 Å was utilized to look at the short-range van der Waals and Coulomb interactions. The simulations were run with constant temperature, pressure, and Berendsen thermostat settings and trajectory data were saved every 250  ps to analyze the outcome of the simulation. 57 , 58 The topology files for the ligands were automatically generated using the General AMBER Force Field (GAFF) along with AM1BCC charges. In our study, the conformational stability was tested for both the apoprotein and complex systems by analyzing the following parameters: Root Mean Square Deviation (RMSD), Root Mean Square Fluctuation (RMSF), Radius of gyration (Rg), Solvent Accessible Surface Area (SASA), hydrogen bond interactions (H-bond), and MM-PBSA binding free energy. 59

sections.title: Binding site identification and grid box generation
sections.text: 3.1 The VP28 trimer protein was analyzed using the CASTp web server, which discovered a total of 87 distinct surface pockets. Out of these choices, pocket ID 1 was selected as the topmost binding pocket for docking analysis, with a surface area (SA) of 1360.263 Å 2 and a volume (SA) of 845.255 Å 2 , as illustrated in Supplementary file Fig. S1 . The amino acid residues that made up pocket ID 1 were listed in the Supplementary file Table S1 . The selected binding site was utilized to construct a receptor grid box for molecular docking simulations.
path: Binding site identification and grid box generation

sections.title: Virtual screening-based molecular docking
sections.text: 3.2 Pharmaceutical research and development require knowledge of how small-molecule ligands recognize and interact with proteins. Molecular docking is predominantly employed for achieving this goal, as it facilitates analyzing critical molecular processes, including mechanisms of ligand binding and the associated intermolecular interactions that sustain the ligand-receptor complex. 60 Adhering to successful molecular docking between the previously predicted binding region of the VP28 trimer protein and a library of 187 phytochemicals, we determined that the binding affinity varied from −3.1 to −10.2 kcal/mol. The compound CID:8067 demonstrated the lowest binding affinity, with a docking score of −3.1 kcal/mol, while the compound CID:441071 showed the highest binding affinity, achieving a docking score of −10.2 kcal/mol. The compounds were systematically ranked according to their relative binding affinities, which were calculated using PyRx, allowing for the identification of the most promising candidates. The top 30 compounds were selected based on their binding scores, which showed affinities between −8.5 kcal/mol and −10.2 kcal/mol. Considering the fluctuations in molecular docking scores observed in various trials, we performed docking experiments on the top 30 compounds three times. This method enabled the calculation of average scores, enhancing the reliability of our findings before ranking the compounds based on their binding affinity. Table 1 presents the molecular properties of the top 30 compounds, including the name, PubChem identity, molecular weight, source plant, binding affinity, and 2D structures. A compound is anticipated to exhibit activity against a protein if its binding energy is below −6.0 kcal/mol. 61 The binding affinity scores derived from the CB-Dock2 tool provided comparable results regarding binding affinity, as presented in Table 1 , along with the interactive residues and their binding patterns depicted in Supplementary file Fig. S2 . Therefore, the higher binding affinities of these chosen compounds to the target envelope protein VP28 trimer indicate that these may demonstrate enhanced potency in addressing the WSSV infection. However, additional evaluation of these compounds' pharmacokinetic and toxicity profiles is needed to identify the most promising lead candidates.

sections.title: Protein-ligand interactions
sections.text: 3.2.1 The most important factor to consider when crafting a new drug is the configuration of weak or covalent bonds in the protein–ligand complex. The measurement of bonding distance, binding site, and protein–ligand interaction enhanced understanding of how the compound and the protein interact with each other. 62 To enhance comprehension of the intermolecular interactions between chosen compounds and VP28 trimer, we utilized BIOVIA Discovery Studio Visualizer and UCSF Chimera to visualize ligand–protein docked complexes. The molecular interactions of the VP28 trimer with the four most potent compounds, which are epicatechin, kaempferol, luteolin, and apigenin, were presented, with the binding interaction patterns illustrated in both 2D and 3D formats Fig. 4 and Fig. 5 . Our observations revealed that each molecule displayed a variety of non-bonded and bonded interactions with multiple binding site residues or those in the vicinity. Epicatechin formed six conventional hydrogen bond interactions with four residues of the VP28 trimer protein, namely Asn A:154, Ser B:156, Met C:139 (double H-bond), and Ser C:156 (double H-bond). The bond distances ranged from 1.90 to 2.92 Å, and there was additionally one Pi-donor hydrogen bond involving Gln A:138. Similarly, kaempferol demonstrated six conventional hydrogen bond interactions with five residues of the VP28 trimer protein, namely Asn A:154, Ser B:156, Met C:139 (double H-bond), Asn C:154, and Ser C:156. The bond distances range from 1.94 to 2.66 Å. Additionally, there was one carbon-hydrogen bond with Ser C:156 and two Pi-donor hydrogen bonds involving Gln A:138 and Gln C:138. Conversely, apigenin and luteolin contributed to the establishment of five conventional hydrogen bonds. Apigenin interacted with Met A:139, Met C:139, Asn C:154, and Ser C:156 (double H-bond), while luteolin engaged with Met A:139, Ser B:156, Met C:139 (double H-bond), and Ser C:156. Both compounds formed two Pi-donor hydrogen bonds with Gln A:138 and Gln B:138. This study revealed that the four lead molecules, epicatechin, kaempferol, luteolin, and apigenin, had similar interaction patterns with the VP28 trimer, characterized by the formation of conventional hydrogen bonds, van der Waals interactions, and pi-donor hydrogen bonds. The analogous intermolecular interactions observed with the VP28 trimer can be attributed to the identical structural characteristics of these compounds, featuring a flavonoid backbone characterized by a polyphenolic structure that consists of hydroxyl groups on the aromatic rings. The arrangement of the hydroxyl groups shows minor differences in these compounds; however, the interactions and the key residues involved in the binding of these four lead molecules to VP28 remain consistent. The residues, such as Asn154, Ser156, and Met139, reliably established conventional hydrogen bonds with the hydroxyl groups found on the benzene rings (A and B rings) of these compounds throughout all docking scenarios. Gln138 played a pivotal role in the formation of pi-donor hydrogen bonds. However, some specific residues involved in these interactions showed a degree of variability; particularly, apigenin and luteolin interacted with both Met A:139 and Met C:139, while epicatechin and kaempferol interacted specifically with Met C:139. Similarly, Gln B:138 showed specificity for luteolin and apigenin, whereas Gln C:138 was specific to kaempferol. In a nutshell, the lead molecules demonstrated comparable interactions, mainly defined by hydrogen bonding, van der Waals forces, and pi-donor hydrogen bonding, with certain differences in the residues participating in these interactions. The consistent and robust intermolecular interactions, especially the hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic contacts, significantly contribute to the substantial binding energies observed for these lead molecules, indicating their strong affinity for the VP28 trimer. Fig. 6 illustrates the regions involved in hydrogen-bond donation and acceptance during the three-dimensional interactions between the VP28 trimer and the four best-selected compounds. The hydrogen bonds played the most crucial role in defining the strength and specificity of the interaction between the protein and ligand. As shown in Table 2 , the post-dock analysis showed that all of the ligands also had strong hydrophobic interactions with the VP28 trimer. According to Tang X et al., the VP28 trimer has important functions. It may help the trimer anchor to the viral envelope membrane, which lets it interact with the host receptor during the infection cycle. Our analysis of protein–ligand interactions indicates that ligand binding may disrupt trimer formation and hinder viral entry into the host cell.

sections.title: Pharmacokinetic properties
sections.text: 3.3 In the field of drug development, using methods like in silico pharmacokinetic analysis is very important because it helps figure out the chemical and physical properties of compounds, which makes the process more efficient and cost-effective. 63 The pharmacokinetic analyses using SwissADME revealed the pharmacokinetic properties of the top 30 compounds discovered through the virtual screening-based molecular docking analysis, as detailed in the Supplementary file ( Table S2 ). The analysis primarily focused on physiochemical aspects, which include water solubility, lipophilicity, pharmacokinetics, drug-likeness, and medicinal chemistry, to evaluate the pharmacokinetic profiles of the selected ligands. According to the results, 19 out of 30 compounds (63%) met all of Lipinski's requirements. The compounds exhibited a water solubility range of −2.08 to −6.86, demonstrating moderate to high solubility in biological systems. The compounds with values ranging from − 10 to − 6 show poor solubility; those exceeding − 6 but less than − 4 demonstrate moderate solubility; compounds falling between − 4 and − 2 are classified as soluble; and compounds with values from − 2 to 0 are regarded as highly soluble. 64 It is noteworthy that 22/30 compounds (73%) were identified as soluble, suggesting their potential for favorable bioavailability. The findings revealed that 20 out of 30 compounds (67%) demonstrated high gastrointestinal absorption, as shown in the Supplementary file ( Table S2 ). Drug candidates that violate any of the Lipinski rules, exhibit moderate or poor water solubility and demonstrate low gastrointestinal absorption are excluded from the study prior to further toxicity evaluation. Out of the 30 compounds demonstrating notable binding affinities, epicatechin, kaempferol, luteolin, and apigenin emerged as the four drug candidates with the most favorable pharmacokinetic properties. Table 3 presents a concise overview of the pharmacokinetic outcomes. The selected compounds met the Lipinski rule of thumb, which was utilized to assess their drug-like properties. All of the selected compounds had a molecular weight below 500 Daltons, a maximum of 5 hydrogen bond donors, and less than 10 hydrogen bond acceptors. The number of rotatable bonds often increases with molecular weight, reducing bioavailability. Nevertheless, a minimum of one rotatable bond was identified for each compound. In addition, they exhibited an outstanding LogP (Partition Coefficient) value below 5, indicating their highly efficient partitioning between lipids and water, which affects their ability to traverse cell membranes. The water solubility (Log S) values are important in determining the disintegration of compounds in water. This is critical because it influences absorption efficiency within the gastrointestinal system. The findings of this study indicate that all four ligands exhibited high solubility, ranging from −2.22 (epicatechin) to −3.94 (apigenin). Moreover, all the compounds exhibited high gastrointestinal absorption characteristics and adhered to the Ghose, Veber, Egan, and Muegge rules without any violations, which was satisfactory for drug-likeness. The bioavailability score was determined to be 0.55 for each of the four compounds, while the synthetic accessibility varied from 2.96 to 3.50, indicating that these compounds are relatively simple to synthesize and appropriate for drug development. Our thorough pharmacokinetic assessments demonstrated that all four selected compounds are convertible into drugs, making them suitable for subsequent toxicological assessment .

sections.title: Toxicological evaluation
sections.text: 3.4 Ensuring safety is of the utmost importance in the drug development process, which includes the assessment of various toxicities and adverse pharmacological effects in both preclinical and clinical trial stages. 65 Toxicity refers to the extent of damage that a chemical compound may inflict on an organism or its different parts, such as cells and tissues. The four chosen drug candidates were subjected to toxicological assessment using the ProTox 3.0 server, emphasizing parameters including cytotoxicity, hepatotoxicity, carcinogenicity, mutagenicity, and immunotoxicity, with the results presented in Table 4 . The results showed that none of the chosen compounds demonstrated cytotoxicity, immunotoxicity, or hepatotoxicity, indicating that they are unlikely to cause liver toxicity in humans or experimental animals, provoke adverse immunological responses, disrupt normal immune function, or lead to cell death or damage under particular conditions. Furthermore, all of the ligands analyzed, except luteolin, showed no mutagenic or carcinogenic properties, whereas luteolin was predicted to have slight carcinogenicity.

sections.title: Molecular dynamics simulation
sections.text: 3.5 Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were run for 100 ns on the native VP28 trimer (without ligand) and the docked complexes it forms with four top-performing compounds to examine their dynamic behaviors and time-dependent structural stability at the atomic level. The strategy provides an intricate illustration of their movement, offering important insights for applications in drug discovery, comprehension of physiological processes, and capturing structure–function relationships. 66 In this study, MD simulation, valuable for post-dock analysis, was used to check the conformational integrity and rigidity of the docking conformation to ascertain whether the ligands were maintained at the VP28′s binding site. It was revealed that all selected ligands appeared to consistently remain within the protein's binding pocket throughout the simulation. This suggests a high probability of stable complexes being retained in a physiological setting. Consequently, the aforementioned time-frame-based inquiry facilitated the discovery of effective inhibitory compounds. The present study implemented several assessment metrics extracted from MD trajectory data, including root mean square deviation (RMSD), root mean square fluctuation (RMSF), radius of gyration (Rg), solvent accessible surface area (SASA), and hydrogen bonding counts. The metrics covered pertain to both the VP28 trimer and the optimal docked ligand complexes, and the contrast of the early and final structural behavior of the complexes is plotted in Fig. 7 and Fig. 8 .

sections.title: Structural stability and compactness assessment through RMSD analysis
sections.text: 3.5.1 In this study, we performed a quantitative assessment of structural changes, stability, and dynamics in biomolecular systems through root mean square deviation (RMSD) analysis. RMSD is considered one of the most useful metrics for evaluating the stability and integrity of a protein's structure. Upon the binding of a ligand to the binding site, structural changes may occur that influence the protein's conformational stability. The analysis of molecular dynamics trajectories, along with the evaluation of RMSD plots, provides a valuable initial assessment of the stability of the simulated protein–ligand complexes, as noted earlier. Maintaining stability in a simulated system typically requires RMSD fluctuations to remain within an acceptable range of 1 to 3 Å. The consistent RMSD value with minimal fluctuation serves as an accurate confirmation of a converged system. 67 However, when significant variations beyond the previously mentioned magnitude occur, it suggests that the protein may undergo a structural shift. In this study, the RMSD values of carbon alpha atoms in apo-protein were utilized as a reference frame for the RMSD calculations. Fig. 7 (A) illustrates how RMSD values change over time for the C-alpha atoms in the ligand-bound and reference proteins. The RMSD trajectory for the apo-protein (blue) manifested a slight shift during the initial 20 ns of the simulation, with RMSD values spanning between 1.32 and 2.1 Å. An upward trend was noted at 21 ns, with RMSD values reaching a peak of 3.1 Å at 31 ns, followed by a sharp drop to 2.1 Å at 33 ns, which retained within the acceptable range. Subsequently, additional upsurges were recorded, peaking at 3.64 Å at 45 ns and progressively culminating in the maximum deviation for the apo-protein at 67 ns, where the RMSD value reached 4.65 Å. Immediately after this maximum peak, the C-alpha backbone RMSD exhibited a trend towards stability, as indicated by its gradual decline throughout the remaining phase of the simulation, indicating a converged system. The apo-protein exhibited a mean RMSD value of 2.99 Å during the simulation period. Therefore, while there were slight variations, they did not significantly impact overall stability or cause notable structural changes. Throughout the simulation, the RMSD profile of the VP28 trimer-epicatechin complex (orange) showed a mean RMSD value of 1.95 Å. Minor fluctuations were noted, with a peak deviation recorded at 62 ns, reaching an RMSD value of 2.68 Å, and subsequently attaining a stable state thereafter, suggesting that the ligand helps stabilize the protein structure through interactions with favorable residues. Similarly, the RMSD descriptor for the VP28 trimer-kaempferol complex (green) showed an average RMSD value of 2 Å, demonstrating an initial upward trend with minor fluctuations, ultimately culminating in a peak RMSD value of 2.5 Å at 50 ns, after which it stabilized for the rest of the simulation time-frame. The VP28 trimer-apigenin complex displayed the highest RMSD of 2.93 Å, the lowest of 1.2 Å, and an average RMSD of 1.94 Å. At around 10 ns, the RMSD value reached a steady level of 2.47 Å, maintaining this state until 52 ns, with only minor fluctuations. A significant drop was noticed at 55 ns, with the RMSD falling to 1.4 Å, before gradually rising again to attain a peak RMSD of 2.93 Å at 98 ns. Throughout the simulation, the RMSD value consistently remained within the acceptable range. In a similar manner to the VP28 trimer-epicatechin, VP28 trimer-kaempferol complex, and VP28 trimer-apigenin complex, the VP28 trimer-luteolin complex (cyan) exhibited an initial rise, attaining an RMSD value of 2.6 Å at 29 ns and sustaining a stable condition with irregular oscillations until 80 ns. The highest peak observed was 2.87 Å at 80 ns, subsequently followed by a gradual decrease. The average RMSD value observed was 2.21 Å. The RMSD analysis results revealed a significant observation: the complexes' RMSD descriptors consistently stayed below 3 Å, demonstrating lower RMSD values than apo-protein. This suggests that the proteins maintained their structural integrity, indicating that even with minor variations between complexes upon ligand binding, there were no large deviations or structural alterations in the protein structure.
path: Structural stability and compactness assessment through RMSD analysis

sections.title: RMSF analysis
sections.text: 3.5.2 The root mean square fluctuation (RMSF) is a valuable metric for determining local alterations in protein chain residues and ligand atom dynamics in reaction to specific temperature and pressure conditions. Furthermore, the RMSF plays an essential part in evaluating the flexibility of individual atoms, providing important insights into how ligand binding influences the overall flexibility of the protein. The low RMSF values of the amino acid residues indicate that the complex has achieved enhanced stability, whereas higher values imply a reduction in stability. 68 As a result, the RMSF values for the chosen natural compounds epicatechin (orange), kaempferol (yellow), apigenin (green), and luteolin (cyan), alongside the VP28 trimer protein, were assessed. Fig. 7 (B) displays the peaks associated with the regions of the amino acid residues that show the greatest fluctuations during the 100 ns simulations. The variation noted in the complex systems' initial amino acid residues exceeded that of any other protein region, which can be assigned to the arrangement of the N and C-terminal domains. The terminal RMSF values are anticipated to be relatively higher than those of the in-between region due to the greater fluctuations observed at terminal sites. The trimeric structure of the apo-protein exhibited a considerably higher RMSF value in the N-terminal region across all three chains, indicating increased flexibility in this region. Tang X et al. reported that, alongside various hydrophobic interactions, there exist ten hydrogen bonding contacts among the trimer monomers. 19 Notably, there are no covalent bonds among the monomers that make up the trimer, which can be associated with the significant fluctuations observed in the N-terminal. Nonetheless, no amino acid residue exceeded the RMSF threshold of 2 Å, except for the N-terminal amino acids, and the mean RMSF value was 1.49 Å, suggesting that the variations were minimal throughout the simulation. Afterwards, the reference apo structure was analyzed in comparison with the structures of epicatechin, kaempferol, apigenin, and luteolin when complexed with the protein. Interestingly, a relatively lower fluctuation at the N-terminal was observed for each complex, indicating that ligand binding significantly contributed to stabilization of the protein across all complexes. The VP28 trimer exhibited minimal fluctuations during the simulation with the compounds epicatechin, kaempferol, apigenin, and luteolin, as nearly all amino acids had RMSF values below 3 Å except for the N-terminal regions and Val_112 of the A chain, which had an RMSF value of 3.11 Å. The mean RMSF values for epicatechin, kaempferol, apigenin, and luteolin in complex with apo-protein were 1.20 Å, 1.23 Å, 1.29 Å, and 1.23 Å, respectively. The stability observed in this region can be attributed to the presence of secondary structure elements, including alpha helices and beta strands, which usually show more rigidity in comparison with unstructured loop regions of the protein. In our in-depth study of RMSF, the N-terminal residues showed the highest peaks for all complexes that were not connected to ligand binding. The remaining residues, including those at the binding site, consistently fell within an acceptable range. This suggests that the overall interaction is not decisively unfavorable, highlighting the necessity to consider additional parameters.

sections.title: Radius of gyration (Rg) analysis
sections.text: 3.5.3 The radius of gyration (Rg) is an essential parameter for understanding the stable, compact, and folded structure of a protein. An increase in Rg value enhances the likelihood of forming a flexible ligand, consequently rendering it unstable. Conversely, lower Rg values suggest a dense and tightly packed conformation. 69 The local conformational stability of the systems was assessed by calculating the radius of gyration (Rg) of the backbone atoms of both free and bound VP28 proteins. Fig. 8 (A) illustrates that each of the top four complexes maintained a consistent Rg profile over the trajectory, showing minimal deviation. The minor fluctuations in the Rg value for all complexes align with the stable characteristics of the docked complexes. Comparable stability was observed in both the apo-protein form and the protein–ligand complex form. The VP28 trimer's mean Rg value was found to be 22.77 Å. In comparison, the mean Rg values for epicatechin, kaempferol, apigenin, and luteolin in complex with the VP28 trimer were 22.83 Å, 22.80 Å, 22.72 Å, and 22.92 Å, respectively. This signifies that no structural switching was detected in the VP28 trimer in the presence of the top four compounds, and it attained a stable Rg equilibrium, suggesting the complex's stability throughout the simulation trajectory.

sections.title: SASA analysis
sections.text: 3.5.4 The solvent-accessible surface area (SASA) value of all simulated complexes was measured. A higher SASA profile reflects an increase in protein surface area, whereas a lower SASA profile indicates a decrease in surface area. The mean SASA values for the five systems (apo-protein, epicatechin, kaempferol, apigenin, luteolin) were 20503.73, 20583.25164, 20501.03019, 20645.09262, and 20650.69371 Å 2 , respectively. Throughout the MD simulation, it was observed that luteolin had a high surface area, whereas kaempferol had a low surface area. Fig. 8 (B) illustrates that all complexes displayed a trend akin to the apo form, with only minor fluctuations noted except epicatechin, which had a downward peak in the first 50 ns, followed by an upward peak in the last 50 ns within the SASA profile. Despite this, during the 100 ns simulation, the SASA value did not show a significant increase for any of the complexes. These findings indicate that all complexes exhibited similar levels of solvent accessibility, suggesting comparable flexibility, exposure to functional sites, or potential for interactions. The observed consistency in SASA values indicates that the ligand-binding regions in all complexes likely offer comparable roles or functions.

sections.title: Hydrogen bonds analysis
sections.text: 3.5.5 The analysis of hydrogen bonds is critical in MD simulation studies because of their critical role in influencing the structure, dynamics, and interactions of biomolecules. To gain insight into the hydrogen bonds and their contribution to the stability of the five systems, we conducted a quantitative assessment of the hydrogen bonds. The results indicate that the hydrogen bond patterns for all complexes showed an increasing trend up to 25 ns, as shown in Fig. 8 (C). This finding suggests that in the early stages of the simulation, hydrogen bonds were being formed, which may indicate structural changes or interactions among the components. Subsequently, stable hydrogen bond profiles were consistently maintained, showing remarkable similarity throughout the entire 100 ns simulation time-frame. The mean hydrogen bonds found in five different systems were 383 for apo-protein, 386 for epicatechin, 391 for kaempferol, and 390 for luteolin. When ligands were bound to proteins, the number of hydrogen bonds increased slightly.

sections.title: MM-PBSA binding energy calculation
sections.text: 3.5.6 The MM-PBSA binding energy allows for a quantitative evaluation of the overall energy variation that takes place during the protein–ligand complex formation, in contrast to the separate unbound protein. In this study, we employed Molecular Mechanics/Poisson-Boltzmann Surface Area (MM-PBSA) calculations to examine the binding free energy related to protein–ligand interactions. During the 100 ns simulation time, the binding free energies were calculated using the MM-PBSA method for each complex, as shown in Fig. 8 (D). The findings of our investigation indicated that the average MM-PBSA binding energies for the four complexes—VP28-epicatechin, VP28-kaempferol, VP28-apigenin, and VP28-luteolin—were determined to be − 321.76, −249.37, −86.84, and − 206.44 kJ/mol, respectively. The MM-PBSA binding energy profiles for the four complexes showed distinct patterns of stability. Interestingly, even with the differences in profiles, the binding free energies of the complexes showed remarkable consistency over time. The findings show that the VP28-apigenin complex had a weaker binding interaction compared to the other complexes. On the other hand, the VP28-epicatechin complex had the strongest binding interaction, as shown by the fact that its MM-PBSA binding energy was significantly lower. In conclusion, through a comprehensive approach involving molecular docking, pharmacokinetic and toxicity assessments, molecular dynamics simulations, and MM-PBSA calculations, this study identified epicatechin, kaempferol, apigenin, and luteolin as promising compounds with the potential to inhibit WSSV by targeting VP28.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.text: 4 The WSSV represents a significant challenge to the shrimp industry and human food security, as there are currently no effective antiviral treatments available to address the virus. In the past three decades, an alarming incidence of mass shrimp mortality has been observed in aquaculture systems. The entire population was eradicated within a few days, leading to substantial economic losses on a global scale. Therefore, this computational method has been employed to discover some natural and effective antiviral candidates designed to inhibit WSSV attachment to the host and maintain non-infectivity in shrimps. The compounds epicatechin, kaempferol, luteolin, and apigenin were discovered as promising drug candidates derived from the plants A. indica and B. monnieri using integrative in-silico methods encompassing virtual screening, molecular docking, pharmacokinetic analysis, and MD simulations. The uncovered antiviral compounds demonstrate promise in mitigating the economic losses experienced by the shrimp industry because of WSSV. This computational study will provide significant insights into VP28 associated with WSSV, as well as improve the treatment of fish viruses in an obvious and significant manner. We suggest additional in vivo and in vitro investigations are crucial for assessing the practical efficacy of these phytochemicals in combating WSSV.

AI-based Modeling & Design.title: Disrupting SARS-CoV-2 Spike Protein Activity: A Virtual Screening and Binding Assay Study
AI-based Modeling & Design.abstract: Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) is a respiratory virus that emerged in late 2019 and rapidly spread worldwide, causing the COVID-19 pandemic. The spike glycoprotein (S protein) plays a crucial role in viral target recognition and entry by interacting with angiotensin, converting enzyme 2 (ACE2), the functional receptor for the virus, via its receptor binding domain (RBD). The RBD availability for this interaction can be influenced by external factors, such as fatty acids. Linoleic acid (LA), a free fatty acid, has been shown to bind the S protein, modulating the viral infection by reducing initial target recognition. LA interacts with the fatty acid binding pocket (FABP), a potential drug target against SARS-CoV-2. In this study, we aimed to exploit the FABP as a drug target by performing a docking-based virtual screening with a library of commercially available, drug-like compounds. The virtual hits identified were then assessed in in vitro assays for the inhibition of the virus–host interaction and cytotoxicity. Binding assays targeting the spike–ACE2 interaction identified multiple compounds with inhibitory activity and low cytotoxicity.
